A CA minted before the strict-clean change parses but carries no Subject Key Identifier; the leaf remint that a host change triggers read the missing extension and exited, and Restart=always looped the daemon forever (observed live on a long-lived state disk after #146 changed the bind host). Such a CA is now replaced wholesale — a stderr line names the replacement beside the new fingerprint — instead of crash-looping. Current strict-clean pairs keep leaf-only remints (same CA fingerprint).
  • Strict-clean minted TLS certificates (#141). The CA and leaf msksd generates now carry Subject/Authority Key Identifiers and the CA a keyCertSign KeyUsage, so Python 3.14 clients — whose default SSL context enables VERIFY_X509_STRICT — verify the pair instead of rejecting it. Existing state directories keep their current pair; removing the msks-ca*.pem/msks-cert*.pem files under the state dir lets the next start mint the strict-clean replacement.
  • Mid-session console stalls no longer wedge a session open (#103). The guest console helper's byte pump blocked on whichever direction stalled first, so a wedged vsock transport froze the whole session — input echoed but never executed, no output, no close. The pump now moves each direction independently and a stream that accepts no writes for 300 s ends the session; on the daemon side, console_stall_timeout_s (MSKSD_CONSOLE_STALL_TIMEOUT_S, 60 s default, 0 disables) closes a console websocket with 4502 when client input draws no guest bytes for the window — msks shell names the close, and reconnecting opens a fresh session. The echo-off caveat (password prompts) and the helper-window relationship are documented in docs/cli.md and docs/config.md.

  • Egress DHCP/DNS under uvloop-running daemons (#144). The development venv pulls uvloop (via uvicorn[standard]), which does not implement loop.sock_recvfrom/sock_sendto; egress workspaces created by such a daemon never received a DHCP lease or DNS answer. The DHCP and DNS services now receive datagrams through a loop-portable helper and behave identically under asyncio and uvloop. This was also the real cause behind the "guest NIC up but no frames" symptom recorded on #143 — not the container boundary.

  • /home could fail to mount on slow boots (#14). The guest fstab mounted the home volume by label under x-systemd.device-timeout=2s; that clock starts at sysinit job enqueue, before udevd runs, and on a first boot from a fresh overlay (every root read a copy-on-write miss) the udev label probe can exceed what is left of the budget — home.mount then fails for the whole boot (nofail keeps the boot moving and never retries). The device timeout is now 30s, so the mount rides out a slow coldplug; a boot with no volume at all waits the same 30s once and continues.

  • Egress workspaces never took a DHCP lease on fast hosts (#36). The guest reaches multi-user immediately after sysinit, and a networkd that enumerates its NIC while udev is still renaming it (eth0 to ens3) never manages the renamed link — DHCP never runs. The guest image orders networkd after systemd-udev-trigger.service and systemd-udevd.service, so the interface name is final before the first enumeration.

  • ws_url quotes the token and workspace id (#36). The console URL interpolates MSKSC_TOKEN raw into the query string; minted tokens are urlsafe today, so this was theoretical, but any future charset with +, &, =, or % would have mangled it. The token now passes through urllib.parse.quote_plus (a query value), and the workspace id through urllib.parse.quote with no safe characters (a path segment, where + would reach the server literally).

  • Workspace cleanup and image import release their resources (#56). cleanup now stops the workspace's VMM before deleting its directory — tracked or pidfile, like kill — where it previously orphaned the process. Image import closes the container-image archive after unpacking; each import previously left the archive's file handle open until garbage collection.

  • Workspace shell input now echoes (#61). The vsock console's guest pty ran with echo=0,icanon=0 while the client keeps the local tty raw, and the service environment's TERM=dumb left bash's readline off — so typed characters reached nothing that would show them. The pty is now a plain canonical terminal (echo=1,icanon=1) and the unit sets TERM=xterm: line editing and history work, and programs reading stdin directly get normal tty echo. The console ships in the workspace image; a workspace keeps the image it was created with, so delete existing workspaces and the old image from the catalog — new workspaces then bind the new image.
  • devenv shell no longer runs the pre-commit suite at shell entry (#32). A devenv 2.3.x scheduler regression pulled devenv:git-hooks:run into the shell's task graph, so a failing hook (e.g. the xenon complexity gate) aborted shell entry before it opened — with no way to use the shell to fix the failure. The suite still runs on git commit and as the msks-xenon task.

items.title: The CLI client
items.text:
Along with invoking the TUI, the msks command is a client for the daemon's /api/v1 REST surface.

Here's an overview of the common command set:

msks                         # the workspace tree TUI
msks ls                      # what exists, and what state is it in
msks create ws                # make a workspace
msks clone ws fork            # copy a workspace into a new one
msks console ws               # boot it if needed, then work inside it
msks forward ws 22            # bridge a guest TCP port to stdio
msks key ws                   # fetch the workspace's ssh identity
msks ssh ws                   # log in over the forward (boots it if needed)
msks rsync ws -- -av ./src/ root@:/src/  # copy files over the forward
msks home export ws           # download its /home volume (backup, seed)
msks start ws                 # boot it without attaching
msks stop ws                  # power it off
msks rm ws                    # delete it (and its data)

The client and the daemon ship in the same Python distribution, but they might be run from different installation directories, so daemon and client versions may not be in sync, which may cause problems. To cope with this, every command makes one best-effort /health roundtrip by the client to the daemon to do a version compatibility check. If the daemon is a different version than the client, the invocation prints one stderr line giving both and a remedy. This is most usually encountered on MacOS, because the daemon runs in a Lima VM separate from the client. If you see this on MacOS, rerun msks-setup-macos-host on the Mac to update the daemon in the Lima VM.

items.title: Client environment
items.text:
The client reads environment variables prefixed MSKSC_ (client) to stay apart from the daemon's MSKSD_* (server) namespace. Each of the environment variables has a config-file equivalent.

Variable Config file key Meaning Default MSKSC_URL url The remote daemon's base URL, the TCP + TLS + token shape; the client dials TCP only when a URL gives one unset (the local socket answers, else the client refuses) MSKSC_SOCKET socket The local listener's socket path: peer-credential authentication, with no token and no TLS unset (the default socket is looked for) MSKSC_TOKEN token_file A daemon bearer token (see tokens below); a socket connection needs none — (required for a URL) MSKSC_CAFILE cafile A PEM file to verify the daemon's TLS certificate; a socket connection verifies nothing (the kernel vouches for both ends) unverified with warning MSKSC_EXPECTED_IMAGE expected_image An image reference the operator sets; msks ls compares it with the image the daemon reports in /health and reports drift unset (no check) MSKSC_CACHE_DIR cache_dir The directory the per-workspace host-key caches live under; the per-workspace directories are created below it ~/.cache/msks MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE identity_file Your own private key file, the ssh identity msks create plants into every workspace (msks generates none; the identity section owns the whole story); a leading ~ expands unset (pubkey_file answers, else msks create refuses) MSKSC_PUBKEY_FILE pubkey_file Your key's public half, what a bare msks create plants instead of reading identity_file. The form for a key you keep encrypted (your agent holds it; msks reads no private half); same naming rule, global-only unset (identity_file answers) MSKSC_TERMINAL_TITLE terminal_title The title template for the workspace-shell windows the workspace page opens (the file key's section lives in The TUI); {workspace} resolves to the workspace's id unset (the terminal's own title) MSKSC_IMAGE_MANIFEST_URL image_manifest_url Where the TUI's Import image action (i on the workspace list) reads the published channel's manifest (a fork's or self-hoster's channel gives its own); the picker shows each row's ref, description, and size, and the pick POSTs the row's URL to the daemon's import endpoint this repository's latest release's images.json

MSKSC_CACHE_DIR exists because the host-key cache is disposable: a swept cache costs one trust-on-first-use re-pin. Pointing it at a per-project, disposable location is the intended use.

Each directory-valued setting takes an absolute path (a relative value is refused with a line giving the fix; a leading ~ expands; an empty value counts as unset). The per-workspace directories are created below it.

MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE points at a file, not a directory: your own private key, read in place. msks derives the public half from it at create. msks ssh and msks rsync sign through your own ssh-agent when it holds that key (ssh-add it). The match is on the key material, so the file it came from and its name do not matter. Otherwise they stage the private half in memory. The key file itself is never copied into msks's state.

A key msks stages itself is an unencrypted OpenSSH-format key (ed25519, ecdsa P-256/P-384/P-521, or rsa). An encrypted key no agent holds is refused with a line giving the fixes in order: ssh-add the key, decrypt a copy, or pass --pubkey at create.

MSKSC_PUBKEY_FILE points at your key's public half, a .pub file (the identity section owns the agent requirement this form carries). A create with it set plants that one line as the identity and reads no private material at all. It is the form for a key you keep encrypted: the public half is in a .pub file while the private half answers from your agent.

A missing MSKSC_TOKEN is an error before any network activity (the client gives the variable and exits), unless the daemon is reached through the local socket, where the kernel vouches for the client and no token exists to read.

An unconfigured client (no MSKSC_URL, no MSKSC_SOCKET, no config-file daemon) looks for the default socket a same-host daemon binds ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/msks/msksd.sock) and connects through it with peer credentials alone. Finding none, it exits with the paths it looked for and the two settings that pick a daemon outright. The client never dials a TCP address implicitly: a well-known port could belong to any daemon.

The daemon serves TLS with a self-signed certificate. Point MSKSC_CAFILE at the daemon's CA (msks-ca.pem under its state directory) and the client verifies the certificate chain. A cafile that is missing or holds no parsable certificate is a one-line refusal giving the daemon's CA file.

items.title: The client config file
items.text:
The environment variables above have a durable home: a YAML file at ~/.config/msks/msks.yaml (relocated by MSKSC_CONFIG_DIR, or XDG_CONFIG_HOME). The variables keep working beside it, and each one overrides the same key in the file. A fresh devenv shell with its presets exported behaves exactly as it does today. Precedence, highest first:

--daemon flag > MSKSC_* environment > the file's daemon aliases >
    the file's global keys > built-in defaults

A bare msks reads the default path and, on the first run, generates a commented near-empty template there (the directory 0700, the file 0600). --config <path> reads exactly that file: a missing one is an error, and an explicit path is never generated. --config=none reads the environment and the built-in defaults only.

Every scalar key is its MSKSC_* variable with the prefix stripped and lowercased (MSKSC_URL → url, MSKSC_EXPECTED_IMAGE → expected_image), with the same semantics as the variable. A leading ~ expands, and a key set to nothing (key: with no value, or "") is the unset form. Hyphens and underscores spell the same key: token-file and token_file are one key (klangk's file spelled kebab; msks's variables spell snake). A file that carries both spellings of one key is refused, the second treated as a duplicate.

token_file is the one key whose variable carries a different shape: the file points at a file holding one daemon token. The config tree therefore stays free of inline credentials, and the token keeps the permissions of the file that holds it. MSKSC_TOKEN still carries an inline token when the environment is the more convenient place for one. For the invocation, the token is read out of its file into the process environment, the substrate every reader already speaks, where child processes (console shells, the terminal launcher) inherit it. The file itself stays the durable, permissioned home. An unreadable or empty token file is an error before any network activity, giving both places a token can come from.

identity_file follows the token_file pattern for a different secret: it gives your private key file by path, read in place and never copied (see the create default below). It is global-only, and a daemons: entry that carries it is refused, because an ssh identity belongs to you, not to one daemon connection.

Unknown keys and duplicate keys are refused at load, each error giving the key and the valid ones, the same fail-fast rules msksd's config file carries.

items.title: Daemon aliases
items.text:
daemons: specifies one entry per daemon you talk to. An entry picks its daemon one way: url for a remote daemon, or socket for a local listener (peer-credential authentication; the entry carries no token_file and no cafile). The keys token_file, cafile, and expected_image override their globals for that alias:

url: https://127.0.0.1:8660
token_file: ~/.config/msks/dev.token
daemons:
  lab:
    url: https://hv-1.lab.example.com:8660
    token_file: ~/.config/msks/lab.token
    cafile: ~/.config/msks/lab-ca.pem
    expected_image: msks/debian13:1.1
  local:
    socket: /run/user/1000/msks/msksd.sock

active_daemon: lab

active_daemon gives the alias a bare msks addresses. The --daemon <alias-or-url-or-path> flag picks one for a single invocation and also takes a raw URL or an absolute socket path. The two selections sit at different layers of the precedence rule. A --daemon alias outranks the environment for that invocation, because you picked the daemon and its entry's keys win over the ambient exports. An active_daemon alias sits below the environment: the devenv presets keep winning. A worktree shell still talks to its own dev daemon beside a user config file that picks another.

items.title: ssh_options
items.text:
ssh_options remembers ssh options for every ssh session msks runs: msks ssh, the workspace page's shell action (it runs msks ssh; The TUI documents the action), and msks rsync's ssh transport. The value is the ssh options you would type after -- on the msks ssh command line, the options themselves. A -- token in the value is refused: msks adds the options to its own, and a remembered separator would turn msks's transport into the remote command:

ssh_options: -A -o ServerAliveInterval=30   # string form (shell-split)
ssh_options:                                # list form (tokens stay whole)
  - -A
  - -o
  - ServerAliveInterval=30

ssh_options's environment form (MSKSC_SSH_OPTIONS) overrides the file value with the string form.

The remembered options sit behind the command line's own, so an option you pass for one invocation wins over the remembered one. msks's own transport settings (the forward as ProxyCommand, the per-workspace known_hosts, the identity) stay defaults beneath both, the same first-obtained precedence stock ssh applies.

Agent forwarding gets the one extra rule the ordering alone cannot give. When the command line carries any forwarding setting (-A, -a, or a ForwardAgent value), the remembered forwarding options are dropped for that invocation and the command line decides alone. Otherwise a remembered -A would reassign a typed -a, because ssh's flags assign in order. A remembered -A forwards your agent, the one SSH_AUTH_SOCK gives, exactly as a typed one does: the guest receives your keys, not the workspace identity.

The remembered options carry the command-line passthrough's full power, including the ability to override msks's transport for every session (a remembered ProxyCommand=, UserKnownHostsFile=, or IdentityAgent= re-routes or re-keys every ssh msks runs). The command-line passthrough has the same power per invocation; the remembered form persists it, so the key is the one to check first when a remembered option breaks the seam.

msks console is a websocket session, not ssh, so ssh_options applies to the ssh surfaces above and leaves it untouched.

items.title: Workspace identity
items.text:
A workspace carries two identity fields. The name is the label you choose at create, the positional argument of every command, unique among the daemon's workspaces. The id is minted by the daemon at create: 10 hex digits (5 random bytes, re-rolled until it collides with nothing on this daemon), immutable, and never reused while its workspace lives.

Every host-side surface keys on the id: the artifact directories under the state dir, the catalog row, and the client-side caches. Deleting a workspace and creating another under the same name yields a different id, with nothing of the first instance left to collide. The second workspace's msks ssh works on the first try, with a fresh host-key cache of its own.

Every command that takes a workspace accepts either reference: msks console ws and msks console 1a2b3c4d5e reach the same workspace. The name is the everyday reference. The id is the reference no other workspace shares.

items.title: msks ls
items.text:
Prints one line per workspace the daemon knows, aligned in seven columns: name, id, status, egress mode, created date, image (catalog reference, or the digest when the catalog cannot resolve one),

$ msks ls
name          id          status                    egress       created     image             host
my-workspace  1a2b3c4d5e  running                   interactive  2026-05-14  debian:13.6       hv-1
scratch       77eedd0199  created                   allow        2026-06-01  -                 hv-1
refs-reader   9c1d2e3f4a  running, 1 mount skipped  allow        2026-06-18  9f2c41a…de1234ab  hv-1

The status column speaks the daemon's lifecycle vocabulary: created (row exists, never booted), starting, running, paused, stopped, unknown, absent. A workspace whose mounts skip carries the count beside its status (running, 1 mount skipped above), a standing marker that lasts until the config and the row agree again; the mounts chapter lists every kind of skip and its reason.

A digest the catalog cannot resolve to a reference reads as its middle-clipped form (the image column's own budget). A - in the name column is a workspace without a label (created nameless through the API, or before the id/name split), addressed by its id alone. A - in the image column means the workspace boots explicit kernel/rootfs paths instead of a catalog image.

--json replaces the table with one JSON document, the API's workspace rows verbatim: id, name, kernel, initrd, rootfs, cmdline, cpus, mem_mib, image_hash, image_ref, host, root_mib, home_mib, egress, egress_slice, egress_mode, secret_coverage, egress_allowlist, mounts, user_data, ssh_pubkey, login_user, status, created_at, and mount_issues (the derived per-mount state behind the status marker):

msks ls --json | jq -r '.[] | select(.status == "running") | .name'

A daemon with zero workspaces prints nothing (an empty table) and an empty JSON array under --json.

items.title: msks storage
items.text:
Reports the state-disk budget and its consumers: the budget line, each workspace's cost beside its ceiling, and each catalog image's cost:

$ msks storage
state disk    used 23.4G of 40G    free 16.6G    pressure ok

┏━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━┓
┃ workspace ┃ root cost/ceiling ┃ home cost/ceiling ┃ cost ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━┩
│ ws4       │ 3.1G / 10G        │ 812M / 2G         │ 3.9G │
│ scratch   │ 61M / 10G         │ 12M / 2G          │ 73M  │
└───────────┴───────────────────┴───────────────────┴──────┘

┏━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━┓
┃ image     ┃ imported         ┃ cost ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━┩
│ debian:13 │ 2026-09-21 12:03 │ 3G   │
│ debian:13 │ 2026-08-02 05:11 │ 3G   │
└───────────┴───────────────────┴──────┘
  • cost is the disk blocks the artifact occupies on the state disk. An idle artifact costs its content, not its ceiling (the files are sparse), and an overlay's cost runs a little above what the guest's own df shows for its root (qcow2 bookkeeping).
  • imported is when the image archive came in, local time to the minute; entries that share a reference (a rebuilt image imported again) read as distinct through it, and the listing orders them oldest-first.
  • ceiling is the size fixed at create; the guest sees it as its quota and its user can watch it fill with df inside the workspace.
  • pressure gives the state-disk condition: warn at or past MSKSD_STORAGE_WARN_PCT (default 90) percent used, critical below MSKSD_STORAGE_FLOOR_MIB (default 512) free. Below the floor, workspace creates, image imports, and home-volume imports answer a named 507 until space comes back. msks storage gives the consumers; msks rm and msks image rm remove them. The message's other escape is lowering the floor; raising it refuses more, not fewer.

msks storage <workspace> narrows the workspace table to one workspace, by name or id. --json prints the API's GET /api/v1/storage document verbatim.

items.title: msks create
items.text:
POSTs the API's create body. The positional argument gives the workspace's name and follows the daemon's workspace charset: lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, starting with a letter or digit, up to 64 chars. The daemon mints the workspace's immutable id; the name is the label the other commands address it by. The create request's field is name (an id field is accepted as the same thing, the earlier spelling).

Flags map onto the create request's fields (the identity flags below generate theirs):

Flag API field Meaning --image image Catalog ref: name:version, bare name, or hash --kernel kernel Explicit kernel path (skips the catalog) --initrd initrd Explicit initrd path --rootfs rootfs Explicit rootfs path (skips the catalog) --cmdline cmdline Explicit kernel cmdline --cpus cpus vcpus, 1–64 (daemon default: 2) --mem-mib mem_mib Guest memory MiB, 64–32768 (daemon default: 8192) --root-mib root_mib Persistent root overlay size (daemon default) --home-mib home_mib Persistent /home volume size (daemon default) --user-data user_data First-boot provisioning payload file; - reads stdin --pubkey ssh_pubkey (verbatim) Use a public key you already own as this one workspace's identity; - reads stdin --user user The workspace's login user; default: your username --share mounts A host directory mounted into the guest: HOST_PATH:GUEST_PATH:MODE, repeatable

Only the flags you pass are sent. Unset flags let the daemon apply its own defaults. An --image reference resolves against the daemon's image catalog (docs/images.md); explicit --kernel and --rootfs bypass it. Size ranges are enforced server-side; a value outside them comes back as a validation error (below).

--share gives a host directory, the absolute guest path it lands at, and a mode (ro or rw, defaulting to rw when the mode is omitted):

msks create ws1 --share /srv/projects:/mnt/projects --share /srv/refs:/srv/refs:ro

The host path must sit under one of the daemon's allowed roots (mount_host_roots, configuration), resolved against symlink escapes. The mounts apply at the workspace's next start. A --start create attaches them on its first boot. The mounts chapter holds the behavior: the two gates, the mode bound, and the coherence between guests sharing one tree. msks mount and msks umount change the set later.

--user NAME records the workspace's login user, and the name is carried on the row. The guest's first boot seeds the account: useradd -m; a home on the persistent /home volume, populated from /etc/skel; the workspace identity in its authorized_keys; and the same passwordless-sudo grant the image's own workspace user carries. msks ssh, msks rsync, and msks console then use the recorded name as their default login. A workspace therefore answers the same identity for every operator that reaches it.

Without --user the create fills the invoking user's name: a bare create lands your own account. The name must fit the login-name charset (lowercase letters, digits, dashes, underscores; a lowercase letter or underscore first; at most 32 characters). A username that does not (a capitalized one) is refused with a line pointing at --user.

Naming root or the image's msks account keeps the shipped account and seeds nothing new. A name that lands on a system account the image already ships (Debian carries charset-valid names like sync and man) seeds nothing either. The first boot says so in its log, and the login stays with the accounts the guest already serves. Pick a name the image uses for no one.

The name is create-time and immutable, like user_data: a workspace created before records no user of its own. msks ssh and msks rsync dial it as root, and the image's msks account stays reachable by giving it directly.

--start boots the workspace right after creating it:

$ msks create my-workspace --image debian:13 --start
created my-workspace (id 9f2c41ab77)
attach with: msks console my-workspace

The confirmation line prints both halves of the workspace's identity, the label you chose and the id the daemon minted, as soon as the create succeeds and before the boot is attempted. A failed boot still leaves the workspace created; the error message says so. The recovery command:

created my-workspace (id 9f2c41ab77)
msks: 503: vmm launch failed
msks: 9f2c41ab77 is created; boot it later with: msks start my-workspace

Creating without --start prints the same line and exits; boot it whenever with msks start, or just msks console it: the console command boots a not-running workspace on its own (below).

--user-data is the first-boot provisioning hook: the file's contents travel to the daemon and run once on the workspace's first boot (see docs/images.md for the seed-disk mechanism, the payload forms each image provisioner accepts, and the create-time immutability). It composes with --start:

$ printf '#!/bin/sh\napt-get update\n' | msks create ws --user-data - --start
created ws (id 77eedd0199)
attach with: msks console ws

One operator key is the identity: msks create plants it as every workspace's identity, one key across workspaces, the daemon holding the public half only. The key is yours and msks generates nothing: identity_file (or MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE) gives your private key file (the config file or the environment), and a create with neither that nor --pubkey refuses with a one-line error giving both.

msks does not scan ~/.ssh and never guesses which of your keys to take. The create sends the key's derived public half only and writes nothing per-workspace. Your private key file stays where it lives, read in place and copied nowhere. The confirmation gives the identity it used:

$ msks create my-workspace --image debian:13 --start
created my-workspace (id 9f2c41ab77)
identity: /home/you/.ssh/id_ed25519
attach with: msks console my-workspace

msks ssh and msks rsync resolve the same key at session time. A workspace re-created under the same name therefore keeps your access: a new id, the same key. Session resolution consults your own ssh-agent first: when SSH_AUTH_SOCK gives a live agent holding that key, the session signs through the agent and the key file's encryption stops mattering.

--pubkey FILE builds the workspace around a public key you already own: the file's one line travels to the daemon at any well-formed key type, the private half stays wherever you keep it, and nothing is written client-side. msks ssh and msks rsync work on such a workspace when the operator identity resolves to that key (identity_file pointing at it). A key that resolves nowhere keeps the direct route: ssh -i through a forward, or the Host msks-* alias with IdentityFile pointing at it. msks ssh exits with a line saying exactly that.

items.title: msks clone
items.text:
Copies one stopped workspace into a new one (POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id-or-name}/clone) and prints the new workspace's label and id:

$ msks clone seed task-42
cloned seed into task-42 (id 9a8b7c6d5e)

A clone is a full fork. The daemon copies both disks — the root overlay and the /home volume. Where the state filesystem can share blocks (a reflink), the copy costs its metadata; where it cannot, the copy writes the source's allocated bytes. The new workspace's row carries the source's create-time config: the image and its pin, the sizes and topology, the egress mode, the mounts, the login user, and the user_data payload. The clone's own factory reset re-provisions from that payload. The cloning chapter holds the whole story: what copies, what stays behind, and the in-guest secrets property.

The source must be stopped. A clone of a running workspace is refused with the reason, and the new name follows the create grammar (lowercase letters, digits, and dashes).

The clone's egress allowlist starts empty under the copied mode: a static clone answers every name NXDOMAIN until its list is set, an interactive one earns each allow. The --copy-allowlist flag opts the clone into the source's list verbatim. The cloning chapter holds the whole story.

items.title: msks start
items.text:
Boots one created workspace (POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id-or-name}/start) and prints the result:

$ msks start my-workspace
my-workspace running

The start request answers after the VMM finishes booting: a few seconds on an idle host, longer under load. The client waits up to two minutes before reporting a timeout, and a timeout message notes that the daemon may still finish the boot.

items.title: msks stop
items.text:
Powers one running workspace off (POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id-or-name}/stop) and prints the result, mirroring msks start:

$ msks stop my-workspace
my-workspace stopped

The stop asks the guest for a graceful, deadline-bounded power-off: the daemon presses the ACPI power button and the guest's systemd runs a full shutdown. The write-out can take a moment. The deadline is the daemon's (MSKSD_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_S); there is no client-side timeout flag, and like msks start the client waits at most two minutes on the answer. A stop that misses the daemon's deadline answers 503 with the endpoint's detail on one line, exit non-zero.

Stopping a workspace that is already stopped is a no-op success: the daemon reports it stopped either way, and the client asks without pre-filtering on local state. The same holds for a workspace that was never booted: the row records stopped without a launch ever happening. The data survives the stop: the root overlay and the /home volume come back on the next msks start.

items.title: msks resize
items.text:
Moves a stopped workspace's disk sizes and topology (the ceilings its guest sees as quotas, and the cpus and memory it boots with) through POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id-or-name}/resize:

$ msks resize ws4 --home-mib 4096
resized ws4: root 10240 MiB, home 4096 MiB

$ msks resize ws4 --cpus 4 --mem-mib 4096
resized ws4: root 10240 MiB, home 4096 MiB, cpus 4, mem 4096 MiB
(the new topology applies on its next boot)
  • --home-mib grows or shrinks the /home volume. The daemon quiets the filesystem, resize2fs moves it, and a shrink that would cut into used blocks answers a named 409 (free data in the workspace or shrink less).
  • --root-mib grows the root overlay only; the next start's cloud-init fills the larger device for free (the command's output says so when the root moved; a home resize's bytes are already in place). The grow-only rule is measured against the overlay's actual virtual size, which sits above the row when create clamped it to the base image. Shrinking the root stays unsupported: msks rm and a fresh create, or a factory reset, reclaim a root instead.
  • --cpus and --mem-mib set the vCPU count and guest memory. The daemon records them in the workspace row and boots it with the new topology at the next msks start. A running workspace is never reconfigured live. The bounds are create's (--cpus 1–64, --mem-mib 64–32768 MiB), and the command's output carries the boot note when they changed. The flags mix freely with the disk flags: one invocation can move the disks and the topology together.

The workspace must be in a free lifecycle state (created, stopped, absent); a running or paused workspace answers 409. The row follows immediately (msks ls --json, msks storage show the new ceiling), and a completed resize is announced on the events channel (workspace.resized). At least one flag is required.

items.title: msks mount
items.text:
Adds one host share to a workspace's mounts (POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id-or-name}/mounts); the spec is the create's own --share grammar:

$ msks mount ws1 /srv/refs:/srv/refs:ro
ws1 mounts /srv/projects:/mnt/projects:rw, /srv/refs:/srv/refs:ro (next start)

The outcome line gives the resulting set, and the next-start note joins it while the change is pending: setting mounts never touches a running VM, and the next msks start attaches exactly this set. The row carries mounts_pending: the daemon compares the configured set with the set the last start attached. The note rests once a start has taken the set, and an edit that returns the list to its attached shape shows the set alone. (what a mount is states the lifecycle: the seed each boot carries bakes the current set, so a restart after a change lands it and prunes the dropped mounts.) The daemon validates the whole list against its gates and the row rules (a host path appears once per workspace, guest paths are absolute and mutually disjoint); a refusal prints its reason on one line.

items.title: msks umount
items.text:
Removes a workspace's mounts of one host path, every guest path the share occupies:

$ msks umount ws1 /srv/refs
ws1 mounts /srv/projects:/mnt/projects:rw

A host path the workspace does not mount is one local line. The example returns the list to the shape the last start attached, so the outcome drops the next-start note. A removal that leaves the configured set differing from the attached shape keeps the note. The next start attaches the remainder, and a workspace whose last mount leaves this way mounts nothing at its next boot. The mounts chapter states the lifecycle.

items.title: msks rm
items.text:
Deletes workspaces (DELETE /api/v1/workspaces/{id-or-name}): the row, the VMM (stopped first, killed if wedged), and the persistent artifacts, the root overlay and the /home volume. The data does not come back. Creating a workspace under the same name mints a fresh id and starts from the image's pristine root, with nothing of the deleted instance left to collide with. One workspace or several:

$ msks rm my-workspace
my-workspace deleted
$ msks rm scratch-1 scratch-2
scratch-1 deleted
scratch-2 deleted

Workspaces are removed one at a time, in the order given. A failure stops the run there with the API's one-line error, and the ones already removed stay removed (each success printed its confirmation line). There is no confirmation prompt: deleting is what rm means, and a workspace is recoverable by recreating it. A workspace recorded on another host answers 409 with the host mismatch given in the error, like every lifecycle command.

items.title: msks image
items.text: Manages the daemon's image catalog, the surface docs/images.md documents over HTTP, as CLI subcommands. Every subcommand uses the same client environment as the workspace commands.

items.title: msks image ls
items.text:
One line per registered image (reference, hash (first 12 hex chars), the default designation, the kernel facts, and when the image entered the catalog) on the measured grid every listing shares:

$ msks image ls
ref            hash          default  kernel                description                      imported
debian:13.6    9f2c41ab77de  default  6.12.107+deb13 (raw)  Debian 13.6 cloud image, kernel…  2026-09-22 14:03
alpine:3.20    33aa9db1c4ef  -        6.12.7 (raw)          -                                2026-09-19 09:41

The image the daemon designates as default carries the default flag. A bare msks create resolves to it. The description column carries the identity the build baked into the image, capped for the row. image info prints it at full length, and an image whose manifest carried none keeps the column with a dash. The imported column shows the moment the archive entered the catalog, in local time to the minute.

An entry re-imported under the same reference moves the time forward with it. A renamed row adds an origin column beside the ref, showing the archive's own pair where it differs from the registered one. Rows whose archive pair matches keep the column with a dash. --json prints the listing as the API returns it (GET /api/v1/images, each row's imported field in ISO 8601 UTC, each row's origin_name/origin_version carrying the manifest pair), stable for scripting.

items.title: msks image import
items.text:
Registers an archive in the catalog (POST /api/v1/images). The source is a daemon-side path (the daemon reads the file from its own filesystem; the command uploads nothing) or an https:// URL the daemon downloads itself:

$ msks image import /srv/images/debian-13.tar
imported debian:13 (9f2c41ab77de)

$ msks image import https://images.example.com/debian-13.tar
imported debian:13 (9f2c41ab77de)

$ msks image import /srv/images/debian-13.tar --name mine --version 1.0
imported mine:1.0 (9f2c41ab77de)

A --name/--version override registers the archive under an operator-chosen pair. Either key alone, the other comes from the archive's own manifest, whose pair stays recorded as the row's origin (see docs/images.md). The archive bytes and the content hash stay exactly as they were. A pair another row already holds is refused with a named error.

A URL source is fetched into the catalog's staging area under the import ceiling and deadline (MSKSD_IMAGE_IMPORT_MAX_MIB, MSKSD_IMAGE_IMPORT_TIMEOUT_S), verified against system TLS roots, and imported from the downloaded copy. The recorded hash therefore always reflects the fetched bytes, and the same content imports once regardless of source. The first image imported into an empty catalog also becomes the daemon's default. An archive the daemon cannot read, parse, or fetch answers 400 with the reason on one line.

items.title: msks image rename
items.text:
Changes a cataloged image's registered name/version; the bytes, the hash, the manifest origin, and workspaces already booting the image stay put:

$ msks image rename debian:13 --name mine --version 1.4
renamed debian:13 to mine:1.4 (9f2c41ab77de)

$ msks image rename mine:1.4 --version 1.5
renamed mine:1.4 to mine:1.5 (9f2c41ab77de)

Either key alone keeps the other at its registered value. Pass at least one. The reference forms are the same as image rm's: name:version, a bare name (its newest version), name@hash, a full hash, or a unique hash prefix. The rename goes through the daemon (PATCH /api/v1/images/<hash>) after resolving the reference against the listing. A pair another row already holds is refused with the daemon's named error (409), and a pair the reference forms cannot carry (: or @ inside a value, or an empty one) is refused with a named error too. After a rename the old name:version stops resolving; name@hash (with the new name) and bare-hash references keep booting the same bytes.

items.title: msks image check
items.text:
Boots an image locally and verifies the guest contract point by point, the pre-import gate docs/images.md describes. The command runs on the image author's host: it needs /dev/kvm and nothing else from msks (no daemon, no state):

$ msks image check workspace-mine-1.0.tar
PASS archive        imported mine:1.0 (1d6a5e782fc0), root autologin getty on the console port
PASS boot           guest answered the console in 3.4s (kernel 6.12.107+deb13-amd64)
PASS console        root autologin getty on the console port
PASS user-data      seed payload ran on first boot
PASS acpi-shutdown  clean shutdown within 120s
PASS root-rw        root is writable and the write survived a stop/start (overlay)
PASS home-label     /home mounted by label msks-home and its write survived a stop/start (volume)

A broken contract point fails its row and the exit code is 1, with the first failure given. --keep preserves the throwaway state dir (serial logs) for inspection. --egress adds the DHCP point (the guest must take a global address over the daemon's own net stack) and needs root plus an egress-capable default route (--uplink gives another interface).

items.title: msks image rm
items.text:
Removes an image from the catalog. The reference accepts every form the daemon resolves for workspace create (name:version, a bare name (its newest version), name@hash (the full 64-hex hash), a full hash) and a unique hash prefix (the 12 chars image ls prints):

$ msks image rm debian:12
debian:12 deleted

The removal is keyed by the image's hash after resolving the reference against the listing. An image a workspace still boots is refused (the API's 409 gives the workspace), and a reference that matches nothing exits with the catalog spelled out so the next try can be copy-pasted. An ambiguous hash prefix lists the images it matches. Use the full hash or name@hash. (Two imports of the same name:version, a rebuilt archive, are the usual ambiguity, and only the hash forms still identify one of them.)

items.title: msks image info
items.text:
Prints one image's full record from the same listing data: reference, the archive's own pair (the origin), hash, kernel facts, cmdline, and the default designation:

$ msks image info debian:13
ref          mine:1.4
origin       debian:13.6
hash         9f2c41ab77de0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000
kernel       6.12.107+deb13 (raw)
description  Debian 13.6 cloud image, kernel 6.12.107+deb13, cloud-init, the egress module set and consent stack
cmdline      console=ttyS0 root=/dev/vda rw
seed         provisioner - (none declared)
default      yes

The reference forms are the same as image rm's. The description row is the identity the build baked into the image's manifest. An image whose manifest carried none prints - (none baked).

items.title: msks image default
items.text:
Designates the image a bare msks create boots (the row image ls marks), or clears the designation with --unset:

$ msks image default debian:13.6
designated debian:13.6 (98ccf2e1f2db) as the default image

$ msks image default --unset
default designation removed; a bare create falls back to the sole
entry debian:13.6 (98ccf2e1f2db)

The reference forms are the same as image rm's: name:version, a bare name (its newest version), name@hash, a full hash, a unique hash prefix. The designation goes through the daemon (POST /api/v1/images/default), survives restarts, and the next image ls marks the row. A fresh MSKSD_DEFAULT_IMAGE import at daemon startup still reclaims the slot. The command is the operator's designation between restarts. A reference that matches nothing exits with the catalog spelled out, the same miss image rm answers.

--unset clears the designation (DELETE /api/v1/images/default) and reports the fallback a bare create now takes. The sole catalog entry stays what it boots (the line above). On a catalog holding several images, a bare create needs --image until one is designated again, and the line says so.

items.title: msks home
items.text:
Moves a workspace's /home volume through the daemon, useful for backup, migration to another daemon or seeding a fresh workspace with data.

msks home export my-workspace              # writes my-workspace.ext4
msks home export my-workspace other.ext4   # gives the output file
msks home export my-workspace - | gzip > backup.ext4.gz
msks home import fresh-ws my-workspace.ext4
msks home import fresh-ws - < backup.ext4

The workspace must be stopped (a volume under a running VM answers 409; stop it first, msks stop is enough). A boot that arrives during a move waits for it and boots the volume the move left. Moves, boots, and deletes serialize per workspace, and the waiter answers a named 409 after MSKSD_MOVE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S instead of hanging.

Export streams the volume file's bytes verbatim and prints one confirmation line (exported my-workspace (2097152 bytes) to my-workspace.ext4). - writes the bytes to stdout and moves the note to stderr, so a pipe stays clean for gzip or ssh. A reader that goes away mid-stream (| head, a compressor on a full disk) prints one line on stderr and exits non-zero. Import uploads the named ext4 image (or stdin, for -), the daemon replaces the volume with it, and the reply is the byte count: imported 2097152 bytes into fresh-ws.

The daemon refuses with one line and exit 1. Refused: a file that is not an ext4 image (msks: 400: the request body is not an ext4 image ...), a workspace in the wrong state, and everything the API's refusals give (a foreign host). An import keeps the workspace's existing volume until the upload completes and passes the ext4 check. A cut-off upload changes nothing.

The typical pairings are backup (export, later import back into the same workspace after a rm + create) and migration (export on one daemon, create + import on another). Seeding is the third: build an ext4 image with the data a fleet of workspaces starts from, then import it into each fresh one. Inside a workspace with egress, git and rsync over the forward (docs/networking.md) carry day-to-day code. The volume moves are for the whole /home at once.

items.title: msks secret
items.text:
Mint a secret placeholder (daemon-wide by default, scoped with --workspace) and the daemon keeps your value as per-recipient ciphertext blobs in its database. See also docs/secrets.md.

# from a password manager, nothing touches disk: daemon-wide,
# one sentinel for every workspace on the daemon
op read 'op://Vault/github/credential' \
  | msks secret mint --name github_api \
      --dest api.github.com --secret-file -

msks secret mint --workspace myws --name pypi \
  --dest .pypi.org --dest pypi.org \
  --ttl 86400 --secret-file ./token    # scoped, suffix + exact

msks secret mint --workspace ci,deploy --name pypi \
  --dest .pypi.org --secret-file ./token   # one row, two workspaces

msks secret ls                           # placeholders + coverage + lock state
msks secret unlock                      # decrypt the pending blobs the
                                         # configured identity key opens
msks secret renew --workspace myws --name pypi --ttl 86400
msks secret revoke --name github_api     # the daemon-wide row of the label
msks secret revoke --workspace ci,deploy --name pypi
msks secret coverage myws scoped         # exempt myws from daemon-wide rows

--secret-file takes a path or - for a pipe, and the value is whitespace-stripped at both ends. The secret is never accepted as a command-line argument, because argv appears in process lists and shell history.

An empty file is refused before any network roundtrip. --dest repeats and binds the swap: an exact host (api.github.com) or a suffix that covers every host under a domain (.github.com). --workspace takes one ref or a comma list and repeats. Omitted, the mint covers every workspace on the daemon (one row, one mskssec2_ sentinel), while a scoped mint prints a mskssec1_ sentinel, so the string alone gives its reach. The mint prints the sentinel; the listing and the audit omit it (secret ls never shows one). The daemon serves a row's sentinel back on demand over the token-authenticated API. revoke and renew take the same targeting the mint took. revoke takes effect on the next request and retires the whole row everywhere at once, and renew extends a --ttl lifetime in place with the sentinel unchanged.

items.title: msks console
items.text:
An interactive shell inside a workspace, over the daemon's console websocket. This is useful when msks ssh is not working properly, because it works when the ssh daemon is not responding for whatever reason. The command boots the workspace first when the daemon reports it as not running. The notices print on stderr while the boot runs, then the session attaches:

$ msks console my-workspace
msks: my-workspace is stopped; starting it
msks: my-workspace running
(workspace prompt)

The session is a root shell: the console is the failsafe path, served by the guest's autologin root getty on the virtio-console port. It is a raw byte stream over the daemon's authenticated websocket, with no user selection and no in-band protocol. Reach a workspace user's shell with su - <name> inside the session, or over ssh for the full interactive posture:

$ msks console my-workspace
(workspace prompt, as root)

A workspace that is already running attaches with no preamble. Two states get special handling:

  • starting: another client's boot is in flight. The console waits for it (polling up to two minutes) and attaches when it lands, instead of racing a second boot into the daemon's double-launch guard.
  • paused: refused with the honest reason, because the daemon has no resume; the message gives the recovery (msks stop it, then msks start again).

A start that loses a race (the daemon reports stopped, another client boots it in the gap) re-checks and attaches to the winner.

Ctrl-] detaches and leaves the workspace running. Ctrl-C and Ctrl-D reach the guest. To type a literal Ctrl-] into the guest, press it twice quickly (the second press within 50 ms): the pair delivers one Ctrl-] byte. A single Ctrl-], or one followed by any other byte, detaches, and the byte that followed the escape is consumed with it, so a paste that happens to contain a lone Ctrl-] detaches the session. Large pastes travel as a few websocket frames (4,096-byte chunks), not one frame per byte. The session needs a tty on both stdin and stdout.

items.title: msks forward
items.text:
Forwards a guest TCP port on this command's stdio over the daemon's forward websocket. The command boots the workspace first when the daemon reports it as not running (the same notices as msks console), then bridges bytes unexamined in both directions: a tty is not required, and binary protocols (ssh, rsync) pass through it cleanly:

msks forward my-workspace 22                  # stdio: ProxyCommand shape
msks forward my-workspace 8080 --local 8080   # loopback listener

--local PORT binds 127.0.0.1:PORT instead of stdio. Every accepted connection opens its own forward websocket, so parallel clients (a browser and a curl, two ssh sessions) are independent sessions. Refusals print one line (the daemon's close codes give the cause: no NIC, not running, service not listening, still booting), while a clean end of stream (the guest service closed, stdin EOF) leaves exit code 0.

items.title: msks egress
items.text:
Decide, watch, and inspect a workspace's outbound-destination egress consent verdicts. A workspace in interactive mode holds each new outbound connection's first packet until a decider allows or denies it. static workspaces allow only their create-time allowlist. allow workspaces (the create default) record off-list destinations and pass them.

msks egress rules ws-dev          # the mode, allowlist, and in-effect verdicts
msks egress requests ws-dev       # the consent rows (audit trail), newest first
msks egress requests ws-dev --decision pending
msks egress decide ws-dev <request-id> allow --duration 5m
msks egress decide ws-dev <request-id> deny --duration forever
msks egress revoke ws-dev <request-id>
msks egress mode ws-dev interactive          # switch the posture;
msks egress mode ws-dev static --allow .debian.org   # --allow replaces
msks egress mode ws-dev static --offline     # ... the allowlist (--offline
                                              # confirms an empty static)
msks egress watch ws-dev          # stream frames; registers this client as
                                  # a decider (holds wait only while one is
                                  # connected)
msks egress watch ws-dev --decide --duration forever
                                  # the same, prompting y/n per request

decide and revoke identify the request by the id watch and requests print (the full id, copy-pasteable). Both act only on the given workspace's requests. A portless destination (a non-TCP/UDP flow) prompts as host (all ports): an allow opens every port on the host for the duration. Durations: once (this connection only; a reconnect re-prompts), 5m, 15m, tilrestart (until the workspace VM stops; the default), forever (the workspace's lifetime, replayed at every boot). revoke undoes an in-effect verdict immediately: the flow rules and the destination's live connections drop, and new connections gate again.

mode switches a workspace's posture without recreating it. A running workspace swaps live: the whole firewall table re-applies in one transaction, established connections survive (an attached msks ssh session stays up), the resolver flips with the chain, and any held request answers deny when the switch leaves interactive. A stopped workspace builds the new posture at its next start. The command's output line says which happened.

Verdicts carry across switches: an allow forever granted under interactive keeps acting under static. Switching to static therefore freezes the workspace at everything approved so far: name-keyed verdicts in full and, on a direct gated-to-gated switch, the kernel-side pins too. A round-trip through allow rebuilds the pins from the durable rows (forever verdicts re-pin at entry; a timed address-keyed allow re-prompts or re-learns on the guest's next resolution). --allow SPEC (repeatable, create's grammar) replaces the allowlist. Omitted, the workspace keeps its list. Switching to static with nothing effectively allowed (an empty allowlist and no in-effect allowed verdict) is refused with a message giving the fix: pass --allow entries, or pass --offline to run the switch anyway. That posture answers every name NXDOMAIN: an offline workspace reachable only by ssh.

items.title: msks key
items.text:
Displays the workspace's ssh identity. Every workspace a local-backend daemon creates carries the public half its create sent, the operator's key, whose line the guest's first boot planted into authorized_keys for root and the workspace's login user. The fetch takes the same MSKSC_URL/MSKSC_TOKEN/MSKSC_CAFILE environment as every other command:

msks key my-workspace                    # the public authorized_keys line

The command is public-only: the private half is the operator's own key, and it never crossed the API to begin with. It lives wherever identity_file points, or in the agent that holds it.

items.title: msks ssh
items.text:
Use ssh to access a workspace, using a forward.

msks ssh my-workspace              # as the workspace's login user
msks ssh my-workspace -- -l root   # the recovery login
msks ssh my-workspace -- -A        # forward your agent ($SSH_AUTH_SOCK)
msks ssh my-workspace -- -L 8080:localhost:80

Options you pass here win for the invocation. The config file's ssh_options key remembers a set for every session instead. See its section for the precedence between the two.

The command boots the workspace first when the daemon reports it as not running (the same notices as msks console). It then fetches the identity over the authenticated API and runs ssh with the forward websocket as its ProxyCommand (msks forward <ws> 22).

A session that booted its workspace waits out the guest's first boot. The daemon reports running while the guest's sshd is already up but the identity seed has yet to land in authorized_keys. The command therefore probes the login first, with a throwaway true as the remote command, retried for up to 30s with a one-line notice between attempts. It opens the real session, interactive or one-shot, once the guest accepts the workspace key. A remote command runs exactly once either way.

The probe carries only the session's login user and agent-forwarding setting, plus msks's own transport, its quiet flag, and a true command. A session's tunnels and other ssh options therefore cannot hold the wait open or alter it. The session itself keeps every option.

The API serves the public half, and the private half resolves at session time. Your own agent comes first: when SSH_AUTH_SOCK gives a live agent holding the workspace's key, matched on the key material (so the file it came from and its name do not matter), the session signs through that agent. The private half never enters the msks process, encrypted or not. Then the operator identity: identity_file (or MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE), the same key the create planted. When neither holds the workspace's key, the command exits with one line giving both rungs and the ways back in (ssh-add the key, point identity*file at it, or ssh -i directly).

Host keys land in a per-workspace known_hosts under the msks cache root, under accept-new. The root is the cache_dir key (MSKSC_CACHE_DIR) when it is set, else XDG_CACHE_HOME or ~/.cache/msks, then <workspace-id>/known_hosts. The cache keys on the workspace's immutable id, so a workspace recreated under the same name starts with a fresh cache and trusts its own first-boot keys again. Every invocation pins under that one id alias, whichever way the workspace was addressed: msks ssh <name> and the TUI's shell action record the same known_hosts entry, and an operator's own ~/.ssh/config Host <name> block no longer matches the session (the id is the hostname msks ssh dials; use the id in a matching block instead).

Host keys persist across stop/start on the workspace's overlay, so the first-connection entry keeps matching. When the daemon recreates the overlay under a live workspace (a healed loss, a factory reset), the guest regenerates its host keys: the daemon advances the workspace's disk epoch, the cache rotates with it, and the next connection pins the fresh keys with a notice marking the recreation instead of refusing. A rotation leaves the previous epoch's cache behind (the <id>/ directory, then <id>.e1/, <id>.e2/, ... as rotations accumulate); those directories are dead: delete them at will. The alias block keeps its own known_hosts under ~/.cache/msks/msks-<ws>/; the two paths record the same host key independently.

Agent forwarding asked for on the command line (-A, or -o ForwardAgent=yes) forwards your agent, the socket SSH_AUTH_SOCK gives. ssh-add -l inside the workspace lists the same keys as on the host, and git push git@github.com, ssh, and friends sign with the host's credentials.

The session authenticates through a transient in-process agent (above), and stock ssh would forward that one when asked to forward at all. msks therefore rewrites the request into ForwardAgent=<your socket>, an explicit path. An OpenSSH client 8.2 or newer parses the form. An older client exits with its own usage error (RHEL 8's 8.0, for one). The workspace identity stays an authentication credential and reaches the guest as nothing else. A request that already gives a socket (-o ForwardAgent=/path/to/sock) keeps its own. -A with no live agent behind SSH_AUTH_SOCK exits with one line marking it. Forwarding set by an ssh config file keeps the stock meaning under this command (it forwards the session agent); the command line is where your agent is given.

Everything after the workspace id (the -- is optional; any argument ssh would take works verbatim) is passed to ssh. A passthrough that starts with a plain word is a remote command (msks ssh my-workspace -- uname -a). When it starts with an option, ssh's own separator carries a command after the options (msks ssh my-workspace -- -A -- uname -a). -A forwards your agent, the same forwarding the paragraphs above describe (before it forwarded the session agent, the workspace identity, which served nested logins to the same workspace: ssh from inside to localhost). That use now points at the identity explicitly instead: identity_file gives your own key, and your agent holds it for the nested login.

The exit code is ssh's own (255 for ssh failures), not the msks command set. The session agent lives exactly as long as the msks ssh process; ControlPersist/mux sessions that outlive it belong to the alias path, whose identity is a key file. Explicit passthrough options override the injected defaults (your own UserKnownHostsFile, a different ProxyCommand) exactly as with stock ssh: ssh takes the first value a repeated option receives, and the passthrough comes first.

The login user is the workspace's recorded login user: the create-time --user, defaulting to the creating operator's name. A workspace created before records none, and the dial is root. ssh arguments that give a user (-l root, -o User=root) override it. The host argument ssh sees is the workspace id itself; the transport is the proxy, so the name never resolves. The ProxyCommand runs this very client, in the absolute interpreter and module form, so msks need not be on the ssh child's PATH. It inherits your environment: MSKSC_URL, MSKSC_TOKEN, and MSKSC_CAFILE must be set where ssh runs. The networking chapter's alias workflow covers the Host msks-* configuration that hides all of this.

items.title: msks rsync
items.text:
Stock rsync against a workspace over an ssh forward, with the identity staged in memory: one command does the whole setup itself. The workspace boots when needed, the identity stages in memory, and the copy opens its own forward:

msks rsync my-workspace -- -av ./site/ root@:/root/site/    # push
msks rsync my-workspace -- -av root@:/root/out.tar ./out.tar  # pull
msks rsync my-workspace -- -aP ./src/ :src/         # as the login user

Everything after the workspace id (the -- is optional) is given to rsync. msks parses no rsync flags. The one shaping pass is the empty host: a path whose host is empty (:/root/site/, or root@:/root/site/) targets the workspace this command gives, its host filled in as the copy runs. The direction, push or pull, comes entirely from the rsync arguments, and the login user comes from the paths the same way. root@:/root/site/ logs in as root; a bare :src/ logs in as the workspace's login user, whose home is the persistent /home volume (the shape for copies under your own account). A path that gives a host keeps it, and the transport is the proxy either way, so the name never resolves. ::module paths are rsync's daemon protocol against port 873; the workspace image runs no rsync daemon (sshd stays its one inbound service), so that form is left as typed and fails as rsync's own error.

A word that starts with a colon reaches this fill even when it is the split-apart value of an rsync option (--filter :rules), because msks does not parse rsync's flags to tell the two apart. That spelling uses the attached form (--filter=:rules), which msks never touches.

The command boots the workspace first when the daemon reports it as not running (the same notices as msks console), fetches the identity over the authenticated API, and runs the host rsync with the same transport msks ssh uses. That transport is the forward websocket as the ssh ProxyCommand (each rsync connection opens its own), the per-workspace known_hosts under accept-new, and the identity staged in a transient in-process ssh-agent. The private half exists only in memory. rsync's ssh children identify it by its public half and sign through the agent socket, and the command writes no key file. The operator identity (identity_file), a --pubkey workspace, and the earlier row shapes (daemon-minted, client-minted) all work: the private half resolves where it lives. That may be the operator's agent first (the same key-material match msks ssh applies), the operator's own file, the API, or the per-workspace file. A key that resolves nowhere on this client exits with the line giving where it can be. A session that booted its workspace waits out the guest's first boot exactly as msks ssh does: a probe login retries behind the identity seed (up to 30s, one line between attempts), and the copy runs once the guest accepts the workspace key.

The login user is the workspace's recorded login user, stated as a generated per-session ssh config, so rsync's own user@ path spelling overrides it (root@:/root/site/ logs in as root). An explicit -e in the passthrough replaces msks's remote shell entirely (rsync takes the last -e, and the empty-host fill keeps pointing at the workspace id your own transport must then reach), the same override shape ssh passthrough options have. The host prerequisites are ssh and rsync. The exit code is rsync's own.

items.title: Errors, exit codes, and timeouts
items.text:
Every command fails with one readable line on stderr and exit code 1, never a traceback:

msks: set MSKSC_TOKEN to a daemon token (MSKSC_URL for a non-default daemon)
msks: cannot reach https://192.168.77.2:8660: [Errno 113] ...
msks: 401: invalid or revoked token
msks: 409: workspace exists
msks: 422: body.id: String should match pattern '^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$'

The status lines carry the daemon's detail field verbatim. A validation failure (422) reports each problem as field: message, joined on one line: the same facts the API returns, minus the JSON scaffolding. A timeout says so explicitly, because the daemon may still complete a request the client stopped waiting for. Argument errors exit with code 2 (the convention the argparse-era CLI set and the typer-based one keeps); success is 0; a Ctrl-C during a long boot prints msks: interrupted and exits 130.

items.title: Cloning workspaces
items.text:
Cloning copies one workspace's state into a new workspace. The new workspace boots with a copy of the source's disks and the source's create-time configuration, under its own id and a new name.

Use the CLI form msks clone ws ws2 to clone ws into ws2. The TUI's workspace page offers the same action (Clone) with a name prompt.

items.title: What a clone carries
items.text:
• Both disks. The daemon copies the root overlay and the /home volume. Everything the guest wrote arrives with the clone: installed packages, /etc changes, repos and files under /home. The copy is a reflink where the state filesystem supports one (the blocks are shared, the copy costs its metadata).
  • The create-time config. The root and home sizes, the CPU and memory topology, the egress mode, the host-share mounts, the login user, and the user_data payload all copy. The clone's own factory reset re-provisions from the payload, exactly like the source's would.

items.title: What stays behind
items.text:
• The egress allowlist. The clone's list starts empty. Its posture is the mode it inherited over nothing allowed, so a fork under interactive mode earns its own destinations. A fork under static mode answers every name NXDOMAIN until the operator sets its list — an offline workspace reachable only by ssh, the same posture msks egress mode static --offline builds. msks clone seed fork --copy-allowlist opts the clone into the source's list verbatim, for the seed-to-fleet case where the seed's approved set is meant to propagate.
  • In-effect egress verdicts. Every allow forever the source earned under interactive mode stays with the source. The clone re-earns each allow, with or without --copy-allowlist.
  • Workspace-scoped secret placeholders. A placeholder minted against the source's id does not swap on the clone's tap. Mint or re-scope one for the clone when it needs the credential. Daemon-wide placeholders cover the clone with nothing to decide, like they cover every workspace.

items.title: The stopped-source rule
items.text: The source must be stopped to be cloned. The daemon refuses a clone of a running workspace.

items.title: Cloning gotchas
items.text:
A clone copies everything the source's disks carry. The clone and the source carry the same ssh host keys, the same machine-id, and the same application secrets any first-boot process minted (session signing keys, self-signed certificates). Anything that trusts the source's identity silently trusts the clone too: a known_hosts entry, a deploy key.

There is no automatic regeneration. Rotate what matters before trusting the clone as a separate machine: regenerate the guest's ssh host keys, re-key anything the workspace registered with an external service, or treat the clone as the same trust domain as its source.

items.title: Typical uses of cloning
items.text:
• Seed workspace. Prepare one workspace with the toolchain, repos, and login state, then clone it per task or per agent with --copy-allowlist: the seed's approved destinations propagate, and each clone still re-earns its interactive verdicts.
  • Experiment fork. Clone before a risky session; the original keeps its state while the clone takes the risk.

items.title: The msksd configuration file
items.text: msksd reads its settings from a YAML file, from MSKSD_* environment variables, and from built-in defaults. The file is the durable home for a deployment's settings, committed to the deployment's own storage and human-reviewable, while the environment variables stay available as per-invocation overrides.

items.title: Precedence
items.text:
Values resolve in this order (highest first):

  1. Environment variables (MSKSD_*): override the file
  2. The config file: the YAML file msksd resolves at startup
  3. Built-in defaults: the settings dataclass defaults

A variable set in the process wins over the same key in the file; a key set nowhere uses the default. An environment variable set to an empty string is the unset form: the file value applies.

items.title: The --config flag
items.text:
msksd resolves its config file in three modes:

Invocation Behavior msksd Reads $MSKSD_CONFIG_DIR/msksd.yaml (default ~/.config/msksd/msksd.yaml, honoring $XDG_CONFIG_HOME). A missing file is generated as a commented template pointing at this chapter: the first run writes the file so its location is discoverable, and the daemon then runs on environment variables and defaults. msksd --config /path/to/msksd.yaml Reads exactly that file. A missing file is a startup error giving the path. Explicit paths are never auto-generated. msksd --config=none Reads environment variables and built-in defaults only; the in-tree user is the smoke-test daemon, and the deployment-host module passes an explicit --config path.

MSKSD_CONFIG_DIR is read before anything else and exists only as an environment variable: the config file cannot relocate the directory it lives in, so the tree root must be resolvable before the file is located.

items.title: msksd doctor
items.text: msksd doctor checks the host for the tools the daemon and the client exec, reading the config the same way the daemon does: the --config flag, the environment, and the file, under the precedence above. The host doctor chapter owns the check rows, the report's markers and hints, and the exit codes.

items.title: Key mapping
items.text:
A config-file key is its MSKSD_* variable with the prefix stripped and lowercased, one rule with no lookup table:

Environment variable Config-file key MSKSD_PORT port MSKSD_EGRESS_SUBNET egress_subnet MSKSD_STATE_DIR state_dir

The file is flat: one key per setting, no sections. For example:

host: 0.0.0.0
port: 8660

sets the same settings MSKSD_HOST, MSKSD_PORT, and MSKSD_CONSOLE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S would. Either spelling is recoverable from the other by the rule, and the daemon enforces it in code: the key↔variable table is derived mechanically, so the two forms cannot drift apart.

The underscore is the canonical spelling, and a hyphen may be written for it: egress-dns-upstream and egress_dns_upstream are one key spelled two ways. The llm_models entries' keys follow the same rule, so an operator used to kebab-case YAML can write it naturally. Both spellings of one key in the same file is a startup error giving the two spellings, and the valid-keys list an unknown key reports is the snake_case one.

One mapping detail worth knowing: state_dir places the database too. state_dir feeds both the local driver's workspace artifacts and the server's sqlite database (<state_dir>/msks.db); there is no separate db_path key, matching the environment variable, which also drives both.

items.title: Native scalar types
items.text:
Numeric, boolean, and string fields accept their natural YAML scalars: port: 8660, access_log: true, socket_wait_timeout_s: 12.5. Quoted strings (port: "8660") work everywhere and parse identically. A key with no value (bootstrap_token:) is the unset form; the environment (for its variable) and then the default apply. Values must be scalars: a list or mapping where a number, boolean, or string belongs is a startup error, and so is a duplicate key (a second port: does not silently win). Merge keys (<<: *anchor) are refused with their own message: the file is flat and every key is spelled out.

Booleans deserve care. true and false are the spellings to use; PyYAML also parses the YAML 1.1 forms yes/no/on/off as booleans, so those work too. The single letters y and n are plain strings to YAML 1.1, so a boolean key set to either reads as false; the environment variable follows the same string rule. A bare 1 or 0 is an integer, which also reads as false. Write true or false.

items.title: Unknown keys fail fast
items.text: A key the daemon does not know is a startup error giving the key and the valid ones, so a typo'd prot fails at boot instead of being silently ignored. The environment has no such guard: a typo'd variable name is simply never read. Invalid values fail the same way whichever source they came from, and the error message gives the MSKSD_* variable: vmm_driver: firecracker reports MSKSD_VMM_DRIVER must be one of ('local',). Non-finite numbers (.nan, .inf) are rejected from either source.

items.title: Key reference
items.text: The tables below group the keys by the subsystem that reads them; the file itself carries them all at one level.

items.title: The API listener
items.text: Key Environment variable Type Default What it does host MSKSD_HOST string 127.0.0.1 The HTTPS + WSS listener's bind address. port MSKSD_PORT int 8660 The listener's port. socket MSKSD_SOCKET string (unset) Binds a second, local listener at this unix socket path: same-host clients connect through it with peer-credential authentication, with no token and no TLS. Unset binds the default path, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/msks/msksd.sock. A daemon without a runtime dir (a container, a hand-written system unit pointing MSKSD_SOCKET at a path its RuntimeDirectory creates) serves TCP alone until this setting gives a path; the empty string always serves TCP alone. The socket file is mode 0660: chgrp it to a shared group to admit that group's members. Membership counts every supplementary group the account database holds for the user (including the nesting a directory backend expands itself), and the daemon keeps no membership cache, so a removal takes effect at the next request once the account database serves the change. The systemd user unit the setup tools generate creates $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/msks for this listener through its RuntimeDirectory, the client's own default candidate path. Read at startup; a reload applies a change at restart. tls_cert MSKSD_TLS_CERT string (unset) Path to the operator-provided TLS certificate. Both cert and key unset: a self-signed CA is generated on first run and its fingerprint printed for trust-on-first-use pinning. tls_key MSKSD_TLS_KEY string (unset) Path to the operator-provided TLS key. event_poll_s MSKSD_EVENT_POLL_S float 1.0 Seconds between watcher scans (workspace status reconciles and the state-disk pressure probe), read at loop start; a running daemon applies a change at restart. bootstrap_token MSKSD_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN string (unset) Seeds the first bearer token at first boot. The plaintext must fit the HTTP token grammar (letters, digits, and the separator characters RFC 9110 allows): the token travels the Authorization header on the REST surface and the websocket handshake alike, whose value grammar rejects the rest. access_log MSKSD_ACCESS_LOG bool false Writes uvicorn's access log: request lines (method, path, query), never headers. Websocket tokens travel the Authorization header, not the URL, so the log holds no credentials.

items.title: The local cloud-hypervisor driver
items.text: Key Environment variable Type Default What it does vmm_driver MSKSD_VMM_DRIVER string local The backend that runs workspaces: local (cloud-hypervisor). state_dir MSKSD_STATE_DIR string ~/.local/state/msksd The daemon's state directory: the sqlite database (<state_dir>/msks.db) and per-workspace artifacts. ~ expands. The database runs in WAL mode: -wal/-shm sibling files sit beside it while the daemon runs and are removed again at a clean shutdown. A copy of the database taken mid-run should take the siblings with it. cloud_hypervisor MSKSD_CLOUD_HYPERVISOR string cloud-hypervisor Path to the cloud-hypervisor binary the local driver execs. socket_wait_timeout_s MSKSD_SOCKET_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S float 10.0 Seconds the driver waits for the VMM's API socket at workspace start. request_timeout_s MSKSD_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S float 5.0 Seconds per cloud-hypervisor API request. shutdown_timeout_s MSKSD_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_S float 20.0 Seconds a workspace stop waits for the guest to power off. console_wait_timeout_s MSKSD_CONSOLE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S float 15.0 Seconds to wait for the guest's console device at boot (generous: nested-virt guests arm the device slower). forward_wait_timeout_s MSKSD_FORWARD_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S float 15.0 Seconds a forward websocket retries its guest dial at boot (a freshly booted guest races DHCP against its services); past the deadline the refusal gives the cause. console_stall_timeout_s MSKSD_CONSOLE_STALL_TIMEOUT_S float 60.0 Seconds a console session stays open after client input drew no guest bytes; then the websocket closes with 4502. 0 disables the close. An idle session (no input) never trips it. move_wait_timeout_s MSKSD_MOVE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S float 120.0 Seconds a boot or volume move waits for the workspace's other volume move (a stalled export reader holds its lock as long as its connection lives); the waiter answers a named 409 past the bound instead of hanging. 0 is fail-fast. default_image MSKSD_DEFAULT_IMAGE string (unset) A container-image tar imported into the catalog and designated default on first boot. seed_images MSKSD_SEED_IMAGES list (unset) Container-image tars imported into the catalog at every start, warm when unchanged; never designated default.
