A bare-name image reference resolves the newest version, with import recency breaking ties between builds whose versions carry the same leading numbers. qemu_img MSKSD_QEMU_IMG string qemu-img Path to qemu-img, which builds the per-workspace root overlay. mkfs_ext4 MSKSD_MKFS_EXT4 string mkfs.ext4 Path to mkfs.ext4, which builds the per-workspace /home volume. resize2fs MSKSD_RESIZE2FS string resize2fs Path to resize2fs, which moves a /home volume's size. e2fsck MSKSD_E2FSCK string e2fsck Path to e2fsck, which quiets a volume before a resize. mkisofs MSKSD_MKISOFS string mkisofs Path to mkisofs, which builds the user_data cidata seed disk. host_name MSKSD_HOST_NAME string (the hostname) The host name recorded as owning locally-created workspaces. root_mib MSKSD_ROOT_MIB int 10240 Default workspace root overlay size, MiB (a per-create request overrides). home_mib MSKSD_HOME_MIB int 20480 Default workspace /home volume size, MiB (a per-create request overrides). storage_warn_pct MSKSD_STORAGE_WARN_PCT int 90 State-disk percentage used that moves pressure to warn; 1–99. storage_floor_mib MSKSD_STORAGE_FLOOR_MIB int 512 Free state-disk MiB below which pressure is critical and workspace creates, image imports, and home-volume imports answer 507. image_import_max_mib MSKSD_IMAGE_IMPORT_MAX_MIB int 8192 The size ceiling a URL image import accepts: a download whose declared or streamed size passes it is refused by name. The storage floor still counts the imported archive twice, like a path import. image_import_timeout_s MSKSD_IMAGE_IMPORT_TIMEOUT_S float 600.0 The overall deadline a URL image import download runs under; a slow source fails with a named error instead of hanging the request.

items.title: Per-workspace egress networking
items.text: Key Environment variable Type Default What it does egress_enabled MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED bool false Arms per-workspace NICs, DHCP, NAT egress, and the DNS forwarder at startup (needs CAP_NET_ADMIN); a running daemon applies a change at restart. egress_subnet MSKSD_EGRESS_SUBNET string 172.31.0.0/16 The IPv4 pool per-workspace /30 slices are carved from. egress_uplink MSKSD_EGRESS_UPLINK string eth0 The host interface egress is NAT-masqueraded out of (the base NAT table applies at startup; per-workspace rules read the live value). egress_dns_upstream MSKSD_EGRESS_DNS_UPSTREAM string (unset) The resolver the daemon's DNS forwarder relays to; unset reads the host's own /etc/resolv.conf. ip_tool MSKSD_IP_TOOL string ip Path to the ip binary (taps and addresses). nft_tool MSKSD_NFT_TOOL string nft Path to the nft binary (per-VM firewall tables). egress_lease_s MSKSD_EGRESS_LEASE_S int 3600 DHCP lease seconds offered to guests. egress_dns_timeout_s MSKSD_EGRESS_DNS_TIMEOUT_S float 3.0 Seconds the forwarder waits on the upstream resolver. egress_mode MSKSD_EGRESS_MODE string allow The consent mode workspaces get at create when the request gives none: allow, static, or interactive. egress_consent_timeout_s MSKSD_EGRESS_CONSENT_TIMEOUT_S float 120.0 Seconds a held first packet waits for a decider before the hold expires to a deny (inside the kernel's ~127 s SYN budget). egress_consent_rate_limit MSKSD_EGRESS_CONSENT_RATE_LIMIT int 8 The per-workspace pending-prompt cap (the prompt-spam bound); 0 removes it. egress_consent_retention_days MSKSD_EGRESS_CONSENT_RETENTION_DAYS int 30 Days a consent row lives past its terminal timestamp; 0 disables retention pruning. egress_consent_row_cap MSKSD_EGRESS_CONSENT_ROW_CAP int 1000 The per-workspace consent-row ceiling (the flood bound); 0 disables the cap. egress_queue_base MSKSD_EGRESS_QUEUE_BASE int 1024 The base per-workspace NFQUEUE numbers derive from (base + pool slice); must leave room under 65535. conntrack_tool MSKSD_CONNTRACK_TOOL string conntrack The tool revocation uses to drop a revoked destination's established connections. interceptor_port MSKSD_INTERCEPTOR_PORT int 8643 The TCP port every armed workspace's interceptor listener binds on its own tap address. probe_port MSKSD_PROBE_PORT int 8644 The TCP port every workspace's probe service listener binds on its own tap address. The guest still dials 443 (the redirect catches it); the interceptor repoints its upstream dial to this port, so a host service on 443 cannot break the probe. audit_hmac_key MSKSD_AUDIT_HMAC_KEY string (unset) When set, every consent row is written with an HMAC-SHA256 tag over its data columns (tamper-evident audit); unset stores no tags.

items.title: Host share mounts
items.text:
Host paths are the one share surface (mounts chapter for the behavior): a workspace gives a host directory through the daemon's two gates, and this table is the second one's config. The named-share list (mount_shares) was removed; a config that still carries the key fails at load with the removal message pointing at these keys.

Key Environment variable Type Default What it does mount_host_mode MSKSD_MOUNT_HOST_MODE text identity How a host-path mount's path reaches the daemon's filesystem: identity (the daemon runs on bare Linux and the path is its own) or prefix (the daemon runs in its own VM, the macOS host, and share roots mount under the reserved /mnt/msks, so the path composes onto that prefix, the WSL /mnt/c shape). mount_host_roots MSKSD_MOUNT_HOST_ROOTS list (unset) The allowed host-share roots, as host paths (translated by mount_host_mode at gate time): a host-path mount must resolve under one of them. Unset allows nothing: the host-share surface stays off until the operator lists one. Refusals give this key. The environment form is a JSON array string. virtiofsd MSKSD_VIRTIOFSD string virtiofsd Path to the virtiofsd binary each attached share spawns. A value with a slash is used exactly as given; a bare name resolves on PATH first, then the locations the distro packages install the binary at (/usr/libexec/virtiofsd, /usr/lib/qemu/virtiofsd; Debian's and Ubuntu's virtiofsd packages install it off PATH). The resolution runs at settings load and again on SIGHUP: a binary installed after the daemon started is one reload away.

items.title: The placeholder secret store
items.text:
Where the real secrets behind placeholder tokens live (secrets chapter for the flow). The store is per-recipient ciphertext blobs; plaintext returns only through an operator's unlock when the first store operation finds it absent.

Key Environment variable Type Default What it does secret_store_unlock_timeout_s MSKSD_SECRET_STORE_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT_S float 86400.0 How long unlocked plaintext lives in the daemon's cache after the unlock POST that supplied it; the timer resets on an unlock itself: websocket traffic and keepalives never extend it. Zero holds plaintext only while at least one operator websocket stays connected: the last disconnect drops it, and an unlock over HTTP alone holds nothing past the reply. llm_port MSKSD_LLM_PORT int 8770 The port each workspace's LLM proxy listener binds on its tap. llm_models MSKSD_LLM_MODELS string/list "" The model list: provider/model:api_base:api_key entries, comma-separated strings, or the file's list of strings and LiteLLM-native dicts; see docs/llm.md. llm_api_key MSKSD_LLM_API_KEY string "" A default key for entries that give none; file:/cmd: indirection works.

items.title: SIGHUP reload
items.text:
Send SIGHUP to a running msksd and it re-reads the config file (and the environment) into its live settings. Subsystems read settings off the app's state at call time, so the swap propagates with no per-module reconfiguration: a changed egress_subnet or host_name applies to the next request that reads it.

Several things keep their startup values until a restart. A reload that gives a new one changes nothing:

  • the listener's address, port, TLS material, and access logging, all bound at startup; the access log is also snapshotted into the listener's config
  • state_dir and the database path it places: the engine is open, and the local driver resolves every workspace's artifacts from the state dir live, so the daemon latches the startup value (moving it mid-run would orphan running workspaces)
  • default_image (imported into the catalog once, at first boot)
  • the watcher scan's event_poll_s (sampled at loop start): both the workspace status reconcile and the state-disk pressure probe use it
  • the egress machinery's startup inputs. egress_enabled latches the subsystem's state when the daemon boots. The base NAT masquerade's egress_uplink also latches: per-workspace firewall rules read the live setting, but the base table that actually masquerades out the uplink keeps its startup value, so change egress_uplink only with a restart scheduled.

One reload does re-stamp the base table. A change that alters the LLM proxy's loopback guard shape (llm_models gaining or losing entries, llm_port, egress_subnet) re-applies the table at the next workspace start, masquerade included, from the live egress_uplink.

mount_host_roots reads live after a reload: each workspace's next start derives its attachments from the roots the reload left. A root the reload removed reads as a skip at start (the mounts chapter gives the skip behavior); running VMs keep the devices they attached. virtiofsd reads live too: the next start spawns the binary the reload gives.

A config that fails to load or validate is refused: the daemon reports the error on stderr and keeps the previous settings. A default-path file deleted since startup is likewise refused rather than regenerated, because a reload is not a first run and regenerating the template would silently revert every file-set value to its default.

items.title: Development environment
items.text:
Msks uses devenv as development environment. A checkout of this repository presets, seeds, and runs for development via devenv shell or devenv processes up. The published chapters describe the deployed product; this one describes the developer's tree: the shell, the dev daemon, the client presets, and the dev identity.

Apologies for the quality of these docs, they have not been edited carefully and probably won't make much sense except in snippets. Until they are edited into some sense, if you would like to participate in development, and need help, ask via a GitHub issue.

items.title: The dev daemon
items.text:
A development host (this repository's checkout) runs the daemon through devenv. msks-dev seeds a per-worktree state dir with its own port, token, and socket, and execs msksd through /run/wrappers/bin/msks-caps, the wrapper the host's NixOS configuration installs; on a host NixOS does not manage the script finds the setup tool's /usr/local/bin/msks-caps by itself (DEV_CAPS gives another path outright). The tool is msks-setup-debian-host on a Debian host and msks-setup-fedora-host on a Fedora host.

The same daemon is the default devenv processes up process: the manager runs scripts/dev-daemon.sh in the foreground, and Ctrl-C stops it through the daemon's own graceful path.

items.title: Developing on a macOS host
items.text:
The devenv shell carries the same edit→lint→test loop on a Mac that it carries on Linux: msks-preflight runs every commit gate (with the suite under the off-Linux coverage floor), the client talks to any daemon the Mac can reach, and the docs build renders. The daemon itself is a Linux program (it drives cloud-hypervisor on /dev/kvm), so the dev daemon, the msksd process, and the smoke tests run on a Linux host, and the msksd process is registered on Linux hosts only. On a Mac, devenv processes up exits at once (No 'processes' option defined, then No processes defined), and msks-dev refuses with a pointer back to this chapter; both refusals are the platform split working as designed, a broken devenv.nix they are not.

Two paths take a Mac to a live daemon.

items.title: The Linux dev host, from the Mac
items.text:
The daemon runs under this chapter's dev-daemon workflow on a Linux host (a dedicated dev machine or the same checkout elsewhere), and the Mac's client talks to it through an ssh tunnel: the daemon binds 127.0.0.1 and mints its certificate for that name, so the tunnel keeps verified TLS end to end.

Copy the remote worktree's dev-daemon state trio (port, bootstrap-token, msks-ca.pem) into the Mac worktree's own state dir:

mkdir -p .devenv/state/msksd
scp <linux-host>:<remote-tree>/.devenv/state/msksd/{port,bootstrap-token,msks-ca.pem} \
    .devenv/state/msksd/

The trio is exactly what The client presets reads: with the three files in place, every fresh devenv shell on the Mac exports MSKSC_URL, MSKSC_TOKEN, and MSKSC_CAFILE by itself, pointing at 127.0.0.1 and the port the port file gives. The tunnel's local side matches that port, so the preset URL arrives on the forward:

ssh -fN -L 8660:127.0.0.1:8660 <linux-host>   # 8660 = the port file's
                                               # port, both sides

A different local port works when 127.0.0.1:8660 is already spoken for (the Lima path below claims it too): forward that port instead and re-point MSKSC_URL inside the shell. The state trio's preset wins over a value exported before entry (the port file gates it), so unset or override the variable after the shell opens.

msks console reaches a running workspace from the Mac over the same trio. msks ssh and msks rsync additionally authenticate with the dev identity that created the workspace, the Linux tree's .devenv/state/msksc/identity. Copy that file over the Mac's own minted one, or point MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE at the same personal key on both hosts (see The dev identity).

items.title: The product Lima host, from a build in hand
items.text:
msks-setup-macos-host (the installation chapter's Apple Silicon section) runs msksd inside its own Lima VM on the Mac and writes the client config: an end-to-end daemon with no separate Linux host. The tool installs the PyPI release matching its own version; --wheel installs a build from this tree instead:

devenv --quiet shell -- uv build                 # dist/msks-<version>-py3-none-any.whl
devenv --quiet shell -- msks-setup-macos-host --wheel dist/msks-<version>-py3-none-any.whl

The VM runs the built wheel, not the working tree: each iteration rebuilds the wheel and re-runs the tool (every phase is idempotent, and the daemon restarts through its systemd unit). Use this path to verify a change end to end on the Mac itself; the Linux dev host above stays the faster inner loop.

items.title: The daemon's config file
items.text: The dev daemon runs bare: scripts/dev-daemon.sh points MSKSD_CONFIG_DIR at the devenv root. The daemon's durable settings therefore live in <repo>/msksd.yaml, generated as the commented template on first daemon start and untracked, so local edits stay personal. The environment the dev script exports (API port, state dir, egress wiring) wins over file values under the precedence the Configuration chapter documents.

items.title: The client presets
items.text:
The devenv shell presets the client's connection to the worktree's own dev daemon. Once the dev daemon has served once, a fresh devenv shell needs no exports: the token and CA come from the dev-daemon state dir, .devenv/state/msksd/:

msks ls        # presets: https://127.0.0.1:8660, the worktree's
               # token, and .devenv/state/msksd/msks-ca.pem
               # (verified TLS)

The same shell presets MSKSC_CACHE_DIR at the worktree's own .devenv/state/msksc/cache/, so each checkout's client state stays its own and one tree's cache entry is never read by another. A non-empty value exported before entering the shell survives the preset; an empty one counts as unset.

Targeting a hand-run bare-host daemon instead (no managed process; msks-dev-ready then msksd from a shell) takes the explicit pair from its state, with its own CA:

export MSKSC_URL=https://127.0.0.1:8660
export MSKSC_TOKEN=$(cat .devenv/state/msksd/bootstrap-token)
export MSKSC_CAFILE=.devenv/state/msksd/msks-ca.pem

items.title: The dev identity
items.text: A checkout's devenv shell presets MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE at the worktree's own dev identity (.devenv/state/msksc/identity), minted passphrase-less the first time the shell opens, so the smokes and msks-dev have a key without touching yours. The preset fills an unset variable: a non-empty MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE you exported before entering the shell survives, and so does the file's identity_file (the environment preset lands only when you gave nothing). Pointing the dev identity at your own key (a symlink over the minted file) works, with the identity chapter's rules: the passphrase prompt appears when the daemon's rows are locked under it and no agent holds it. See The key files.

items.title: Doctor on the dev host
items.text: The dev daemon runs bare: scripts/dev-daemon.sh points MSKSD_CONFIG_DIR at the devenv root. A hand-run msksd doctor in the shell therefore resolves the same <repo>/msksd.yaml the daemon serves with. The environment the dev script exports (API port, state dir, egress wiring) wins over file values under the precedence the Configuration chapter documents.

items.title: Development
items.text:
Install nix and devenv on any Linux host (a NixOS host is not required). Enter the environment (Python 3.14, uv venv, cloud-hypervisor + ch-remote, qemu, the pytest toolchain, xenon):

devenv shell

All scripted/CI invocations disable dotenv loading:

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- <command>

Run the test suite the way CI runs it (-n auto is never optional; see AGENTS.md for the coverage story):

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- unit-tests

Scoped iteration picks only tests whose coverage touches changed lines:

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- testmon

Complexity gate (also runs as a pre-commit hook):

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks-xenon

The Python-side pre-commit gates' full offender list in one pass: all ruff and deferred-import findings, every xenon offender, and the jscpd report, plus (when sources under src/msks/ changed) every missing coverage line and branch arc for the changed files after one gated suite run:

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks-preflight

items.title: Build outputs
items.text:
The release artifacts each build on their own store path, without evaluating or building the others:

devenv build outputs.server        # msksd with the full daemon closure
devenv build outputs.client        # the msks CLI/TUI with the client closure alone
devenv build outputs.guest-image-debian  # the Debian workspace image archive
devenv build outputs.guest-image-nixos  # the NixOS workspace image archive

The daemon and client outputs are two dependency closures over the one wheel (nix/msks-pkg.nix, nix/msks-client-pkg.nix): the server output runs msksd; the client output runs msks and msks-term-popup. The same outputs build from the flake with plain nix (no devenv in the environment) against the same pinned nixpkgs (flake.lock and devenv.lock pin the same revision, so each flake attribute is the same store path its devenv build twin builds):

nix build .#server .#client .#guest-image-debian .#guest-image-nixos

items.title: Wheel installs
items.text: The msks wheel is pure Python on every platform: nothing compiles at install time. Egress consent is the one runtime library need: the daemon's vendored NFQUEUE binding loads libnetfilter_queue.so.1 by soname, so a daemon host with interactive egress carries the runtime package (libnetfilter-queue1 on apt, libnetfilter_queue on dnf and pacman, libnetfilter_queue1 on zypper, libnetfilter_queue on apk). A host without it boots workspaces without egress and refuses an egress boot by name. msksd doctor gives the package for the detected package manager when the load fails.

items.title: VM guest assets
items.text:
The workspace guest is Debian 13 (trixie), straight from Debian's official genericcloud cloud image: systemd as PID 1, apt, cloud-init, and Debian's own kernel, initrd, and modules, booted directly (no BIOS/UEFI) by cloud-hypervisor. The image is pinned by its dated cloud.debian.org URL and sha512, and the build turns it into the msks boot contract (vmlinux (Debian's bzImage, CONFIG_PVH=y), initrd, a pristine ext4 base rootfs, and guest-manifest.json) with a small overlay of msks systemd units (vsock console, serial autologin, the /home mount, the cloud-init dropins that pin NoCloud and keep cloud-init off the guest's networking). Extraction is fully unprivileged: qemu-img convert, partition slice, debugfs rdump, mke2fs -d. Measured boot on bare-metal KVM: the vsock shell prompt at ~2.8s, the serial login prompt at ~7.5-8.6s against a <5s interactive goal. Root writes persist through the per-workspace overlay, and /home is the workspace's own ext4 volume; apt reaches the upstream through the workspace's egress NIC, served by the daemon's consent stack whenever the daemon holds CAP_NET_ADMIN. The repack runs under fakeroot so the image is root-owned with sane password-file modes, and the setuid binaries the workspace user's sudo needs pass through the same fakeroot session as uid-0 inodes. Stopping a workspace presses the ACPI power button (vm.power-button): the guest's systemd-logind runs the clean poweroff that flushes its persistent disks.

Every step of the build runs inside the repo on any Linux host with nix:

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks-build-guest

The artifacts (plus a guest-manifest.json describing them and the boot cmdline) are written to .devenv/state/guest/ (relocatable with GUEST_DIR). Boot one interactive VM from them with:

msks-demo-vm

It attaches the guest's serial console to your terminal (poweroff -f inside the guest or Ctrl-C stops it) and leaves ch-remote reachable on the printed API socket path.

Boot tests self-provision: when .devenv/state/guest/ holds built artifacts and /dev/kvm is usable, the smoke tests find them without any exported variables (TEST_VMLINUX / TEST_INITRD / TEST_ROOTFS / TEST_CMDLINE keep precedence when you do export them). When the artifacts were never built, or /dev/kvm is missing or not accessible to your user (add yourself to the kvm group, users.users.<name>.extraGroups = [ "kvm" ]; on NixOS, then re-login), the smoke tests skip themselves.

items.title: Running the daemon (msksd)
items.text:
devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell --
MSKSD_STATE_DIR=/tmp/msksd MSKSD_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN=dev-secret MSKSD_PORT=8660 msksd
  • Trust: with no MSKSD_TLS_CERT/MSKSD_TLS_KEY, msksd generates a self-signed CA + certificate into the state dir on first run and logs the CA fingerprint: pin it on first connect (trust-on-first-use, like SSH). The CA key lives beside the database under the state dir.
  • First credential: MSKSD_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN seeds one bearer token, inserted once when absent; it is visible in the process environment to the same user (acceptable for a single-user local daemon; unset it after minting real tokens). --no-tls serves plain HTTP for development.
  • Events: wss://host/api/v1/events streams workspace status transitions. The websocket handshake authenticates with the same Authorization: Bearer header the REST surface uses, so the token never appears in a URL. Uvicorn's access log prints request lines (method, path, query) and not headers, so turning it on (MSKSD_ACCESS_LOG=true) does not persist credentials. A bad token closes the websocket with code 4401.
  • Rotating the bootstrap token: setting MSKSD_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN to a new value adds a token; the previous bootstrap credential stays valid until revoked via the API.
  • Config file: settings also live in a YAML file: msksd --config /path/to/msksd.yaml reads exactly that file, --config=none reads env vars only, and a bare msksd resolves $MSKSD_CONFIG_DIR/msksd.yaml (default ~/.config/msksd/msksd.yaml), generating a commented template on first run. Env vars override the file; see docs/config.md for the key-by-key reference.
  • Schema: the SQLite database is created and upgraded by Alembic at startup (inside the package: msks/migrations).

items.title: The dev daemon (the default processes up)
items.text:
msksd runs FIRST-LEVEL on the dev host (cloud-hypervisor on the real /dev/kvm, per-VM taps, the egress consent stack in the host kernel) through the msks-caps capability wrapper the host's NixOS config installs. devenv processes up runs it attached in the foreground (Ctrl-C stops it, workspaces get their stop cycle); msks-dev runs the same script by hand in a terminal. Each worktree state dir (.devenv/state/msksd, MSKSD_STATE_DIR relocates) seeds its own bootstrap token, API port, and port-derived egress subnet, so concurrent worktrees run one daemon each; a state-dir lock refuses a second daemon on the same catalog. The client presets below land in every devenv shell. (An older hand-run flow without KVM, msks-dev-ready, still exists for API/client-only work:)

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks-dev-ready
export MSKSD_STATE_DIR="$PWD/.devenv/state/msksd" MSKSD_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN="$(cat .devenv/state/msksd/bootstrap-token)"
msksd &                                    # serves https://127.0.0.1:8660
MSKSC_URL=https://127.0.0.1:8660 MSKSC_CAFILE=$PWD/.devenv/state/msksd/msks-ca.pem \
  MSKSC_TOKEN="$(cat .devenv/state/msksd/bootstrap-token)" msks ls

The state lives in .devenv/state/msksd/ (TLS CA, bootstrap token, sqlite catalog, workspace volumes). The dir honors MSKSD_STATE_DIR: export it before msks-dev-ready to relocate it, as an absolute path. The script anchors a relative value below the repo root while the daemon resolves one against its own CWD, so only an absolute value moves both to the same place. Gitignored but NOT disposable-clean: git clean -xfd deletes all of it, along with the dev daemon's personal msksd.yaml at the repo root. Egress (and msks ssh, whose forwards travel the egress NIC) needs CAP_NET_ADMIN: the dev host's wrapper grants it, so egress workspaces run first-level; on a host without the grant a workspace created without --no-egress refuses to start (the 503 gives MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED, and the fix is --no-egress or the host config in nix/module.nix). Daemon edits restart with Ctrl-C and re-run (--reload restarts on tree change).

Known quirk: cloud-hypervisor v52 rejects writes to sector 0 on disks without an explicit image_type (a QCOW2 misdetection guard), which breaks any guest writing an ext4 superblock: every disk the daemon creates declares image_type: Raw.

items.title: The image catalog
items.text:
Images are plural: msksd holds a catalog under <state_dir>/images/, every registered archive keyed by content hash, with the boot files unpacked once per hash (workspace launches never unpack anything). The whole /api/v1 surface is its own chapter; these curls are the import and list forms:

curl -sk -H "authorization: Bearer $MSKSC_TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"source": "/nix/store/...-msks-guest/workspace-debian-13.6.tar"}' \
  https://127.0.0.1:8660/api/v1/images        # import
curl -sk -H "authorization: Bearer $MSKSC_TOKEN" \
  https://127.0.0.1:8660/api/v1/images        # list (name/version/hash/default)

A workspace create selects an image by reference: "image": "debian:13.6" (or a bare name for its newest version, or a hash); with no image and no explicit artifacts the designated default resolves. The first import becomes the default; MSKSD_DEFAULT_IMAGE points the daemon at an archive to import on first boot, and the dev daemon seeds it from its state dir's default-image symlink (msks-build-guest-archive converges it), so a bare POST /workspaces works on a fresh daemon with nothing else imported. Explicit kernel/rootfs fields still win over the catalog (the shape the tests and dev flows use).

items.title: The client CLI (msks ls, msks create, msks start, msks stop, msks rm)
items.text:
The client also covers the non-interactive half of the operator flow:

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks ls
devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks create my-workspace --start

msks ls prints one line per workspace (name, id, status, image hash, host); --json prints one JSON document for scripting. A workspace carries two identity fields: the name you choose at create (the label every command addresses it by) and the id the daemon mints, immutable and never reused, keying the artifact paths and the client caches; either reference reaches the same workspace.

msks create POSTs the same body the API accepts: --image picks a catalog reference, --cpus/--mem-mib/--root-mib/ --home-mib size the VM, --user-data attaches a first-boot provisioning script (a cidata seed disk the guest's provisioner runs once), and explicit --kernel/--rootfs (with optional --initrd, --cmdline) bypass the catalog. --start boots the workspace right after creating it, so msks create ws --start then msks console ws is the two-step path from nothing to a shell. msks start <ws> boots an existing workspace later, msks stop <ws> powers one off (a graceful, deadline-bounded shutdown; the data survives), msks rm <ws>… deletes one or more workspaces together with their persistent root overlay and /home volume, msks console <ws> boots one itself when the daemon reports it as not running (a notice prints on stderr while the boot runs), and msks home export/import <ws> moves the whole /home volume through the daemon for backup, migration, and seeding. All commands use the same MSKSC_URL/MSKSC_TOKEN/MSKSC_CAFILE environment as msks console; failures (unreachable daemon, timed-out request, bad token, API or validation errors) print one readable line instead of a traceback. See docs/cli.md for the full command and environment reference.

items.title: Workspace egress networking
items.text:
Workspaces are networked from creation, and the whole path lives in the daemon's own net stack. msks create ws, or a bare "id" on the API, boots with egress; msks create ws --no-egress (or "egress": false) boots NIC-less:

workspace VM ──virtio-net──► per-VM tap ──► per-VM nftables chain
                                                │  guest → uplink: accept
                                                ▼
                                     NAT (masquerade) → host uplink

The daemon is the guest's only DHCP server and resolver: each egress workspace gets a dedicated /30 from MSKSD_EGRESS_SUBNET, a DHCP offer that gives the tap as gateway and resolver, a small DNS forwarder on that resolver, and NAT out the host's uplink (MSKSD_EGRESS_UPLINK). Everything derives deterministically from the workspace id, so stop/start cycles rebuild the same network; stop and delete tear the tap, chain, and services down again. The guest side is just the image's DHCP client (systemd-networkd + resolved in the overlay); a workspace without egress presents no NIC, on every backend.

Egress arms while MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED=true and the daemon holds CAP_NET_ADMIN: the dev host's wrapper grants the capability, and nix/module.nix does the same for a deployment host. A daemon that cannot arm the plumbing still serves everything else, and an egress workspace refuses to boot with the cause given (boot those with --no-egress). See docs/networking.md for the full reference.

items.title: The docs site
items.text:
The documentation builds into a static site (the same build the Deploy Docs workflow publishes to GitHub Pages on every push to main and every release tag). Preview it locally. The preview serves whatever the checkout holds (the current branch's docs, so edits review against the tree that will ship), and while it runs, every edit to the chapters or the site config re-renders the open tab in realtime:

devenv shell
msks-docs              # serves http://127.0.0.1:8923/ live

DOCS_SERVE_PORT relocates the port. The chapters live under docs/; the TUI chapter's screen renderings regenerate with RENDER_DOCS_SCREENS=1 pytest -q src/msks/tests/test_render_docs_screens.py.

items.title: The workspace LLM proxy
items.text: Each workspace's tap carries its own proxy service when the daemon is configured for it: an OpenAI-shaped proxy (/v1/models, /v1/chat/completions, streaming included) served by msksd at MSKSD_LLM_PORT, admitted by that workspace's input chain from that tap only, and authenticated by a per-workspace credential the first-boot seed plants (/etc/msks/llm.token plus the MSKSWS_BASE_URL/MSKSWS_API_KEY exports). Provider credentials live host-side: MSKSD_LLM_MODELS entries with file:/cmd: secret indirection, a single * entry for single-upstream passthrough, any other list through the litellm router. See docs/llm.md.

items.title: Developing msks inside a workspace
items.text:
The dev-workspace bootstrap seed turns a pristine Debian workspace into an msks development environment over the workspace's own egress NIC. One create with the seed and egress is the whole of the setup: the image catalog serves the pristine Debian base unchanged:

msks create dev --egress --user-data scripts/dev-workspace.sh \
  --mem-mib 8192 --root-mib 20480   # the in-guest suite's budget
msks start dev   # first boot provisions; later boots resume

Cloud-init runs the seed once per overlay lifetime: it installs uv (which fetches its own Python 3.14), clones the repo, and runs uv sync, all into the persistent root overlay, so stop/start cycles keep it and a factory reset re-provisions from the same seed. Every step checks before doing, so re-running the script is a no-op. Progress is guest-observable in /root/.msks-bootstrap/state (the running step name, then done), so msks console into a booting workspace shows where setup stands. The suite runs inside the guest the way the unit-tests task runs it: the task's exec line, from the venv uv built:

msks console dev
uv run python -m pytest src/msks/tests -v -n auto

devenv and nix remain an optional developer comfort inside the guest, off the seed's critical path: building them there exercises upstream toolchains for tens of minutes and gigabytes and tests nothing msks owns.

The seed's downloads (PyPI, uv's Python builds, the git remote) all travel the egress NIC the daemon serves. The end-to-end proof is the opt-in root smoke test_local_dev_workspace_bootstrap (TEST_EGRESS=1). A baked dev image (the same substrate the guest build uses) remains an optional cold-start accelerator on top of the seed, not a prerequisite.

The workspace's whole /home also moves through the daemon: msks home export dev streams the volume to the client's machine (backup, or migration to another daemon), and msks home import restores or seeds one from an exported image:

msks stop dev
msks home export dev - | gzip > dev-home.ext4.gz   # whole-home backup

Day-to-day code in and out travels the workspace's own egress (git remotes, substitutes) and the forward seam (msks ssh, and msks rsync dev -- -av ./src/ :src/ for file copies, with no setup beyond the client environment). Outbound, the push carries its own credentials: logging in through the forward with -A delivers the operator's ssh agent into the workspace, so a git push from inside authenticates to any remote over the egress NIC with nothing stored in the image or the seed (the loop and its proof, test_local_egress_git_out, are in docs/networking.md). See docs/storage.md for the byte-stream endpoints and their contract.

items.title: The workspace console (msks console)
items.text:
An interactive shell in a running workspace, from any host that can reach the daemon:

devenv --quiet -O dotenv.enable:bool false shell -- msks console my-workspace

A devenv shell presets MSKSC_URL/MSKSC_TOKEN/MSKSC_CAFILE from the worktree's dev-daemon state; an outside shell exports the same trio by hand (the URL from the daemon's log line, the token and CA from .devenv/state/msksd/).

The client speaks the daemon's console websocket (/api/v1/workspaces/{id}/console): TLS plus bearer token, the same authentication as the REST surface, with the token on the query string (like /api/v1/events). Ctrl-] detaches (Ctrl-C and Ctrl-D reach the guest); pressing Ctrl-] twice quickly sends one literal Ctrl-] to the guest instead (see docs/cli.md). The session ends cleanly when either side closes. Detaching leaves the workspace running; the shell process inside the guest exits when the stream closes.

Transport, in the preferred vsock-first shape:

  • The workspace VM boots with a virtio-vsock device whose host side is a unix socket cloud-hypervisor listens on (<state>/vms/<id>/vsock.sock). The daemon's proxy connects, sends CONNECT 1023\n, reads the OK <port>\n reply, then pumps raw bytes both ways: no framing; backpressure is websocket/TCP flow control.
  • The guest loads vmw_vsock_virtio_transport (systemd-modules-load) and runs msks-console.service: the msks console helper (/usr/bin/msks-console-helper, a static binary the image builds from src/console-helper), restarted by systemd if it dies. The helper owns the vsock listener, accepts host-originated connections only, and each connection negotiates the identity prelude: the daemon sends the requested user, the client terminal's size and TERM, and the helper answers MSKS OK <user> (or a named refusal) before exec'ing that user's login shell on a fresh pty. The pty is a plain canonical terminal: ISIG, ONLCR, ECHO, and ICANON all on. Ctrl-C generates SIGINT in the guest, output arrives CRLF-terminated, and the line discipline echoes and edits input for programs that read stdin directly. The shell's TERM comes from the client's terminal, so readline engages and provides line editing and history while it is active; a TERM=dumb client gets readline off. The session's user is root by default; msks console --user <name> requests the image's workspace user (users the image does not serve are refused by name).
  • The guest pty is created at the client terminal's size (not a fixed 0x0): the console request carries the geometry at connect, and the pty keeps that size for the session's life. The console stream is a raw byte pipe by design, so a window resized mid-session does not reach it: reconnect for a new size, or use an ssh session through the forward, where ssh's window-change channel resizes the pty live. If console resize ever returns to the queue, it starts with a control-channel decision: a dedicated vsock control port, or another design that keeps the stream raw.
  • MSKSC_CAFILE pins the daemon certificate for verification when you have it (the dev daemon writes msks-ca.pem into its state dir on first serve). Without it the client proceeds with certificate verification off and says so on stderr; the CA fingerprint the daemon logs at startup is the cross-check.

items.title: The VZ virtiofs hardlink landmine
items.text: The macOS host-share design passes host folders to workspace guests over virtiofs twice, and the first hop (Apple's VZ virtiofs server) carried a known instability through macOS 14: creating a hardlink sometimes renumbered the original file's synthetic inode, and the Linux guest's dentry cache went stale (link()/stat() returning ENOENT for files that exist). Docker Desktop answered with a private fs/fuse patch in its VM; the patch never mainlined. The decision for msks: the msksd VM keeps the stock Debian kernel. The instability is no longer reproducible on macOS 15 per the upstream report, and the suite runs clean on macOS 27; the unstable releases sit below the macOS floor the feature needs anyway (Lima refuses nested virtualization, which workspaces require, on older macOS). No stock-kernel mount knob exists that approximates the patch. And UTM shares the same VZ server on its Apple backend, while its QEMU backend's only POSIX-filesystem transport is 9p (directory sharing there is SPICE WebDAV or 9p), the transport every msks Lima template keeps out (mountTypesUnsupported: [9p], a deliberate msks choice Lima's default does not make; the suite ships its own template). The evidence, the re-run procedure, and the escape hatch (the Docker patch carried in a custom kernel, should a future macOS regress) live in the suite's README under scripts/vz-hardlink-repro/; re-run the suite on new macOS releases before shipping rw shares.

items.title: The two-hop virtiofs landmine
items.text:
The second hop of the host-share design, the msksd VM exporting a VZ virtiofs mount into workspace VMs through virtiofsd, is territory no shipping product covers (NFS-serving a virtiofs mount is broken upstream). The scripts/hop2-virtiofsd-suite/ rig builds the real stack (a nested cloud-hypervisor guest whose virtiofs share is the outer VM's rw virtiofs mount) and runs the seven workloads. All pass on stock Debian (virtiofsd 1.13.2, cloud-hypervisor v54, macOS 27): listings are byte-identical across the hop, link/unlink churn is clean, inodes from hop 1 pass through verbatim, a 40k-file tree leaves virtiofsd holding 6 fds, a mid-write kill of the daemon and VMM leaves every file that landed complete, and cross-writer file visibility stays in the milliseconds once a responder is live (the first response after publishing one runs ~1.5s while the guest consumes its command).

Two findings shape the design: cloud-hypervisor's userspace vhost-user master is what makes hop 2 possible on the stock kernel (Debian's cloud kernel builds no /dev/vhost-vfs, so a QEMU-shaped hop 2 would need a custom kernel), and ownership collapses to root across both hops (macOS uid 501 → 0 → 0), which the single-writer contract already covers. The suite's README carries the evidence table, the re-run procedure, and the marker-file protocol for cross-VM signaling on a share.

items.title: The host doctor
items.text:
msksd doctor checks the host for the tools and libraries the daemon and the client exec at runtime. Every reported issue suggests a fix.

Note that msksd doctor is not very useful on macOS: use msks-setup-macos-host --check instead.

msksd doctor

The command takes the same --config flag the daemon takes. It checks the tools this host's daemon will actually exec: the config's tool paths and environment apply.

items.title: What it checks
items.text:
The checks cover runtime needs only: the external dependencies, the cloud-hypervisor VMM, and a few configuration settings.

Tool names resolve on the daemon's search path, not the caller's. The session's own PATH answers first. Then come admin directories (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/sbin, /sbin), because the systemd user manager's default PATH carries them. A session whose PATH lacks these directories still gets the daemon's truth.

When a tool was found only through the admin directories, the run adds a warning. Its fix is to log out and back in (the setup tool adds the directories to ~/.profile), or to run export PATH=$PATH:/usr/sbin:/sbin. A daemon started by hand inherits the session's PATH, so the fix reaches that shape too.

items.title: Reading the report
items.text:
Every row prints with a marker:

  • ✓: present and functional. The binary answered its version probe, the library answered one of its three probes, the binding loaded.
  • ⚠: a warning-grade miss. The daemon does not need this path (the ssh/rsync pair), or a config failed to load.
  • ✗: an error-grade miss. The daemon needs this dependency on a core path.

Each miss carries an install hint matched to the detected package manager, printed as a paste-ready command sequence under the row. The hints use each manager's real package names: genisoimage serves mkisofs, and qemu-utils ships qemu-img.

Some fixes are not distro packages. Where that is so, the hint gives the real source: cloud-hypervisor installs from the upstream static release.

The run ends with a tally (14 passed, or 12 passed, 1 error, 1 warning). When anything failed, a closing block repeats every miss with its fix. The exit code is 0 when every check passes or only warns, and 1 when any check errors.

items.title: Egress consent
items.text:
The consent layer decides, per workspace, whether each new outbound connection is allowed. It uses the per-VM chain the guest networking chapter describes.

The TUI includes a consent decider UI, which allows the user to approve or deny an egress request. Another decider is present in the msks-term-popup UI. A different CLI version of decision is implemented via msks egress.

items.title: The consent mode
items.text:
A workspace picks its consent mode at create time (for example, via msks create --egress-mode). The command msks egress mode switches it afterwards (see switching modes live). Every decider offers a way to switch modes.

The mode decides where each new outbound connection is decided. There are three available modes:

  • allow (the create default). New requests pass. The daemon's resolver records each off-allowlist name the guest looks up.
  • static. The workspace's allowlist is the policy. Allowlisted names resolve through the daemon's resolver, and their addresses are pinned as allowed in the kernel chain for the answer's TTL. For example, apt update against an allowlist of .deb.debian.org might complete with no prompt and no hold. A name not on the allowlist answers NXDOMAIN and the denial is recorded as an audit row. Address-range entries (eg. 10.0.0.0/8, 203.0.113.7:5432) accept in the chain directly.
  • interactive. The first packet of every new flow queues to the workspace's own queue inside the host kernel. msksd holds it until a decider answers.

items.title: Deciders
items.text:
A decider is any authenticated client that announced itself on the events websocket, like the egress consent page of the TUI shown in the image above or msks egress watch <workspace>. New holds wait for a decider only while at least one is connected: the connection is the liveness signal. A hold created before the last decider left still runs its timeout.

Without a decider, a connect against an off-allowlist destination fails fast. The prompt shows the DNS name (e.g. api.anthropic.com:443). The resolver is the one the DHCP lease hands the guest. It remembers which name resolved to which address. A destination given by address prompts with the address itself, and its verdict keys on the address.

Here's a visualisation of the egress networking configuration:

workspace VM ──virtio-net──► tap ──► per-VM nftables chain
                                  │  ESTABLISHED → accept (conntrack)
                                  │  allowlist / prior verdicts → accept
                                  │  NEW → NFQUEUE ──► msksd consent engine
                                  │                        │ verdict
                                  │                        ▼
                                  │             accept + pin / drop + RST
                                  ▼                        / expire
                                NAT → host uplink

The decision table matches the resolver gate's precedence: a standing deny first, then the static allowlist (name specs against the gated name, address specs against the original destination), then a standing allow, then the mode.

Under static, the denial is recorded and the answer is a local HTTP 403. Under interactive, the flow holds through the consent engine, and the same decider endpoints answer the same rows the kernel queue writes. An allow completes the handshake.

A deny answers the 403 locally, and nothing forwards. The 403's body says what happened: consent denied the destination; a decision is already pending (the flow lost the duplicate race); no decider answered (none registered, or the request expired undecided); or the request ended without a decision (the gate failed, the prompt cap refused the hold, or the workspace vanished, stopped, or switched mode mid-hold).

Verdicts and durations are shared: one allow in any decider covers the destination's web flows and its other ports alike.

msks egress revoke therefore stops a destination's next connection and its first plain request on a fresh connection. Connections that already carry consent (established TLS, or a plain connection that already answered that destination) keep it until they close. The kernel path additionally kills established flows with their conntrack entries. The interceptor's connections have no conntrack entry to kill.

items.title: Verdicts and durations
items.text:
Deciders record allow/deny with a duration: once (this connection only; a reconnect re-prompts), 5m, 15m, tilrestart (until the msks VM stops; the default), forever (the workspace's lifetime, replayed at every boot). An allow pins the destination in the kernel for its duration and covers the name.

A decider revoking a verdict undoes an in-effect verdict at once. The destination's live connections die with their conntrack entries (on a shared address that includes the co-resident's), and new connections gate again.

Every row (request, verdict, expiry, revocation) is written to the consent table with its provenance. Rows are pruned past MSKSD_EGRESS_CONSENT_RETENTION_DAYS and the per-workspace MSKSD_EGRESS_CONSENT_ROW_CAP. With MSKSD_AUDIT_HMAC_KEY set, each row also carries an HMAC-SHA256 tag over its columns.

items.title: Switching modes live
items.text:
msks egress mode <ws> <mode> [--allow SPEC]... (or m in the decider TUI or msks-term-popup) moves a workspace between the three postures without recreating it. The row's mode and allowlist change at once. A running workspace swaps its whole per-VM table in one nft transaction (the same maneuver the interceptor's arm/disarm uses). The consent elements (verdict pins, resolver-learned allows) carry across. Established connections survive the switch, and an attached msks ssh session stays up. A stopped workspace builds the new posture at its next start.

The switch keeps three invariants:

  • The queue never dangles. Entering interactive binds the workspace's NFQUEUE consumer before the chain references the queue. Leaving it installs the queue-less table first and unbinds the consumer after. An unbound queue drops, so the order is the whole rule.
  • Held requests answer. A switch away from interactive fail-closes every hold the workspace still owns: the held SYNs answer deny at once, rather than waiting out the timeout against a queue that no longer exists.
  • Verdicts carry. The consent rows survive every switch, and enforcement follows the current mode: an allow forever granted under interactive keeps acting under static. Name-keyed verdicts act at the resolver, and address-keyed ones are re-pinned into the fresh table's sets. static after an interactive session is therefore the frozen consent set: everything approved so far, and nothing else. The pins rebuild from the rows across a direct gated→gated switch and at every gated entry. A round-trip through allow re-pins the forever rows. A timed address-keyed allow re-prompts or re-learns on the guest's next resolution.

A switch to static starts answering off-list names with NXDOMAIN mid-session, and the guest's cached answers run out on their own TTLs. A switch to static with nothing effectively allowed (an empty allowlist and no in-effect allowed verdict) is refused.

items.title: First run
items.text: After the installation process has resulted in a running msksd systemd user service, it's almost ready to use. But you need to supply your ssh keypair and import at least one image used as a base for workspace creation before you can succesfully create one.

items.title: Make sure it's running
items.text:
Before trying to connect to msksd via the client, make sure it's running.

On Linux, to see status and log output from the account the daemon runs as (the service is a systemd user unit):

  systemctl --user status msksd
  journalctl --user -u msksd -f          # follow the daemon's log

On macOS, do the following (the daemon runs inside the Lima VM, as a systemd system unit):

  limactl shell msksd -- systemctl status msksd
  limactl shell msksd -- sudo journalctl -u msksd -f   # follow the daemon's log

When msksd is first started on Linux (or within the Lima VM that runs Linux on Mac), it creates a state dir (~/.local/state/msksd). The msksd.yaml config file is generated within it as a commented template (see Configuration).

The unix listener binds $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/msks/msksd.sock. Same-host Linux clients connect through it on peer-credential authentication. A remote can, if configured, contact a TLS/https listener with a bearer token. That's how it works on macOS.

With the host prepared, the service lingered, and an image imported, invoking the msks (the client) on the same account will find the socket.

items.title: The key files
items.text:
You need to configure an ssh key before msksd/msks will work properly.

Every workspace msks uses your public ssh key as the workspace's operator identity.

Every msks ssh and msks rsync session uses your private half.

msks also allows you to manage secrets for workspaces. The same ssh key locks workspace secrets on the daemon: values a workspace needs at runtime are sealed under the identity, and the client unlocks them with the private half again.

The client names the key in its YAML file (~/.config/msks/msks.yaml) or its environment, with two keys:

identity_file: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # the private half
pubkey_file: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # the public half

If your identity is typically in your ssh agent, you needn't specify the identity-file, just the pubkey_file. But it's more foolproof to specify both at first.

items.title: identity_file: the private half
items.text:
identity_file names your private key file, read in place. msks derives the public half from it at create, and the key file is never copied into msks's state

But session resolution consults your own ssh-agent first. When SSH_AUTH_SOCK names a live agent holding that key, every session signs through the agent and the file's encryption stops mattering. The match is on key material, so the file it came from and its name do not matter (ssh-add it). If your key is saved in your ssh-agent, you needn't name the private half of your key in msks config, only the public one (pubkey_file), and the private half need not be on disk.

If your ssh key is not already in an agent, a key no agent holds is staged in memory as an unencrypted OpenSSH-format key (ed25519, ecdsa P-256/P-384/P-521, or rsa). msks never types a passphrase.

A passphrase-encrypted identity_file raises the session's one passphrase prompt when the daemon's locked secret rows need it. The TUI asks once when the tree opens, and the answer unlocks every locked secret row for the session. Escape or Cancel leaves the secrets locked. They stay named on the secrets page and re-askable there.

items.title: pubkey_file: the public half
items.text:
pubkey_file names a .pub file, and a create with it set plants that one line as the workspace's identity and reads no private material at all. This is the form for a key you keep encrypted on disk: the public half sits in the .pub file while the private half answers from your agent.

msks console will wok to access a wokspace if you've lost your key.

items.title: Where the private half lives at runtime
items.text:
An agent-held key stays in the agent: msks asks it to sign, and the file on disk is never opened. A key msks stages itself runs in a transient in-process agent that dies with the session. And a session you forward your agent into (ssh_options with -A) carries the agent you named into the workspace. The workspace identity msks mints stays separate, and your keys arrive only where you forwarded them.

With neither key naming a usable source, msks create refuses with a line saying so. It is the one command that needs the identity at its start.

items.title: Importing a guest VM image
items.text:
On first run, a workspace image has not been imported, so you are not able to create guest VMs. A workspace image arrives either from the published channel (msks image import in the TUI, or the images chapter's URL form) or from a local build.

These images are hosted on github, and the TUI enumerates them for you and allows you to import one. There are currently Debian, Fedora and NixOS guest images corresponding with the most recent msks release.

items.title: Workspace images
items.text:
A workspace image is one file, a container-image tar: the layout podman load and skopeo already understand. It carries a kernel, an initrd, a rootfs disk, and a manifest that describes all three. This chapter covers the image contract, how to build one, how to check one, how to register it with a running daemon, and how workspaces select an image.

msksd boots the kernel directly and attaches the rootfs as a virtio disk. Nothing ever runs the image as a container. The container-image packaging exists so the file is inspectable and loadable by stock tooling (tar tf, podman load, skopeo copy), and so it can travel through container registries unchanged.

items.title: The image contract
items.text:
The tar follows the containerDisk convention: standard container bookkeeping (manifest.json, an image config, repositories) wrapped around a single uncompressed layer whose root carries the workspace boot files:

workspace-<name>-<version>.tar
├── manifest.json                     # container bookkeeping
├── repositories
└── <image-id>/
    ├── VERSION, json                 # container bookkeeping
    └── layer.tar                     # uncompressed; the containerDisk:
        ├── boot/vmlinuz              #   bzImage kernel
        ├── boot/initrd.img           #   initramfs
        ├── disk/rootfs.ext4          #   raw ext4 root filesystem
        └── disk/image.json           #   the manifest (below)

disk/image.json is what msksd reads; schema 2:

Field Meaning schema 2 arch The guest's architecture, a uname machine name: x86_64 or aarch64. The shipped builders always emit it. Import compares it to the host's own machine and refuses a mismatch, reporting both sides; a foreign-arch kernel would hang wordlessly at boot. An image without the field declares nothing and imports as before name Catalog name, e.g. debian version Catalog version, e.g. 13.6; numeric segments sort correctly cmdline Kernel command line for workspace boots kernel_version e.g. 6.12.107+deb13-amd64 (informational) kernel_format bzImage on x86_64, Image on aarch64 (informational) capabilities Optional capability object; provisioner names the seed consumer (below)

The manifest is self-describing: importing the archive needs nothing beside the archive itself.

items.title: What the host provides
items.text:
Every workspace artifact the guest touches is owned by msksd at runtime. The root and home volumes and the cidata seed disks are created under the state dir (MSKSD_STATE_DIR, the one relocation variable). The console reaches the guest over the virtio-console port of the VMM msksd launched. Both deployment shapes (the NixOS module and the dev daemon) deliver this without host-side scripting. The host itself provides four things, all configuration:

  • /dev/kvm, reachable through the kvm group.
  • Two ambient capabilities for msksd's service user: CAP_NET_ADMIN (taps, addresses, nftables) and CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (the DHCP and DNS listeners).
  • The egress kernel modules: tun and the nftables/NAT set, loaded at boot (the NixOS module's boot.kernelModules).
  • net.ipv4.ip_forward=1, verified by the daemon at start when egress is armed; the module ships it as a sysctl.

The daemon e2e smoke (test_smoke/test_daemon_e2e.py) drives this whole surface against a real msksd process: the image boots, serves its console, and reaches the outside exactly as this section describes.

items.title: What a guest must provide
items.text:
The rootfs and kernel together decide whether a workspace actually boots. A guest image must:

  • Boot a kernel with direct-kernel boot support. cloud-hypervisor loads the kernel and initrd itself and passes cmdline; the guest never runs its own bootloader. Stock Debian/Ubuntu kernels work (a bzImage on x86_64, an Image on aarch64).
  • Serve a root getty on the serial console. msks console bridges the client to the guest's serial device through the VMM's serial socket, so the guest needs an autologin root getty on its serial console. The shipped images run serial-getty@ on the arch's console device (ttyS0 on x86_64, ttyAMA0 on aarch64) with an autologin drop-in. The kernel console (the same device, given on the cmdline) shares the port: kernel messages interleave with the session, which is exactly what a failsafe console wants. Authentication is the daemon's TLS + token listener, and the stream is raw bytes with no in-band protocol. The session keeps the getty's own terminal geometry for its life. A workspace user's shell with the client's terminal size uses ssh through the forward seam.
  • Register the virtiofs filesystem driver when shares attach. Host directories reach a workspace as virtiofs mounts (#667), so the guest's kernel must know the filesystem: built in (both pinned Debian flavours: CONFIG_VIRTIO_FS=y) or loadable (Fedora's image ships the module in its runtime closure and loads it at boot). msks image check's virtiofs row probes the driver. A workspace that attaches shares on an image without it sees the gap reported on the guest's console and cloud-init log at start, and the mounts never come up.
  • Take an address over DHCP when a NIC is present. Workspaces are networked by default: the VM boots with a virtio-net NIC, and the daemon's DHCP service offers the address, gateway, and its own resolver. Debian's kernel ships virtio_net, and the shipped overlay loads it at boot. The overlay carries a systemd-networkd .network unit (Name=en* eth*, DHCP=yes) plus resolved's stub resolv.conf, so the guest configures whatever NIC appears. The offered resolver becomes resolved's per-link upstream: /etc/resolv.conf points at the 127.0.0.53 stub, and the lease's resolver in effect is read from resolvectl dns (the git-out smoke's probe). A workspace created with "egress": false presents no NIC. Nothing matches the unit and networkd stays idle, so the same image serves both postures. The shipped base carries no developer toolchain: git, curl, and uv all arrive over the egress NIC when a seed or the operator installs them.
  • Answer the ACPI power button. stop presses the power button (vm.power-button) and waits; the guest's own handler runs the clean shutdown that flushes its disks (systemd-logind does this by default; an acpid rule works too). A guest that ignores the button is killed at the deadline, and whatever its page cache still held is lost.
  • Tolerate a read-write root. The daemon boots each workspace's root read-write through a per-workspace qcow2 overlay, so the base image stays pristine under copy-on-write. It also attaches an ext4 volume at /home. Mount it by the volume label msks-home (the daemon formats the volume with that label), so the mount stays on the right device whatever the disk order is; nofail keeps boots moving when the volume is absent. A udev rule asks systemd for the mount again when the labeled disk appears, so a boot whose device job expired while udev was still probing mounts the volume moments after the label appears. This holds on every boot the image ships, restarted workspaces included (the daemon's identity seed carries the same retry for first boots on images that predate the rule).
  • Grant passwordless sudo to the wheel group. Both images ship the conventional admin group wheel, whose members administer the VM. Debian does it through a %wheel dropin in /etc/sudoers.d; the image creates the group because Debian's own tree carries none. NixOS does it through a declarative sudo rule. The identity seed creates a named login user, gives it the workspace user's shell, and joins it to the group. The seed never writes sudo configuration, so a guest that is rebuilt keeps exactly the sudo policy its configuration declares.
  • Run cloud-init against the cidata seed disk. A workspace created with user_data or a seeded ssh identity boots with a third, read-only virtio disk: a small iso9660 filesystem labeled cidata, exactly cloud-init's NoCloud seed layout. Its root carries user-data (the operator payload, composed beside the identity's seeding script when a key was supplied) and meta-data. The meta-data holds instance-id, keyed off the workspace id, and local-hostname, the workspace's creation name (the minted id when the workspace was created without one).

The hostname is set at first boot, and a factory reset re-provisions from the seed with it. A stop/start never re-provisions, because instance-id never changes. A launch heal that rebuilds a lost seed carries the hostname as well, but a guest that booted before keeps the hostname it already has. cloud-init sets the hostname per instance, and its per-boot update leaves a hostname it never set untouched, so only a factory reset moves an older workspace's.

/etc/hosts carries the workspace's name as well. The Debian image turns on cloud-init's manage_etc_hosts in the mode that adds the conventional 127.0.1.1 record for the host, in place, on every boot; the file's other entries stay put. A guest first booted before, whose healed seed now carries the name, gets the record with the creation name while its kernel hostname keeps the older one: the module reads the seed, not the kernel. Name resolution does not wait on the record. Both images' resolvers answer the local hostname on their own, via the myhostname NSS module (Debian's genericcloud base ships libnss-myhostname, and it is part of the NixOS base system). The record is the plain files-source entry a tool reading /etc/hosts directly still finds.

The image ships cloud-init (the Debian genericcloud base does), and dropins pin the behavior the msks contract needs. datasource_list: [ NoCloud, None ] makes the seed disk answer immediately, with no EC2 or OpenStack probing and no network timeouts. network: {config: disabled} leaves the image's own networkd unit owning whatever NIC appears, with cloud-init's netplan rendering out of the way. Both payload forms run: cloud-config YAML and #! scripts.

cloud-init's run-once state (the /var/lib/cloud cache) lives on the workspace's root overlay, so stop/start never re-provisions and a factory reset does (the reset drops the overlay). Any distro cloud image that ships cloud-init (Debian's generic and genericcloud, Ubuntu, Fedora, ...) imports as-is and declares "capabilities": {"provisioner": "cloud-init"}.

items.title: Architectures
items.text:
The guests build for x86_64 and aarch64. The bare flavor names follow the building host's uname -m: msks-build-guest on an aarch64 dev host is the arm64 build. The -x86_64 and -aarch64 suffixes pin an arch explicitly (msks-build-guest nixos-aarch64). The Debian and Fedora flavors are fetch-and-pack, so their pinned attrs build on any host. The NixOS closure wants its native evaluator: the arm64 busybox guard in the initrd build refuses a cross-eval and reports the cause.

The arm64 guests run 16K-page kernels (Debian's own arm64-16k flavour, and a kernel patch on the NixOS side). A flat guest's page size is guest-internal, so the image boots on any arm64 host, while nested KVM inside the guest initializes only where the guest's page size matches a 16K host's (#635's Stage-2 scoping): one image covers both. The console differs by arch: the cmdline carries ttyS0 on x86_64 and ttyAMA0 on aarch64, where cloud-hypervisor presents a PL011 UART. The manifest records the arch, the kernel format, and the cmdline together, so the archive stays self-describing.

items.title: The shipped builder
items.text:
msks-build-guest

builds the default image (workspace-debian-13.6.tar) from a date-pinned, sha512-verified Debian trixie genericcloud qcow2, the cloud-init-bearing variant of Debian's cloud image family: cloud-init and its python3 runtime arrive with the base.

The build converts the qcow2 to raw, extracts the root filesystem, and applies the msks overlay and boot diet. It repacks the result as a deterministic ext4 (mke2fs -d under fakeroot; the intermediate is stored in the nix store as one opaque tarball, never as a tree). It then wraps the kernel, initrd, rootfs, and a generated image.json into the container-image tar with byte-stable tar flags (--sort=name --mtime=@1 --numeric-owner). Identical rebuilds hash identically, so the same image deduplicates across hosts.

The output is written under .devenv/state/guest/ (GUEST_DIR relocates it); scripts/build-guest.sh and nix/guest-debian.nix document every step and are the reference for what an image build does.

Both images bake the agent toolchain: pinned Node, the pinned pi coding agent, and the pinned herdr terminal workspace manager (herdr.dev, the release's static binary, with its license). They also bake pinned Claude Code (the npm wrapper plus its linux-x64 native binary, staged in npm's global layout with the wrapper's own post-install linking done at build time) and the pi model-discovery extension in /etc/skel and root's home. The internal docs/llm.md describes what the extension does at pi startup.

The staging differs per image. Debian puts the official Node tarball and the pinned packages under /usr/local. NixOS uses nixpkgs' own Node and the same pinned packages through the system profile. Claude Code's native binary is loader-patched to the closure's glibc, because a stock NixOS ships no usable loader where the published interpreter points. The extension is planted by tmpfiles copy-once rules.

The pins move with an image rebuild: agentNodeTarball in nix/guest-debian.nix; piTarball, npmDepsHash (and, on a pi bump, the table in nix/pi-shrinkwrap-integrity.json), agentHerdrBinary and its license pin, and the two agentClaude* tarballs in nix/agent-toolchain.nix. The build stays pure derivations: pi's dependency closure is prefetched against its shrinkwrap, with the five integrity gaps the published lock leaves closed by hash, and installed offline. A workspace that already booted keeps the toolchain it booted with; a rebuilt image serves the new pins to the next workspace.

pi's own tool dependencies ship in the image too. pi resolves fd and rg from PATH, at interactive startup and again at first tool use, and downloads each from GitHub releases when it finds neither. Without them, a fresh workspace's first agent start would wait on that download, behind the egress interceptor and the GitHub API quota every workspace behind one address shares.

The Debian image stages Debian's own fd-find and ripgrep debs (fdFindDeb and ripgrepDeb in nix/guest-debian.nix, pinned by pool URL and checksum like the kernel and rsync debs) with the same linkage guard rsync gets. fd-find's binary is placed under /usr/lib/cargo/bin with /usr/bin/fdfind a symlink, exactly the layout apt install fd-find leaves, and pi accepts the fdfind name. The Fedora image stages the distro's own fd-find and ripgrep rpm (fdFindRpm and ripgrepRpm in nix/guest-fedora.nix, pinned from the compose's Everything repo, with fd's libjemalloc dependency pinned beside them) under the same guard. Fedora calls the binary fd, the name pi probes first. The NixOS image ships nixpkgs' own fd and ripgrep on the same profile PATH as the toolchain. With both present, a first pi start needs no downloads.

The tools themselves decide some of their own freshness. Claude Code checks for updates on startup and installs a newer self into the user's home when it finds one; its autoUpdates setting and the DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER environment variable are the switches. herdr's herdr update does the same on demand. A workspace user can therefore run a newer tool than the image pin: the pin governs what a fresh workspace starts with, not what a user's home accumulates. A no-egress workspace sees these checks fail quietly.

msks-build-guest nixos

builds the second catalog image (workspace-nixos-<version>.tar) from a NixOS system evaluated against the same pinned nixpkgs the development shell uses: the guest's cloud-init, sshd, and rsync are built by nixpkgs instead of fetched as Debian artifacts. The root filesystem is the whole system closure packed into a fresh ext4 (the same mke2fs -d under fakeroot; no cloud image exists to extract), and every store path resolves from the image itself. The archive carries the same image.json schema with the same declared capabilities (cloud-init); the daemon serves it with nothing keyed off the image's name. The output is written under .devenv/state/guest-nixos/ (GUEST_NIXOS_DIR relocates it); nix/guest-nixos.nix documents every step. The image ships the same agent toolchain as the Debian one: nixpkgs' own Node and the shared pins (nix/agent-toolchain.nix) are on the system profile, with the loader-patched Claude Code and the tmpfiles-planted extension staging described above.

items.title: Rebuilding the system inside a NixOS workspace
items.text:
A NixOS workspace is nixos-rebuild-ready. nix runs as on any NixOS host: the daemon, the build users, and the CLI ship enabled. The image bakes everything a rebuild evaluates against:

  • The store database. Every store path the image ships is registered valid: the build loads the closure's registration into /nix/var/nix/db/db.sqlite. The guest's nix therefore answers reference queries, and a rebuild reuses the shipped closure instead of refetching or rebuilding it.
  • The pinned nixpkgs source. The same revision the image was built from is on the store as root's channel profile, so <nixpkgs> resolves with no network. A nix-channel --update moves to the rolling channel deliberately: that is the stock NixOS posture, and the pin governs what a fresh workspace starts with.
  • /etc/nixos/configuration.nix. It imports nix/guest-nixos-configuration.nix, the very module the image build evaluated, with the module's whole import chain (its package files, the shrinkwrap pair) shipped beside it at the same relative paths. The image build evaluates the shipped chain exactly as a rebuild does, so a configuration a rebuild cannot evaluate fails the build, not a workspace's first boot.

A rebuild re-evaluates the shipped configuration. Edit the module or add settings in configuration.nix and run:

sudo nixos-rebuild switch

  • The nix search path. The same four entries ship in /etc/nix/nix.conf and in every login shell's NIX_PATH: nixpkgs, nixos-config, the nixos-system entrypoint the rebuild tool prefers, and the channels profile. <nixpkgs> therefore resolves identically for the root rebuild path and for the workspace user at the console.

  • The system profile as the boot's init. The kernel cmdline gives init=/nix/var/nix/profiles/system/init, the activation-maintained indirection a nixos-rebuild switch re-points, so a rebuilt system survives a workspace stop/start with no daemon involvement. The VMM always boots the image's frozen kernel and initrd, so a rebuilt system's new kernel takes effect only through a new image; userspace changes apply fully on reboot.

A rebuild that changes nothing but re-activates keeps every msks contract item (the console getty, the sshd posture, cloud-init seed handling, the agent toolchain on PATH), because the configuration it evaluates is the one that shipped.

nix works the same way for the unprivileged workspace user logged in on the console. nix-build '<nixpkgs>' -A <pkg> builds from the baked pin through the daemon; nix-env -iA nixpkgs.<pkg> installs into the user's own profile; nix-shell -p <pkg> builds and enters an environment. Fetches the shipped store lacks come from cache.nixos.org through the workspace's egress path.

The image ships one background consumer of this readiness. The msks-interceptor-ca oneshot folds the daemon's interception CA (staged by the identity seed under /etc/msks, one CA for every workspace) into the system trust bundle. The module reads the staged certificate at evaluation time; the unit runs one nixos-rebuild switch per fresh certificate after cloud-final; a hash marker keeps later boots no-ops. The image build itself refuses a host that carries /etc/msks/interceptor-ca.crt (the module's assertion fails the build), since that evaluation would bake a foreign CA into every guest.

A workspace with egress fetches substitutes from cache.nixos.org through the workspace's egress path like any other traffic. A no-egress workspace rebuilds against what is already in the store; new packages that need a fetch fail with nix's own error until egress is granted. Both images stay the same size class as before: the nix closure, the validity database, and the nixpkgs source grow the NixOS rootfs by roughly a gigabyte uncompressed.

Each image build also executes every staged launcher and fails on one that does not run. The Debian build runs node, pi, claude, fdfind, and rg through the tree's own dynamic loader and libraries, the same world the guest execs them in, because the build sandbox carries no /usr/bin/env or /lib64. herdr, a static binary, runs as-is. pi's and npm's published #!/usr/bin/env node shebangs, which that sandbox cannot resolve, are asserted byte-exact instead. The NixOS build runs the profile binaries directly.

The first image that shipped the toolchain passed every presence check while pi could not start: the npm build had rewritten cli.js's shebang to a build-time Nix store node no guest carries. test -x on a symlink says nothing about the interpreter behind it. The launcher executions turn that class of breakage into a build failure.

msks-build-guest fedora

builds the third catalog image (workspace-fedora-44.tar, #651) from Fedora's date-pinned, sha256-verified Generic cloud qcow2. It is the same fetch-and-pack shape as the Debian build, with Fedora's own divergences adapted at each step:

  • btrfs, not ext4. The cloud image's root filesystem is a btrfs subvolume set (root, boot, home, var). The build extracts it with btrfs restore (unprivileged, no mount), flattens the set into the plain tree a direct-boot guest wants, and packs a fresh ext4 from it (the same mke2fs -d under fakeroot). The extraction runs inside one fakeroot session, and btrfs restore -m restores the distro's own owner/group/mode, setuid bits included, into the session's faked view. The session writes that view out as a manifest, and the pack stage re-applies it, because a faked view cannot outlive its session and untarring it under a new one would make setuid binaries genuinely unreadable (mke2fs -d reads file contents through the real modes).
  • The kernel stays inside the image. Fedora publishes no separate kernel artifact: /usr/lib/modules/<kver>/vmlinuz is the kernel, its config, and the module tree in one pin. The minimal initramfs carries zero modules (Fedora's kernel builds ext4, virtio_blk, and crc32c in), so busybox mounts the root and switch_roots into systemd.
  • SELinux stays off. The build reconstructs the filesystem without SELinux xattrs (btrfs restore drops them, and the unprivileged pack cannot write them), so every file would boot unlabeled and enforcing policy freezes PID 1 before the first getty; the boot cmdline carries selinux=0. The workspace's isolation boundary is the VM itself: the Debian and NixOS images carry no MAC either.
  • NetworkManager owns the NIC. Fedora's image runs NetworkManager, whose default policy takes a DHCP address on any ethernet it finds, so an egress workspace's NIC configures itself with no msks-side unit (the Debian overlay's networkd enablement is the divergence there) and cloud-init's network rendering stays off the same way.
  • The console prompt is pinned to the shared shape. Fedora's default bash prompt is [root@host ~]#; the build appends the PS1 that presents the same root@host:~# every family's console surface answers with.
