  • Boot diet. chronyd and the zram generator's config drop (the generator would stall each boot ~45s on a zram device no workspace VM presents), and the module closure ships the virtiofs module Fedora builds separately from the Debian pair.

The output is written under .devenv/state/guest-fedora/ (GUEST_FEDORA_DIR relocates it); nix/guest-fedora.nix documents every step. The image stages the same agent toolchain as the Debian one (the official Node tarball and the shared pins under /usr/local) and the same fd/rg staging described above, from the distro's own rpm.

items.title: Building your own
items.text:
Any rootfs that satisfies the contract above can become a workspace image. The outline, using a distro's own cloud image as the source:

  1. Fetch the source image and verify it against its published checksum.
  2. Produce a raw ext4 of the guest root filesystem (qemu-img convert + partition extraction, or unpack the cloud image's root archive directly).
  3. Enable an autologin root getty on /dev/hvc0; make sure the virtio_console module is present so the device exists at boot.
  4. Bring up networking. Workspaces boot with a virtio-net NIC by default, so the image must be able to configure one. How it does so is the distro's choice:
  5. a kernel with the virtio_net driver present (module or built-in; on most distros udev autoloads the module when the device appears);
  6. a DHCP client that configures whatever NIC appears and honors the offered address, gateway, and resolver (networkd, dhcpcd, or anything else that speaks DHCP);
  7. name resolution must follow the resolver DHCP names (however the distro wires /etc/resolv.conf);
  8. a boot with no NIC (a workspace created with "egress": false) must still reach a usable login: the same image serves both postures.

The shipped image does this with systemd-networkd + resolved; any equivalent stack works.

  1. Ship cloud-init, configured for the cidata seed. Starting from a distro cloud image (Debian generic/genericcloud, Ubuntu, Fedora: they carry cloud-init and its python runtime) gives you this for free; otherwise install the distro's cloud-init package. Two dropins under /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.d/ pin the msks contract:
  2. datasource_list: [ NoCloud, None ] (the workspace's seed disk answers immediately; nothing probes EC2 or OpenStack sources or waits on the network);
  3. network: {config: disabled} (the network configuration from step 4 owns the NIC; cloud-init's renderer would only fight it).

The guest kernel needs the isofs module present to mount the seed (every stock distro kernel carries it). Declare the consumer in the manifest (step 6) so listings show what eats the seed. An image whose guest runs no cloud-init still accepts user_data at create, but nothing executes it: the daemon cannot tell.

  1. Write disk/image.json describing your kernel and cmdline, and declare "capabilities": {"provisioner": "cloud-init"}.
  2. Lay out boot/ and disk/ as the layer tree and wrap it:
tar --sort=name --mtime='@1' --owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner \
    -C layer-root -cf workspace-mine-1.0.layer.tar .
# then wrap layer.tar in a container-image tar, or simply:
podman import workspace-mine-1.0.layer.tar workspace-mine:1.0
podman save -o workspace-mine-1.0.tar workspace-mine:1.0

podman import/save produce a valid outer layout; msksd accepts both compressed and uncompressed layers (uncompressed layers keep import and in-place inspection cheaper).

items.title: Checking an image
items.text:
The daemon verifies layout and manifest at import, but a tar that parses can still carry a guest that does not boot: the layout is the only thing the daemon can see. msks image check <archive> is the gate an image author runs before publishing. It boots the archive exactly the way a workspace boots (same driver, overlay, home volume, seed disk, and console path, against a throwaway state dir under /tmp) and reports each contract point by name:

$ msks image check workspace-mine-1.0.tar
PASS archive        imported mine:1.0 (1d6a5e782fc0)
PASS boot           guest answered the console in 3.4s (kernel 6.12.107+deb13-amd64)
PASS console        root autologin getty on the console port
PASS virtiofs       the virtiofs filesystem driver answers (mount -t virtiofs works)
PASS user-data      seed payload ran on first boot
PASS acpi-shutdown  clean shutdown within 120s
PASS root-rw        root is writable and the write survived a stop/start (overlay)
PASS home-label     /home mounted by label msks-home and its write survived a stop/start (volume)

Any host with /dev/kvm runs it; nothing else from msks is needed (no daemon, no state). The points map one-to-one onto "What a guest must provide" above. The checks cover the archive layout and manifest, a guest whose console getty answers, the virtiofs driver a share mounts through (#674: an image without it fails its own row with the gap given by name, before a workspace's share attaches as a mount unit that never comes up), a root that accepts writes through the overlay, and /home mounted by its label, both surviving a stop/start cycle. They also cover the seed payload running on first boot (checked when the manifest declares a provisioner; a provisioner-less image reports the point skipped with that reason) and the ACPI power button producing a clean shutdown. A broken point fails its row and the exit code is 1; the summary gives the first failure. --keep preserves the throwaway state dir (serial logs included) for inspection.

--egress adds the networking point: the guest must take a global address over DHCP when the checker boots it with a NIC through the daemon's own net stack. That leg needs root (taps, nftables, the DHCP and DNS listeners on their privileged ports) and an egress-capable default route (--uplink gives another interface). The checker sets net.ipv4.ip_forward to 1 for the pass and restores what it found; a checker killed outright leaves the sysctl at 1. Run the leg on a host that is not serving the real daemon: both bind the same privileged DHCP and DNS ports. The no-NIC half of the posture is the core pass itself: it boots without a NIC and requires a usable login. The write probes (root-rw, home-label, user-data) run over the root console.

items.title: Registering an image
items.text:
Import makes the daemon unpack the boot files once into a per-hash cache and record the image in the catalog. The msks image commands drive this surface from the CLI (msks image import <path>, msks image ls, msks image rm <ref>, msks image info <ref>, and msks image default <ref>; see docs/cli.md). The raw HTTP form:

curl -X POST https://192.168.77.2:8660/api/v1/images \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"source": "/path/on/the/daemon/workspace-mine-1.0.tar"}'

The source is a path on the daemon's filesystem (the daemon reads them from its state dir), or an https:// URL the daemon downloads itself:

msks image import https://images.example.com/workspace-mine-1.0.tar
curl -X POST .../api/v1/images -d '{"source": "https://images.example.com/workspace-mine-1.0.tar"}'

A URL download is written to the catalog's staging area under a size ceiling and a deadline (MSKSD_IMAGE_IMPORT_MAX_MIB, MSKSD_IMAGE_IMPORT_TIMEOUT_S; see docs/config.md). It verifies TLS against the system roots, refuses a redirect that leaves https, and imports from the downloaded copy, so the recorded hash always reflects the fetched bytes. The ceiling also clamps to the bytes the storage floor protects, so the download itself cannot spend the state disk's headroom.

The fetch runs with the calling token's authority. A deployment hands its API token to operators it trusts to import images, and the URL form reaches whatever network the daemon can reach. That is the same trust a daemon-side path import already carries. Either way, the daemon copies privately and hashes that copy. A source file changing underneath the import therefore cannot desync the recorded hash from the imported content, and importing the same content twice is idempotent.

An import registers the archive under an operator-chosen pair when name/version are in the request: msks image import <path> --name mine --version 1.0 on the CLI, or the keys beside source over HTTP. Either key alone moves; the other falls back to the archive's own manifest. The override changes the registered record: the listing, image info, and name:version reference resolution. The archive bytes, the content hash, and the archive's own image.json stay exactly as they were. The manifest's pair stays recorded as the row's origin beside the registered pair, so a usable image's provenance reads from the catalog alone.

A cataloged row renames in place under the same rules:

msks image rename debian:13 --name mine --version 1.0
curl -X PATCH .../api/v1/images/<hash> \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"name": "mine", "version": "1.0"}'

Either key alone keeps the other at its registered value. A rename validates the new pair the same way an import override does: non-empty, and free of : and @ (the reference forms key on them). It refuses a pair another row already holds, with a named error that identifies the holder by hash and by its origin when an override or a rename moved it there. It keeps the origin pair and changes nothing else: the bytes, the hash, the listed import time, and workspaces already booting the image stay put. The refusal holds for overrides and renames; a plain import of a rebuilt archive under a pair a row already holds stays allowed (the long-standing shape: name@hash and bare-hash forms resolve the ambiguity). Re-importing unchanged bytes carries the row's current registration forward; re-importing the same bytes with a new override renames the row the same way a rename does.

Rules worth knowing:

  • The first image imported becomes the default (the one a bare workspace create uses) and keeps the designation while more images arrive. POST /api/v1/images/default re-designates at any time:
# designate by any reference form create's image field takes
curl -X POST .../api/v1/images/default \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"ref": "debian:13.6"}'

# clear the designation; the answer reports the fallback
# (the sole catalog entry, or none)
curl -X DELETE .../api/v1/images/default \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
  • The designation is the catalog's default pointer file. It survives restarts, and msks image ls/image info mark the designated row. With it cleared, a bare create falls back to the sole catalog entry; on a catalog holding several images it answers a named error until one is designated again.
  • MSKSD_DEFAULT_IMAGE (set by the dev daemon from its state dir's image) imports and designates at first boot; on later boots the daemon only re-checks the hash, not a full re-import.
  • MSKSD_SEED_IMAGES imports at every start, warm when the archive is unchanged and never designated; the dev daemon sets it to the NixOS guest's archive whenever msks-build-guest nixos has built one. A rebuilt guest is therefore what a bare-name create boots, without a manual re-import.
  • Listing shows every registered image with its hash, name, version, kernel facts, which one is default, and when each entered the catalog (the imported field, ISO 8601 UTC). A renamed row additionally carries its origin pair (origin_name/origin_version, equal to name/version for an unrenamed row):
curl -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://127.0.0.1:8660/api/v1/images

  • Storage: one image costs roughly twice its rootfs size on the daemon's state dir (the retained archive plus the unpacked boot cache), beside the workspace overlays and volumes; docs/storage.md has the capacity model.

  • An image with workspaces still booting it cannot be removed (DELETE /api/v1/images/{hash} answers 409 naming the workspace); once its workspaces are gone, deletion drops the cache and the retained archive.

items.title: Using an image
items.text:
Workspace create selects an image by reference:

# name:version — exact
curl -X POST .../api/v1/workspaces -d '{"id": "ws1", "image": "debian:13.6"}'

# bare name — resolves to the newest registered version; the
# most recently imported row wins when two builds carry the same
# leading numbers (e.g. a NixOS version's trailing store hash
# differs between builds)
{"id": "ws1", "image": "debian"}

# name@hash — pins identity AND content
{"id": "ws1", "image": "debian@<sha256>"}

# bare hash — content-addressed
{"id": "ws1", "image": "<sha256>"}

# no image at all — the designated default
{"id": "ws1"}

Versions order numerically (13.10 sorts after 13.9). A malformed reference (debian@not-a-hash) is a named 400 rather than a miss. Explicit kernel/rootfs fields still win over the image: the image is the convenient path, not a mandate.

items.title: First-boot provisioning (user_data)
items.text:
A workspace created with user_data gets a customization payload that runs on its first boot, EC2-style, delivered on the workspace's own seed disk:

# a script (any image with a provisioner; the leading #! is what
# makes it one)
msks create ws --user-data provision.sh --start

# cloud-config (needs a cloud-init image)
curl -X POST .../api/v1/workspaces -d '{
  "id": "ws", "image": "mycloud:1.0",
  "user_data": "#cloud-config\nusers:\n- name: alice\n..."
}'

The rules worth knowing:

  • Create-time and immutable. The payload is part of the workspace's identity; user_data is accepted only at create. It is capped at 64 Ki characters (pydantic's 422 gives the bound), an empty payload is a 400, and any mutation attempt answers a named 405 (delete and recreate to change it). cloud-init keys its run-once semantics off the workspace, so changing it after the fact would silently do nothing anyway.
  • The seed is per-workspace state. It is built at create (a few hundred KiB of iso9660 overhead regardless of payload size, cidata-labeled), attached read-only as the third disk, survives stop/start and factory reset, and is deleted with the workspace. It can embed tokens, so the daemon stores it mode 0600 under the workspace's own directory, and creates its database file (which records the payload on the workspace's row) 0600 too. Listing endpoints and msks ls --json echo the payload back over the same TLS + token channel as the console.
  • Both payload forms run. cloud-init executes #! scripts from user_data and applies cloud-config documents alike; declare the image's capabilities.provisioner: cloud-init so operators and tooling can see what consumes the seed.
  • The host's timezone is carried on the seed (#633). A create on a host with a timezone other than UTC captures it, and the seed's script sets the guest's clock to it on first boot: date and logs inside the guest read the operator's wall clock with no operator action. The capture is create-time and immutable like the rest of the seed: a host timezone change later leaves existing workspaces on the zone their seed baked, and only new creates see the new zone. A host on UTC (or whose clock file reads as nothing recognizable) seeds no timezone; the guest keeps the image's own default.
  • A seedless boot needs a quiet create. A workspace created without a payload, a key, mounts, or a timezone to carry boots with two disks and no added cost: cloud-init finds no seed, applies nothing, and the interactive budget is unchanged (~3.0s start→shell).
  • Failure posture is cloud-init's. The console getty starts before cloud-init runs, so the interactive budget is unaffected (the shipped image measures ~3.0s start-to-shell). Payloads run in cloud-init's final stage: a slow or hanging payload delays boot-complete, not the shell. cloud-init status --wait (or the serial log) says when provisioning finished; a factory reset re-runs the payload from the same seed.

items.title: The published image channel
items.text:
Every release publishes the built guest images to a hash-keyed channel on this repository's GitHub releases. Each image lives on its own release tagged images/<hash-prefix>, as a zstd-compressed archive (<flavor>.tar.zst) whose sha256 the catalog records. Importing the compressed form hashes exactly the shipped bytes, and the daemon's import accepts the form directly (the archive reader detects it). An unchanged derivation publishes nothing: the workflow compares the archive derivation's evaluation against the previous manifest and skips the build entirely, and a channel slot that already exists is never rewritten.

The version release carries images.json, the manifest that lists every published image (one row per flavor and arch): ref, description, kernel, arch, size, hash, url, and the source facts (build, built_from). Fetching a published image is one command. Pick the row whose arch field matches the host's uname -m; the import then accepts it without ceremony, and refuses a row for another architecture with the same named error any other foreign-arch import gets:

# the URL from the manifest row
msks image import \
  https://github.com/mcdonc/msks/releases/download/images/<hash>/debian.tar.zst

The description the listing and image info print is baked into the image itself: the build writes one line into the layer's image.json giving the distro, kernel, and shipped stack, and it is carried through the import into any catalog. msks image ls carries it (capped for the row), msks image info prints it at full length, and the manifest rows carry it for the release channel.

The manifest answers from the moment the release exists: the release workflow attaches the previous release's manifest when it creates the version release, and replaces it with the new one when the image builds finish. While the builds run, the manifest gives the previous images and an import pulls those; a release that changes no guest derivation publishes a manifest identical to the one it replaces.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
msks ships as a Python distribution with everything inside: the client (msks), the daemon (msksd), the consent-decider terminal (msks-term-popup), and host setup scripts this chapter describes (msks-setup-debian-host, msks-setup-fedora-host, and msks-setup-macos-host).

msks needs Python 3.14 or newer.

Install the Python distribution using uv:

   curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
   source $HOME/.local/bin/env
   uv tool install --python 3.14 msks

There is an automated setup script for the remainder on Debian-derived, Fedora-derived hosts, and macOS hosts, each described below.

items.title: What the setup lands
items.text:
Each phase runs in order, and the first refusal stops the run with an error. On Apple Silicon, everything except the msks client is installed into a Lima virtual machine.

Packages. The packages required by the server and the client.

The capability wrapper. /usr/local/bin/msks-caps — a root-owned copy of util-linux setpriv carrying file capabilities cap_net_admin and cap_net_bind_service. The daemon's per-VM taps and nftables chains need net_admin; the egress stack's DHCP (port 67) and DNS (port 53) need net_bind_service. The wrapper raises both caps ambient, so they flow to the daemon and every tool it execs. The grant surface is the wrapper's execute permission: any local user able to run it holds the two capabilities through it. After installing it the setup runs the wrapper and verifies the caps.

The routing kernel. /etc/sysctl.d/msks-egress.conf sets net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 at boot, and the value applies immediately: route packets between the per-VM taps and the host uplink. The daemon reads the sysctl at startup and refuses every egress workspace, with the cause named, while it reads 0. /etc/modules-load.d/msks.conf loads the netfilter and tun modules at boot: the nftables machinery, NAT, conntrack, the deny RST, and the interactive consent queue. A module the kernel tree lacks draws a warning naming the kernel package that carries it. Interactive egress consent needs its whole module set, and the run's summary names the verdict.

/dev/kvm. Access arrives through the kvm group on the daemon's user. The setup adds the executing user to the group when missing. The account picks the group up at the next login. An already-running session keeps the old groups until it starts anew.

The login PATH. The account that typed the command (the SUDO_USER under sudo) gains /usr/sbin and /sbin on its login PATH: the setup appends a guarded block to that account's ~/.profile, idempotently, so a re-run never duplicates it. Debian keeps nft, conntrack, and the e2fsprogs trio in /usr/sbin, and a non-root login shell does not carry the directory. The block means the operator's next login can type the names the daemon execs. A daemon started by the systemd user unit finds the directories on its own PATH (the unit manager's default carries them). A daemon started by hand (msks-dev, a bare msksd) inherits the session's PATH, so the same login carries the fix to both shapes.

The systemd user service. On a host systemd manages, the setup writes ~/.config/systemd/user/msksd.service for the executing user and enables it. The unit execs msksd through the wrapper, so the file capabilities grant it the same posture a root unit would have, so it can spawn VMs. It runs with MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED=true and the uplink interface the setup detected, and it creates the unix listener's runtime directory under the user's own $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (RuntimeDirectory=msks, the client's default socket candidate). It restarts the daemon on failure. Finally, loginctl enable-linger keeps the user manager, and the daemon, running across logouts and boots.

Cloud Hypervisor's static release binary. So guest VMs can be started.

The client links. /usr/local/bin/msks and /usr/local/bin/msks-term-popup are symlinks to the console scripts that shipped beside the setup tool. They land in the directory the wrapper and the VMM binary already occupy. Every login shell carries /usr/local/bin, so a bare msks answers for every user on the host with no profile edits. A GUI-opened terminal window resolves the consent-terminal launcher on its own PATH. A regular file or a live link to another target at a path refuses by name: the run never clobbers what it did not land. A dangling link re-points, stale by definition. --uninstall removes both.

PATH manipulation. Adds /usr/sbin to the sudoing user's PATH so various binaries can be found.

The run ends with a summary: the wrapper and its caps, the sysctl, the modules file, the tools' paths, /dev/kvm, the login PATH block, the client links, the consent verdict, the detected uplink, and the service line.

You will need to log out and back in for msksd doctor to return clean after using the host installer.

items.title: Setup on a Debian host
items.text:
You can use the msks-setup-debian-host script to set up msks on Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 or newer, and Linux Mint 22 or newer.

The platform gate accepts the debian, ubuntu, and linuxmint os-release IDs with those release floors: older Ubuntu and Mint archives lack virtiofsd, which the setup requires. One version caveat: host mounts need virtiofsd 1.13.0 or newer, and Linux Mint 22's archive ships 1.10.0. msksd doctor gives the gap, and the workaround is a self-built virtiofsd pointed at with MSKSD_VIRTIOFSD (see mounts).

The msks daemon runs the workspaces directly on the host using cloud-hypervisor and various networking and kernel-y bits need to be satisfied for it to work properly.

The host therefore needs pieces the wheel cannot carry. These are software dependency packages, kernel modules, a routing sysctl, two capabilities for the daemon's user, and a service that keeps msksd running.

On a Debian deployment host, use msks-setup-debian-host console script (installed by the wheel) to do those things.

You can run it like this after installing the msks Python distribution:

sudo "$(command -v msks-setup-debian-host)"

The quoted form matters: the console script lands in ~/.local/bin, which sudo's path does not carry — the bare name would answer "command not found".

Run it as the user the daemon will serve under sudo, the SUDO_USER account is the executing user, and the service the tool registers will belong to your normal user account.

The run is idempotent: re-run any time, and re-run after a util-linux upgrade (the wrapper keeps a copy of setpriv; see below).

items.title: Setup on a Fedora host
items.text:
msks-setup-fedora-host is the way to install msksd on Fedora: it contains a HostProfile (the package map, the probe names, the dnf verbs, the usermod/gpasswd group commands) over the same phases the Debian tool runs (the wrapper, the routing kernel settings, the packages, the kvm grant, the systemd user service, the --uninstall mirror, the VMM download).

sudo "$(command -v msks-setup-fedora-host)"

The run installs through dnf the packages a stock Fedora answers without: conntrack-tools, qemu-img, tmux, virtiofsd, and the consent stack's libnetfilter_queue when the linker cache lacks the soname. A stock install already carries the rest of the probed set (setpriv, setcap, ip, nft, modprobe, sysctl, the e2fsprogs trio, mkisofs, ssh, and rsync), so those probes read present and the run moves on. The CA probe names Fedora's own command, update-ca-trust (the ca-certificates package), where the Debian map probes update-ca-certificates.

The kvm membership runs through usermod -aG kvm, and the uninstall summary's removal line is dnf's.

The same pieces land at the same paths for the same reasons the Debian section above documents: the wrapper at /usr/local/bin/msks-caps with the two capabilities, the sysctl and modules files under /etc, the user unit under ~/.config/systemd/user/, and the cloud-hypervisor static release for the host's architecture. --uninstall reverses the run the same way.

items.title: The same host by hand (if you'd rather not trust msks-setup-{debian,fedora}-host)
items.text:
msks-setup-{debian,fedora}-host is a program the wheel ships, and running it means running shipped code as root. An operator who prefers to read every step first can land the same host in an interactive root shell.

To do so, install the package set. It is the same set msks-setup-{debian,fedora}-host lands, so a host finished by hand comes up clean under the doctor too:

sudo -i apt install iproute2 \
                    nftables \
                    conntrack \
                    procps \
                    util-linux \
                    libcap2-bin \
                    kmod \
                    e2fsprogs \
                    qemu-utils \
                    genisoimage \
                    libnetfilter-queue1 \
                    libnfnetlink0 \
                    openssh-client \
                    rsync \
                    tmux \
                    ca-certificates

ca-certificates is the set's one self-serving package: the CA bundle the next step's curl to github.com needs for its TLS verification.

The capability wrapper is a fresh root-owned copy of setpriv, with the two capabilities set and read back. A filesystem without capability xattrs takes the setcap and loses it, so the readback is the proof:

install -o root -g root -m 0755 "$(command -v setpriv)" /usr/local/bin/msks-caps
setcap cap_net_admin,cap_net_bind_service+ep /usr/local/bin/msks-caps
getcap /usr/local/bin/msks-caps

The functional proof — the daemon's exact exec line, with the ambient set inspected in the process it starts (the CapAmb line must carry a nonzero mask):

/usr/local/bin/msks-caps --inh-caps=+net_admin,+net_bind_service \
  --ambient-caps=+net_admin,+net_bind_service \
  -- sh -c "sed -n 's/^CapAmb:[[:space:]]*//p' /proc/self/status"

Routing, at boot and now:

printf '%s\n' \
  '# route packets between per-VM taps and the host uplink' \
  'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' > /etc/sysctl.d/msks-egress.conf
sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/msks-egress.conf

The kernel module set, at boot and now:

printf '%s\n' tun nf_tables nft_chain_nat nft_masq nft_ct nft_reject \
  nf_reject_ipv4 nf_nat nf_conntrack nfnetlink_queue \
  > /etc/modules-load.d/msks.conf
modprobe tun nf_tables nft_chain_nat nft_masq nft_ct nft_reject \
  nf_reject_ipv4 nf_nat nf_conntrack nfnetlink_queue

Interactive egress consent needs nft_reject, nf_reject_ipv4, and nfnetlink_queue loaded — check with grep -w <module> /proc/modules (or lsmod) when a load landed quietly.

/dev/kvm for the daemon's user, picked up at that account's next login:

usermod -aG kvm <the-user-the-daemon-runs-as>

The systemd user service is the daemon user's own piece — leave the root shell and run it as that user. Write ~/.config/systemd/user/msksd.service with the unit below. Adjust the msksd path to where the install put it, and the uplink's default-route interface (default via 192.168.1.1 dev eno4 proto dhcp src 192.168.1.112 metric 100 gives it):

[Unit]
Description=msks daemon (workspaces as cloud-hypervisor microvms)

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/msks-caps --inh-caps=+net_admin,+net_bind_service --ambient-caps=+net_admin,+net_bind_service -- /path/to/msksd
Environment=MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED=true
Environment=MSKSD_EGRESS_UPLINK=<uplink>
RuntimeDirectory=msks
Restart=always
RestartSec=1
TimeoutStopSec=180s

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

Then enable it, as that user:

systemctl --user enable --now msksd.service
loginctl enable-linger <the-user-the-daemon-runs-as>

loginctl enable-linger is the one root command among these — it keeps the user manager, and the daemon, running across logouts and boots.

The daemon's workspace machinery execs cloud-hypervisor (the VMM).

Cloud Hypervisor's static release binary is the sanctioned VMM install — Debian's archive does not carry it.

curl -L -o cloud-hypervisor-static \
  https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/releases/latest/download/cloud-hypervisor-static
curl -L -o ch-remote-static \
  https://github.com/cloud-hypervisor/cloud-hypervisor/releases/latest/download/ch-remote-static
sudo install -m755 cloud-hypervisor-static /usr/local/bin/cloud-hypervisor
sudo install -m755 ch-remote-static /usr/local/bin/ch-remote-static

items.title: macOS on Apple Silicon hosts
items.text:
Running msks-setup-macos-host runs the macOS installer, which is expected to work on M3+ Macs. It installs the Lima virtual machine system (via Brew), and runs msksd within a Lima VM. The msks client runs on the Mac itself.

The msksd VM that msks-setup-macos-host creates from the shipped Lima template is the host that shares Mac folders into workspaces. The VM mounts them under its reserved prefix and forwards each attached share to the workspace that asked for it; see the mounts chapter's macOS section.

items.title: Sizing the msksd Lima VM
items.text:
The VM starts at the template's sizing — 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory, a 60 GiB disk — and the sizing flags change it at creation and on every re-run:

msks-setup-macos-host --cpus 8 --memory 16 --disk 200

A changed value stops the VM, edits its instance, and starts it again: running workspaces stop with the VM, and each starts again with msks start. Equal values change nothing, so the command is safe to re-run in scripts. The disk only grows: a smaller value refuses, naming both sizes — reclaim space with msks storage instead. The disk is sparse, so it fills on demand up to the size you set. The floors are 2 CPUs, 4 GiB of memory, and 20 GiB of disk: the VM must hold the daemon and a workspace.

When the VM's disk runs low, the daemon's storage warning and the 507 refusal name the same grow command. The fix is one re-run away.

items.title: Linux on Mac Hardware
items.text: It doesn't work on Asahi. An Apple Silicon host whose kernel runs KVM in NV mode does not yet deliver guest interrupts (#649): a workspace starts and its kernel boots deep into first boot, then stalls before ssh answers.

items.title: Uninstalling msks
items.text:
msks-setup-{debian,fedora,macos}-host --uninstall reverses the run. It stops and disables the msksd user service and removes its unit file and its enablement symlink; the stop lets the daemon finish its shutdown cycle, workspaces included. It turns linger off, removes the two /etc files the run landed, and removes the capability wrapper. It takes the executing user out of the kvm group; the tool keeps no record of which run added a membership, so any member leaves, and the summary names the adduser line that restores it. It strips the PATH block from ~/.profile and removes the cloud-hypervisor binary. Kernel modules already loaded stay loaded until the next reboot.

After the sysctl file leaves, sysctl --system re-applies every remaining sysctl.d file, the same set a boot applies. A second owner that wrote its own forwarding file keeps its setting. A live-only forwarder the tool never saw keeps its value too. On a host where no remaining file names net.ipv4.ip_forward, the live value the setup run set stays on until the next reboot. The summary names sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 for the operator who wants it off immediately.

The packages the run installed stay installed: they are shared packages, and other software on the host may use them. The uninstall summary prints the ones whose probes answer present, with a copy-paste apt-get remove --purge ... line. You can remove the ones nothing else needs yourself.

The uninstall run is idempotent the same way: a piece already gone is a line in the summary, not an error, and the first real refusal stops the run: the setup run's rule. --no-service holds its meaning: the service is left alone, every other piece still leaves.

items.title: The host doctor
items.text: The The host doctor chapter documents the msksd doctor command that can diagnose installation issues.

items.title: The alternative paths
items.text: A development host (this repository's checkout) runs the daemon through Nix and devenv. The Development environment chapter owns that path. A Mac developing from a checkout has its own chapter — Developing on a macOS host.

items.title: The workspace LLM proxy
items.text:
Every workspace can consume LLM endpoints through msksd. The daemon holds the provider credentials and the routing configuration; each workspace holds only its own proxy credential and talks to endpoints served on its own tap.

Provider keys never enter a workspace, and a workspace uses LLMs with its egress consent untouched. This holds even for a workspace with no egress at all (once one is attached), or a static workspace whose allowlist carries no providers: the daemon makes the upstream connection itself.

msks uses LiteLLM under the hood for this capability.

items.title: Routing modes
items.text:
The model list is one msks.yaml config file setting, llm_models. Its entries are spelled in YAML dict format. The MSKSD_LLM_MODELS environment variable can also be used: the environment form takes them comma-separated ala provider/model:api_base:api_key.

Here's an example of the config file format:

llm_models:
  - model_name: gpt-4o
    params:
      model: openai/gpt-4o
      api_base: https://api.openai.com/v1
      api_key: file:/etc/msksd/openai.key
  - model_name: claude-sonnet-4
    params:
      model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4
      api_key: cmd:pass show anthropic
      rpm: 10

A workspace addresses a model by its logical name: the part after the provider slash for a string entry, or the explicit model_name for a dict one. A request that gives no model, or a name the list does not carry, uses the first configured model. Known providers (openai, anthropic, cohere, mistral, groq, together_ai, deepseek, fireworks_ai) fill their default base when an entry gives none.

Dict keys accept kebab- or snake-case, params is a shorthand for LiteLLM's litellm_params. file:/cmd: indirection works on api_key/api_base inside the block.

An environment string overrides the config file's list wholesale. The colons of the string grammar split with two exceptions, so the common shapes all parse:

  • an entry whose key is a file: or cmd: reference keeps everything from the marker (paths and commands carry colons: openai/gpt-4o::file:/etc/msksd/openai.key);
  • a scheme-bearing base keeps its port and any key after its path (openai/gpt-4o:https://api.openai.com/v1:sk-...).

A single entry whose model name is * is passthrough mode. The entry's base gives one upstream, requests forward verbatim over httpx, and /models is discovered dynamically from the upstream. Every model the upstream serves is available with no further configuration.

llm_models:
  - model_name: "*"
    params:
      api_base: https://api.openai.com/v1
      api_key: file:/etc/msksd/openai.key

Any other list is multi-provider mode: the entries become a litellm router.

An empty list (the default) presents no LLM surface at all: nothing binds on any tap, and the per-workspace input chain admits no proxy port.

items.title: The Anthropic Messages route (for Claude API access)
items.text:
claude is preinstalled in every msks VM.

The LLM proxy serves /v1/messages, the Anthropic Messages API claude-code speaks.

Configuring the proxy exclusively for claude-code API access is one msks.yaml block. The passthrough form names the endpoint, and every model it serves is available:

llm_models:
  - model_name: "*"
    params:
      api_base: https://api.anthropic.com/v1
      api_key: file:/etc/msksd/anthropic.key

The environment form is equivalent: MSKSD_LLM_MODELS='*:https://api.anthropic.com/v1:file:/etc/msksd/anthropic.key'.

An Anthropic-compatible gateway works the same way: point api_base at the gateway's own base.

A multi-provider form serves claude-code beside other clients. An entry whose logical name is the model name claude-code sends answers that model's requests directly; a name the list does not carry falls to the first entry:

llm_models:
  - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-5
    params:
      model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5
      api_key: file:/etc/msksd/anthropic.key
  - model_name: gpt-4o
    params:
      model: openai/gpt-4o
      api_key: file:/etc/msksd/openai.key

With this list, a claude-code request for claude-sonnet-4-5 takes the first entry, and an OpenAI-shaped client asking for gpt-4o takes the second.

In passthrough mode the request forwards verbatim to the upstream's own /v1/messages endpoint. The upstream must serve the Messages API itself for this route: Anthropic's API, or any Anthropic-compatible gateway. The entry's key rides as x-api-key, and the anthropic-version and anthropic-beta headers forward with 2023-06-01 as the default version. A passthrough entry pointed at an OpenAI-shaped upstream still serves the OpenAI pair; the Messages route answers that upstream's own error.

A workspace that wants claude-code on the proxy must export a few envvars by hand. The base URL derives from the seeded MSKSWS_BASE_URL:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="${MSKSWS_BASE_URL%/v1}"
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="msks-local-proxy"

The token is a placeholder; it exists because claude-code refuses a base URL with no credential beside it. Set in a shell profile, the pair reaches every Anthropic SDK client in the workspace, not claude-code alone.

items.title: Subscription claude-code with no stored credentials
items.text:
The LLM proxy cannot successfully be used to access a subscription Anthropic account. Instead, you should almost certainly use the normal Anthropic subscription login process to connect to Claude Code.

But that process does leave Claude credentials on the VM.

If you want to keep Claude credentials off the VM even with an Anthropic subscription instead of an API key, an operator with a claude.ai subscription and no API billing can still run claude-code inside a workspace, with nothing credential-shaped left on the guest's disk: subscription login with RAM-only tokens. The tokens live in a tmpfs for the session and vanish at shutdown.

This is only useful if you use more than one coding agent on the same VM, and you distrust the other to not steal your Claude credentials. Otherwise, it's total overkill. It's better to just silo claude into its own workspace.

Subscription authentication is OAuth, and claude-code holds its tokens wherever it runs (~/.claude on Linux). No msks machinery can hold them for the guest. The proxy and the placeholder swap both present a static credential, and the OAuth token rotates on refresh. What the workspace can do is keep the token off the home volume, so a powered-off workspace holds nothing.

The threat this recipe answers. An agent sharing the workspace (another coding agent, a script a repository asked to run) reads the home volume as the same user. A disk-backed ~/.claude hands it the refresh token, which works from anywhere until you notice. The tmpfs narrows the exposure to sessions where claude-code itself is running. The home volume never carries the token at all. The full answer for untrusted agents is a separate workspace: another workspace's VM reads nothing of this one's, live or at rest.

Keep ~/.claude in RAM. Mount a tmpfs on it before the first login. Tokens, settings, and session history then live in memory alone, and a reboot drops them all:

mkdir -p ~/.claude
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o mode=700,uid="$USER" tmpfs ~/.claude

A workspace where mounting does not fit runs claude auth logout at the end of each session instead. Either way the home volume stays clean. A copied workspace or a home-volume backup carries no credential.

Log in with the paste-code flow. claude auth login prints an authorize URL. Open it on your own machine; any browser works, and the guest is never dialed. Authorize, copy the code the page shows, and paste it at the guest CLI's prompt. A reboot drops the tokens (the tmpfs again), and the next session logs in the same way.

The flow. The token exchange dials platform.claude.com. The session dials api.anthropic.com. claude-code's telemetry hosts (statsig, sentry) and its other non-essential calls dial too; exporting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 keeps them from asking at all.

A static workspace must allowlist the two entries that matter:

msks egress mode myws static --allow api.anthropic.com \
    --allow platform.claude.com

The flags replace the whole list; repeat them to keep entries the workspace already had.

An interactive workspace answers the two prompts instead.

items.title: Integration with the Pi coding agent
items.text:
Each msks VM ships with the pi coding agent installed. Each image bakes pinned Node and the pinned pi coding agent on every account's default PATH: the Debian/Fedora image under /usr/local, the NixOS image through its system profile.

The first-boot VM seed configures the clients: /etc/profile.d/msks-llm.sh exports MSKSWS_BASE_URL, built from the DHCP lease's gateway and the daemon's port. It also exports MSKSWS_API_KEY, a placeholder the proxy never reads: it exists for OpenAI-shaped clients that refuse an empty key.

A pi extension consumes these envvars so that /models within Pi works.

The pi extension is named llm-models.ts. It exists in /etc/skel and root's home. Every account the identity seed provisions copies the skeleton, so each login user ends up with the extension in ~/.pi/agent/extensions/, where pi discovers it. At every pi startup the extension makes one fetch of ${MSKSWS_BASE_URL}/models, aborted at 1.5 seconds, and registers the catalog under the msks provider, so /model always shows the daemon's live model list.

items.title: SIGHUP
items.text: A restart or SIGHUP of msksd is required in order to register changes to the LLM proxy settings.

items.title: Host share mounts
items.text:
A workspace can mount host directory trees into its guest. The daemon's config gives the allowed roots a guest's mounts must sit under via mount_host_roots, and -- on a VM-hosted daemon -- the trees its own VM carries. On the guest side, each workspace gives a host path, the absolute guest path it lands at, and a mode (ro or rw, defaulting to rw).

You can motify mount_host_roots Within the daemon hosts's ~/.config/msksd/msksd.yaml:

# the operator allows the roots (msksd.yaml; reloadable on SIGHUP)
mount_host_roots:
  - /srv/projects
  - /srv/refs

With this configuration active in the msksd daemon, you can successfully mount files from the host's /srv/projects and /srv/ref locations:

# a workspace mounts host paths (applies at its next start)
msks create ws1 --share /srv/projects:/mnt/projects
msks mount ws1 /srv/refs:/mnt/refs:ro
msks umount ws1 /srv/refs

items.title: What a mount is
items.text:
A workspace's mount gives a host path, an absolute guest path, and a mode. The guest path becomes a root-owned mount point inside the VM. The location must be absolute, below the filesystem root, outside the pseudo-filesystems (/proc, /sys, /dev, /run) and outside /home.

Two mounts of one workspace never overlap, and a host path appears once per workspace. Mounts follow next-start semantics, like resize: setting them never touches a running VM, and the next start attaches the current set. A restart after a change lands the new set and prunes the dropped one.

items.title: The mount gates
items.text:
Each host path checks two gates at set time:

  1. The policy gate (every host): the path, resolved against symlink escapes, must sit under one of the allowed roots under mount_host_roots. A path outside them is refused with the instruction to add it or a parent to the daemon's config. A symlink that resolves outside its allowed root is refused the same way.
  2. The mount gate (VM-hosted daemons, mount_host_mode: prefix): the path, translated under /mnt/msks, must sit under a root the daemon's VM actually has mounted. A path whose root is not mounted is refused with the instruction to recreate the VM from a template that mounts it. vz mounts are fixed at VM start, so a config edit cannot add one. This knob is typically only used on MacOS, to account for double-mounting under the Lima VM filesystem.

The spec grammar splits its fields on colons, so a host path containing one is inexpressible on the wire. --share and the TUI editor both refuse it, giving the field that the colon broke.

A mount attaches read-write unless it says ro: the trust decision is made before the mode matters (the root is allowed), and a mount that wants less says ro. Read-write mounts hold no exclusivity: any number of workspaces may attach the same tree.

items.title: The skip behavior
items.text: A start proceeds when a mount cannot attach caused by a root the reload removed from the allowed list, a path whose root the daemon's VM no longer mounts, a symlink that moved out from under its allowed root, or a path that vanished since the set. Each publishes an event (mount.skipped) giving the mount and the reason, and the row carries the standing marker (msks ls prints running, 1 mount skipped) until the config and the row agree again. The workspace's other mounts attach.

items.title: Coherence between guests
items.text: A host tree attaches read-write to any number of workspaces at once, and every attach forces virtiofs cache=never. This means data writes become coherent through the host page cache, and lockfile coordination (O_EXCL creates: git, cargo) works because the host kernel serializes it. Things that do not coordinate between guests on the same share: flock/fcntl locks (each attach is its own virtiofsd), and mmap coherence.

items.title: Shares on a macOS host
items.text:
On a Mac the daemon runs inside its own Linux VM (Lima over Apple's Virtualization.framework, on an M3-or-newer Mac), and a shared Mac folder crosses two hops to reach a workspace: vz virtiofs carries it from macOS into the daemon's VM under the reserved prefix and one virtiofsd per attached share carries it from there into the workspace guest.

The client speaks Mac paths throughout (--share ~/code:/mnt/code), and the daemon's prefix host mode does the translation before the two gates run. The Lima template mounts the invoking user's home under the prefix at VM creation, writable, so the common case needs no edit. A share root outside it (another user's home, a /Volumes tree) is a template edit plus VM recreation, and the mount gate's refusal suggests a remedy.

The far end of the share is the Mac's own volume, and its behaviors cross with the tree. Four of them are contract, not configuration:

items.title: macOS: Watchers poll
items.text:
File events do not cross virtiofs. Changes made on the Mac (an editor's save, a build's output) reach every attached workspace as data, promptly coherent the way coherence between guests describes, but no inotify event follows them: the share carries data, not notifications.

Watchers on shared trees run in polling mode (Vite's server.watch.usePolling setting, jest's --watchAll, or the tool's own poll option), and a tool that can watch only through events cannot watch a share at all. Signaling built on the same polling takes one care: a file's existence becomes visible before its content does (a writer creates empty, then fills). A poller therefore waits for a completion marker the writer emits after the data, never for the file itself.

items.title: macOS: Case and normalization follow the Mac volume
items.text:
The tree a workspace mounts is a Mac volume, and its naming rules cross with it. A Mac's default volume matches names case-insensitively, storing them as typed (case-preserving), and compares them Unicode-normalization-insensitively: a name typed composed (NFC) and the same name decomposed (NFD) are one file.

Tools inside the workspace that expect Linux naming can fail on the share. Two names differing only in case cannot coexist in one directory (a checkout holding both README and readme collapses them), and a tool comparing filename bytes sees NFD where the Mac accepted NFC.

Archive and package tooling that hashes or compares names byte-for-byte can report a mismatch against a Linux-built expectation. A tree that must keep Linux naming rules exactly must live in the workspace's own storage, not on a mount.

items.title: macOS: The rw single-writer contract
items.text:
An rw share allows the workspace as a writer. Locks taken inside the workspace hold there and stop there: flock and fcntl locks end at the workspace's own virtiofsd, and the Mac side honors none of them.

Finder, an open editor, or a Mac-side build writes past any lock the workspace took. Between workspaces, coherence between guests governs: lockfile creates (O_EXCL: git, cargo) serialize through the host kernel and work cross-workspace; flock/fcntl do not cross an attach.

Trees whose tools lock and treat the lock as the whole story (a cargo or bazel cache, a SQLite database, anything with a journal on disk) take one writer at a time: the workspace's, or the Mac's. A Mac that only reads the share (browsing in Finder, opening a file) travels the coherence contract. A Mac-side writer into a lock-using tree races the workspace.

items.title: macOS: External volumes stay busy while shared
items.text:
A file the stack holds open keeps its Mac volume mounted. A disk whose tree is shared into a running workspace therefore refuses to eject (the Finder reports the volume in use) until the workspace stops and its files close.

To allow the volume to unmount, msks stop on the workspace and eject the disk.

items.title: The plumbing
items.text:
Each attached share is one virtiofsd process using the platform's own virtiofsd package, spawned before the VM and stopped with it.

The default virtiofsd binary name resolves on PATH first and then the package's install locations off PATH, so the daemon finds it without configuration. MSKSD_VIRTIOFSD gives a different binary.

The mounts need virtiofsd 1.13.0 or newer: the identity translation and the read-only enforcement both landed upstream there, and an older binary refuses the daemon's arguments at start.

File ownership translates in both directions. Writes from the guest land on the host as the daemon's own user, whatever guest account made them. Host-side ownership stays advisory, as with a typical bind mount.

Files read back inside the guest present as the workspace's own user: the login user the workspace gives, or the image's built-in msks account when it gives none. The share's tree therefore reads as the logged-in user's files, and a file the guest creates stays writable by the account that created it.

Extended attributes remap under one host prefix (user.virtiofs.), so a guest cannot write host security labels or root-owned namespaces through the share.

items.title: Guest networking
items.text:
In msks, each workspace VM gets its own "tap": the VM's virtio-net NIC plugs into one end, the host kernel (nftables chains, the DHCP/DNS services, NAT) sits on the other.

A tap is a Linux TAP device — a virtual network interface created in software (/dev/tap, part of the kernel's TUN/TAP subsystem). Unlike a physical NIC, a program running on the host can open the tap and read/write raw Ethernet frames to it, so anything the VM sends out its NIC appears as packets arriving on the host-side tap, and vice versa.

Creating taps and assigning addresses requires a Linux capability CAP_NET_ADMIN, which is why msksd runs using systemd and a capability wrapper.

A workspace talks to the network only when it was created with egress: true, and when it does, every piece of the path lives in the daemon, where the guest cannot reach it.

For example:

curl -X POST .../api/v1/workspaces -d '{"id": "ws1", "egress": true}'

Or:

msks create ws1 --egress

This chapter covers the plumbing: the NIC, the tap, DHCP, DNS, NAT, and the forward that carries ssh and rsync into the workspace.

The consent layer that gates where a new connection may go is its own chapter: Egress consent holds the first packet of each new connection for an allow/deny decision over the decider channel, built on the same per-VM chain.

items.title: The path
items.text:
workspace VM ──virtio-net──► per-VM tap ──► per-VM nftables chain (host kernel)
                                              │  forward: guest source → uplink: accept;
                                              │  established replies back; all else drops
                                              │  input: only DHCP (67) and DNS (53) in
                                              ▼
                                     NAT (masquerade) → host uplink

Each egress-enabled workspace owns a dedicated /30 carved from the configured pool (MSKSD_EGRESS_SUBNET, default 172.31.0.0/16): the guest holds the first host address, the daemon-side tap the second.

The workspace's tap name, nftables table, and NIC MAC derive deterministically from the workspace id, and the pool slice is recorded on the workspace row at first attach. Stop/start cycles, daemon restarts, and even digest collisions between workspace ids therefore keep the same address.

msksd is the DHCP server. The DHCP offer gives the tap as gateway and as DNS server, and a small forwarder on the tap answers port 53 by relaying to the host's own upstream (MSKSD_EGRESS_DNS_UPSTREAM, or the first nameserver in the host's /etc/resolv.conf).

The resolver speaks UDP. TCP/53 has no listener, so a query needing TCP fallback (DNSSEC validation, very large RRsets) fails fast. The forwarder answers queries from its own guest only. Anything else arriving on the tap is dropped unread, so a spoofed-source datagram cannot turn the daemon into a reflection amplifier. The resolver also grows the naming layer: query cache, name learning for prompts, and the lockout that keeps DNS from being routed around, all behind that same offered resolver.

items.title: What the chain enforces
items.text:
The per-VM table hooks two places, both scoped to the workspace's tap:

  • Forward. The guest's own source address may leave via the uplink, and the replies to connections the guest established may come back. Everything else across the tap drops: traffic from a spoofed source, traffic headed anywhere but the uplink (which is what blocks one workspace from reaching another's tap), and inbound the guest never asked for. Nothing outside initiates a connection into a workspace.
  • Input. The guest may reach a fixed set of ports on the host through its tap: DHCP (67), the resolver (53), the interceptor's listener while armed, and the LLM proxy port when one is configured. Everything else from the tap drops before the host's own services (the API listener among them), so guest root cannot port-scan the host.

What the chain deliberately permits depends on the workspace's consent mode (the egress consent chapter). In allow mode, the destination of a guest-initiated connection is unconstrained: any host reachable through the host uplink is reachable. In static and interactive modes, every new flow passes a destination gate first.

items.title: What runs where
items.text:
On the host: the tap, its address, the per-VM nftables table, the NAT masquerade on the uplink, the DHCP service, and the DNS forwarder are all owned by msksd. It runs as a dedicated service user holding exactly two ambient capabilities. CAP_NET_ADMIN covers taps and their addresses, the nftables tables, and (because ambient capabilities survive exec) the workspace VMM opening its tap. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE covers the DHCP and DNS listeners, UDP 67 and 53. Nothing in the daemon's process tree runs as uid 0; /dev/kvm reaches the VMM through the kvm group. The per-tap service listeners (the interceptor, the LLM proxy, and the probe service) bind ports above 1024 by default. A setting that gives a privileged port needs the capability. The host's firewall is never touched. Containment stays inside the host by design.

Inside the guest: nothing msks-specific. The image overlay ships a systemd-networkd DHCP unit (see images.md); the kernel's virtio_net driver configures the NIC, DHCP configures the address and resolver.

A workspace created with "egress": false presents no NIC at all. The posture is available on every backend, and it needs zero enforcement machinery.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Variable Default Meaning MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED false Arm the egress plumbing at daemon start (the dev daemon and the NixOS module enable it) MSKSD_EGRESS_SUBNET 172.31.0.0/16 The pool per-workspace /30s are carved from MSKSD_EGRESS_UPLINK eth0 The host uplink NAT hides guests behind MSKSD_EGRESS_DNS_UPSTREAM resolv.conf Where the forwarder relays queries MSKSD_EGRESS_LEASE_S 3600 DHCP lease lifetime MSKSD_EGRESS_DNS_TIMEOUT_S 3.0 How long the forwarder waits on the upstream MSKSD_IP_TOOL / MSKSD_NFT_TOOL ip / nft The plumbing tools' paths

A ruleset apply hands nft a file under the daemon's state directory and passes it by path, so the tool configured above runs with the daemon's own read access to that directory. A wrapper that execs the real nft as another user -- or in another mount namespace -- must carry that access along.

Egress needs the daemon to hold CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (the dev host's wrapper and the NixOS module grant exactly those two) and a kernel that routes. The host ships net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 as a boot-time sysctl.d setting, and the daemon verifies it at startup. A daemon that reads 0 refuses every egress workspace with a cause that gives the sysctl key.

Debian and Fedora deployment hosts run their setup tool, msks-setup-debian-host or msks-setup-fedora-host, and the Installation chapter describes the tool end to end. For egress it matters that the tool installs a capability wrapper, lands the sysctl and the module set this section lists, and registers the daemon's systemd user service with MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED=true and the detected uplink. An operator who sets MSKSD_EGRESS_ENABLED=false arms nothing, and every egress workspace then refuses to boot with the cause given.

items.title: Reaching guest services (msks forward)
items.text:
Egress is the guest's outbound path. The forward websocket (msks forward, issue) is the client's inbound one, and it uses the same per-VM tap. The daemon dials the workspace's deterministic tap address on the port the caller gives and bridges raw bytes over its authenticated websocket API. The CLI chapter's msks forward section covers the stdio and --local shapes and the close-code contract.

The workspace image meets the forward with a TCP service plane of its own: sshd (the image's Debian package, enabled) and rsync. sshd listens on all interfaces once the guest's NIC has its address. A boot-time unit holds the port behind DHCP, with a 15s ceiling so a slow lease never blocks it for long. Every login is a key login: PasswordAuthentication no, and root may log in with a key only (PermitRootLogin prohibit-password). Host keys are generated on the workspace's first boot into its persistent root overlay, so a stop/start cycle presents the same host key: the known_hosts entry you recorded on first login keeps matching. The entry lives under the workspace's immutable id, so a workspace recreated under the same name is a new id with a fresh cache: it trusts its own first-boot host keys instead of refusing the first instance's. A workspace without egress carries the same image unchanged: its forward is refused at the API with close code 4501 before any dial, and its console is the virtio-console getty.

items.title: The workspace ssh identity
items.text:
A workspace created through the client carries the operator's key as its ssh identity (issues). identity_file (or MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE) is queried for your private key. Its derived public half travels with the create request, and the first boot plants that line into authorized_keys for root and the workspace's login user.

The daemon stores and seeds the public ssh key only. Its database never holds a private half and its key fetch carries no private field at all. The public half persists across daemon restarts and workspace stop/start: it lives on the workspace's row, and a stop/start cycle serves the same line again. The seed composes the identity's script with any user_data payload as MIME siblings, so a workspace can carry both.

The daemon validates the supplied line by shape: a label in the algorithm-name charset, fields, base64 body, and a blob whose embedded algorithm name agrees with its label. It annotates the line with its own provenance comment (msks-client:<id>). A supplied key is accepted at any type: the guest's sshd, the platform's own, is the authority on which keys it will authenticate.

With the identity materialized, the usual client shapes work over the forward:

msks forward myws 22 --local 2201 &
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -p 2201 root@127.0.0.1
rsync -e 'ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -p 2201' \
    -av ./site/ root@127.0.0.1:/root/site/

The same login works as the workspace's login user (ssh -i ... -p 2201 alice@127.0.0.1, the name msks create --user recorded), whose home lives on the persistent /home volume. A workspace created before records no user of its own. Log in as root, or as msks, the account the image itself ships, given directly.

msks ssh is the zero-step form of the same login: it boots the workspace if needed and runs ssh with the forward as its ssh ProxyCommand.

It signs through the operator's own agent when it holds the workspace's key (ssh-add; matched on the key material, so the file the key came from and its name do not matter). Otherwise it stages the operator identity from identity_file in a transient in-process ssh-agent, and the private half never becomes a file.

It logs in as the workspace's login user by default, and as root for a workspace that records none. -l root is also the recovery login; see the CLI chapter's msks ssh section. When the command itself booted the workspace, it holds the connection back until the guest accepts the workspace key. A probe login retries behind the first boot's identity seeding, so the first attempt lands as a session instead of Permission denied (publickey).

msks rsync is the copy form of the same: it runs the host rsync over the forward with the identity staged in memory, and the copy opens its own forward. msks rsync devbox -- -aP src/ :src/ targets the login user's home; root@:/root/x targets root-owned paths. The CLI chapter's msks rsync section has the details.

The user's own ssh config may carry the same workflow for plain ssh invocations; one wildcard block serves every workspace:

Host msks-*
    ProxyCommand sh -c 'exec msks forward "${1#msks-}" 22' _ %h
    UserKnownHostsFile ~/.cache/msks/%h/known_hosts
    StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
    IdentitiesOnly yes
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.cache/msks/%h.ctl
    ControlPersist 10m

ssh msks-devbox, rsync -aP src/ msks-devbox:/src/, git clone msks-devbox:srv/proj.git, and VS Code Remote-SSH work against the alias; ControlMaster shares one forward connection across concurrent invocations. The block sets no User: plain ssh logs in as its own default, the local username. That is the workspace's recorded login user for the operator who created it (the name msks create --user planted; ssh -l alice reaches a workspace another operator's name recorded). A workspace that records no user dials root, the account every seed provisions a key for. The alias block gives the operator's own key with IdentityFile, the same file identity_file points at. Those paths are the client cache root's defaults and stay where the block writes them. OpenSSH reads its own config, so MSKSC_CACHE_DIR (the variable the devenv shell presets for its command forms) moves only the msks ssh/msks rsync state. A relocated cache takes the alias block's paths with it only when you edit the block to match. msks ssh is the command form that carries the identity per-session from memory instead. Plain ssh invocations against the alias need the file. The ProxyCommand runs msks in the user's environment, so MSKSC_URL, MSKSC_TOKEN, and MSKSC_CAFILE must be set there. ssh -l root msks-devbox is the recovery login. -A forwards the operator's own agent into the workspace, and so does msks ssh -- -A, which rewrites the request onto the same socket without the alias block.

items.title: An operator-supplied key for one workspace
items.text: msks create --pubkey FILE (issue) builds the workspace around a public key chosen for that one create (the key that ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub gives, a hardware token's key, any well-formed OpenSSH line) instead of the configured key. The supplied line travels to the daemon at its own key type and is accepted at any type: the guest's sshd, the platform's own, is the authority on which keys it will authenticate. The daemon re-annotates the line with its provenance comment and seeds it like any other identity. Its database holds the public half only.

items.title: Pushing code out with your own credentials
items.text:
Written for the developer working inside a workspace: your repo's remote (GitHub, a private GitLab host, anything reachable on the network) accepts a push only with your credentials, and the workspace has none of them and should hold none. The workflow is one login with agent forwarding, after which a push from inside the workspace works exactly as it does on your own machine.

On your client machine, load the key into your agent (ssh-add), then log in through the forward with -A:

ssh -A msks-devbox

Inside the session your agent is present: ssh-add -l lists your keys, and every ssh the session starts (git's included) offers them to the remote, so the ordinary push needs no extra setup:

git -C ~/work/proj push origin main

The credential stays on your machine. The agent travels the connection as a socket, so nothing is written to the workspace's disks, the image, or the seed; when the session closes, the workspace keeps no copy of the key. Host-key checking for the remote behaves as anywhere else (the workspace has its own ~/.ssh/known_hosts).

Two msks-specific details:

  • msks ssh my-workspace -- -A, the one-command login with forwarding, forwards your agent too. The command rewrites the request onto the socket SSH_AUTH_SOCK gives, the same agent the alias form above forwards, so no ssh-config block is needed. The plain alias (ssh -A msks-devbox) and the forward port directly (ssh -A -i ~/.cache/msks/msks-devbox.key -p 2201 msks@127.0.0.1) work as always.
  • With the alias's ControlMaster, the agent arrives only on the connection that creates the master. If you connected earlier without -A, close the master first (ssh -O exit msks-devbox), then reconnect with -A, or wait out the ControlPersist window.

What the network allows depends on the workspace's consent mode. allow reaches any destination beyond the host without a grant: remotes, package mirrors, any host reachable through the uplink. static and interactive gate each destination first (the egress consent chapter covers the semantics).

Guest-initiated connections aimed at the host itself stay dropped in every mode (only DHCP and the resolver answer it).

items.title: Backend support
items.text: Egress is a local-backend feature; the consent API itself is enforcement-agnostic (see “Local-only semantics” in Egress consent). A future backend can therefore drive a different mechanism from the same model. The no-NIC posture works everywhere: a workspace created with "egress": false presents no NIC whatever runs it.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text: start arms the tap and services before the VMM boots (the VMM opens the tap by name); stop, kill, and delete tear the tap, its chain, and its services down again. A failed boot unwinds its own plumbing: no half-open path outlives a failed workspace start.

items.title: Placeholder secrets
items.text:
A workspace need never hold a real secret. Instead, it may hold a placeholder: a sentinel token the operator mints once and pastes into the workspace. The secrets page in the TUI and the msks secret command are how you interact with secrets.

The daemon swaps the sentinel for the real secret on the wire. The real secret is the operator's own value, supplied at mint: a file or stdin on the CLI, or a masked field on the TUI form.

The actual secret lives in msksd's secret store (the database's per-recipient age-encrypted blobs) and in the daemon's unlock cache during its window. The secret store is encrypted using the ssh identity.

A mint covers workspaces. With no target it is the daemon-wide placeholder valid on every workspace's tap. An operator running several workspaces against one daemon mints the credential once and distributes the same sentinel everywhere. A workspace target scopes the row to only those workspaces.

The in-flight swap itself is the egress interceptor; the next section documents it. If you don't care much about how this works, you can safely skip it.

items.title: The interceptor (the swap on the wire)
items.text:
A workspace covered by at least one live placeholder is armed. A live placeholder is minted, unrevoked, and unexpired; the coverage is the workspace's own scoped placeholders, or any daemon-wide placeholder while the workspace accepts one.

When armed, the daemon redirects that workspace's TCP flows toward ports 80 and 443 into an in-process HTTPS/HTTP proxy, and the swap happens there. The proxy is mitmproxy, embedded in msksd. Mitmproxy runs one process serving every armed workspace, one listener per workspace's tap, so a guest that spoofs another workspace's source address still lands on its own tap's placeholders.

What each request gets:

  • The swap. The sentinel is exchanged for the real secret in every request header and every query-string pair (duplicate keys included) when the destination matches the placeholder's allowlist (exact host or label-anchored suffix, as minted). Request bodies are not scanned: the sentinel travels headers and URLs, and an operator pasting it into a body payload sends it nowhere the placeholder covers. The origin sees the real secret; the workspace never holds it. On HTTPS, the connection's TLS handshake (its SNI) gives the destination, and the request's Host header is pinned to that same name: a guest cannot claim one name in the handshake and route by another in the header (domain fronting). On plain HTTP the request is dialed by the Host header's name, for the same binding.
  • The splice. An HTTPS destination no placeholder of this workspace covers is relayed undecrypted: the origin's real certificate reaches the workspace, pinned clients keep working, and the sentinel travels raw.
  • The sighting. A sentinel seen toward a destination its own allowlist misses (while another placeholder decrypts the flow) passes through unrewritten and publishes a secret.sighting event on the events channel. The same is true for a sentinel a workspace holds no covering row for. A daemon-wide sentinel used from a workspace scoped against it, or another workspace's scoped sentinel, reads as an off-allowlist sighting: the cross-workspace leak is announced, never serviced. A revoked or expired sentinel passes through the same way; its placeholder is gone, so there is nothing to swap and nothing to report.
  • QUIC stays down while armed. The workspace's UDP flows toward port 443 are dropped, so browsers fall back to the TCP flow the redirect owns: nothing routes around the interceptor.

While a workspace is armed, the redirect takes its web egress (TCP 80 and 443) before the kernel's consent queue, so the interceptor runs the consent gate for exactly those flows. Every web connection is decided on the name the wire carries: the TLS handshake's SNI on HTTPS, the Host header on plain HTTP. The verdict is bound to the address the naming memory holds for the connection. A name claiming an address it never resolved to keys by the address.

A static workspace's allowlist gates its web traffic by that name. An interactive workspace's web connections hold through the same decider endpoints, rows, durations, and session memory every other port uses; msks egress watch and the TUI answer them like any other hold.

An allowed web connection takes the splice or swap path above. A denied one is answered locally with an HTTP 403 giving consent as the reason: the handshake completes against the daemon's interception CA, the request refuses, and nothing forwards. A client that pins the origin's real certificate fails its handshake instead; it is refused closed either way.

Each swap publishes a secret.swap event; mint, revoke, expiry, and unlock publish their own (secret.mint, secret.revoke, secret.expiry, secret.unlock). All six travel the events websocket beside the workspace lifecycle events.

Each gives the placeholder's row id, its workspace and name, and a timestamp. The row id is the durable handle, because the row itself retires on revoke and expiry. A swap or sighting also gives the destination the wire saw; a mint gives the allowlist it was minted with; revoke, expiry, and unlock carry the identity alone.

The msks tui secrets page's audit view (e from the page) shows every workspace's events newest first, daemon-wide. The newest hundred recorded mints, revokes, expiries, and unlocks replay onto it when the view opens, and swaps and sightings stream in live. The off-allowlist sighting is highlighted as the exfil signal, with a header line stating the detection boundary above. Kind and workspace filters narrow the view; a daemon-wide row's events cover every workspace, a scoped row's its members.

We fail-closed on the swap path. A secret the store cannot serve, or a row the database cannot read answers the request locally with a 502 instead of forwarding it. A request that still carries the sentinel never leaves the host.

For TLS connections, the interceptor presents each connection a leaf certificate signed by the daemon's one interception CA. Every workspace's guest trusts the same certificate its seed staged: the identity seed writes /etc/msks/interceptor-ca.crt at first boot, and the trust-store exports and the NixOS fold register it. A workspace whose guest already trusts that CA sees HTTPS toward allowlisted destinations validate normally from the first placeholder. When the daemon's certificate changes under a workspace that already booted (the move from an earlier per-workspace CA, or a future CA rotation), the next boot renews the seed. The seed is rebuilt carrying the daemon's certificate with an instance-id suffix keyed to it. cloud-init re-provisions (the seed script is idempotent, and the operator's payload re-executes with it), and the fold re-registers the fresh certificate. The splice leg needs none of this: it presents the origin's own certificate.

The listeners bind one shared port on each armed tap address (interceptor_port, default 8643; see the key reference). Upstream connections are verified against the CA bundle mitmproxy ships (certifi's Mozilla list), not the platform's own store; pointing verification at the platform bundle is a setting the certification effort brings, never a code change.

items.title: The seeded probe placeholder
items.text: A fresh daemon seeds one placeholder itself at first-time startup: the daemon-wide row named probe, allowlisting secretprobe.msks, carrying the fixed credential blob bXNrczptc2tz as its secret. It exists so an operator can verify interception from inside a workspace with zero minting (the probe endpoint). Its sentinel never needs to be treated as a secret: the credential it swaps to is public and gates nothing beyond the probe's own ok page.

items.title: The probe endpoint
items.text:
The daemon serves one deliberately ordinary HTTPS service every workspace can reach: https://secretprobe.msks/, an emulated external endpoint protected by HTTP basic auth (username msks, password msks). It exists so an operator can verify from inside a workspace that secret interception works end to end. The ok page can only exist when the whole chain ran: redirect, TLS splice, leaf mint, and the sentinel-to-secret swap.

The daemon seeds the machinery itself at first-time startup, and the interception CA is installed at first boot. The seeded placeholder is the daemon-wide row named probe, whose secret is the base64 of the whole credential bXNrczptc2tz. Nothing is left to do by hand. The verification:

# on the host: read the seeded sentinel (token-gated API)
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://msksd/api/v1/probe

# inside the workspace: the sentinel rides as the raw Basic blob
curl -H "Authorization: Basic <sentinel>" https://secretprobe.msks/
ok

A request that reaches the service has already passed the nft redirect (guest TCP 80/443 to the per-tap interceptor listener), the splice tier (the SNI matched an allowlisted entry), and the daemon CA's leaf mint. The swap then rewrote the raw blob into a well-formed credential. The interceptor's upstream dial was repointed to the service's own per-tap port (probe_port, default 8644) and verified against the service CA the daemon mints. The guest's 443 is the redirect's port. The service listener binds the setting's unprivileged number, which a host wildcard cannot squat. The service validated the fixed pair. A broken link answers distinctly: a TLS failure points at the splice or the CA, a 401 points at the swap (or a wrong credential), a timeout points at the redirect.

The endpoint performs one action: it answers the fixed credential with ok. It reads no workspace state, accepts no commands, and returns no other data. The credentials are a fixed probe value shared by every deployment, and the endpoint gates nothing beyond its own ok page. That is also why the seeded row's sentinel is served back over the token-gated API (GET /api/v1/probe): a token holder already owns the daemon.

Two reachability notes. The probe answers only while the workspace is armed. A workspace scoped against daemon-wide placeholders (no covering row of its own) never arms.
