Its direct dial to secretprobe.msks:443 finds nothing admitted and times out. That posture is the documented way to opt a workspace out of interception entirely.

items.title: VM-specific CA configuration
items.text: The guest's trust in its own interception CA is installed at first boot on both images. Debian guests link it into the system trust store. Both guests export three variables for the CA. SSL_CERT_FILE points at a bundle of the platform's own roots with the CA appended. The variable replaces the default lookup, so the bundle must carry both. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS serves node-based clients, and GIT_SSL_CAINFO points git at the same bundle. NixOS's /etc/profile reads no profile.d. Its sanctioned /etc/profile.local hook sources the same exports, which also brings the LLM proxy's environment alive there.

items.title: The mint flow
items.text:
Uses msks secret mint to mint a new credential from the command line UI.

$ op read 'op://Vault/github/credential' \
    | msks secret mint --name github_api \
        --dest api.github.com --secret-file -
minted */github_api for api.github.com
sentinel: mskssec2_9Jm3...kQ
  • The value is the operator's own secret: a file's contents, or stdin for --secret-file - (the example pipes it from a password manager, so it never touches disk). It is whitespace-stripped at both ends and never accepted as a command-line argument, because argv lands in process lists and shell history. It is stored as ciphertext blobs and never echoed; the mint reply carries the sentinel, not the value. The client and the daemon may sit on different machines: the value travels the token-authenticated TLS API. The mint stores ciphertext only: one age-encrypted blob per covering workspace's identity key, and the plaintext travels the daemon's unlock cache until its window ends (below). A covering workspace whose key is outside the store's capable set (ssh-ed25519, ssh-rsa), or that carries no identity key at all, refuses the mint with the workspace named.
  • The mint above carries no workspace target: it is the daemon-wide mint: one row, one mskssec2_ sentinel, valid on every workspace's tap toward the minted destinations. A workspace created later is covered from its first boot; coverage acts as policy, not as a snapshot of the workspace set at mint time.
  • --workspace scopes the mint: --workspace myws (exactly today's single-workspace placeholder), or a comma list (--workspace ci,deploy) for several: one row, one mskssec1_ sentinel, one coverage set either way. A mint produces a single sentinel whether it targets every workspace or a set of one or several; the same label can live on the daemon-wide row and on scoped rows beside it, one row per label per coverage set.
  • --dest repeats: an exact host (api.github.com) binds the swap to that host; a suffix (.github.com) binds it to every host under that domain. A placeholder carries one coverage set, one allowlist, one secret; per-workspace destination scoping stays available by minting a scoped placeholder instead.
  • --ttl SECONDS gives the placeholder a lifetime; without it the placeholder lives until revoked. msks secret renew extends a lifetime in place: the sentinel never changes and nothing is re-delivered.
  • The CLI prints the sentinel at mint. The listing and the audit omit it (msks secret ls never shows one). The daemon serves the row's sentinel back on demand over the token-authenticated API, through the msks tui secrets page's Enter-on-a-row panel, so a sentinel that scrolled away reads back from the daemon. The operator's value alone is never echoed back.

items.title: TUI minting
items.text:
The msks tui secrets page mints too. c opens the form: name, repeatable destinations, coverage (the daemon-wide row, or a multi-select of the workspaces the tree's own list offers), the lifetime (unbounded by default, an hour to thirty days beside it), and the value.

The submit checks the store (msks secret check's endpoint) before it mints. A refusal (a store that cannot answer writes, a name collision on the chosen coverage set, a blank value) gives itself on the form, with the fields kept for a retry.

A successful mint answers with the sentinel's panel. The sentinel opens masked, its prefix giving the reach and its body rendering as bullets. A Show action reveals and hides it again. An OSC 52 clipboard copy works over ssh too, where the terminal honors it, and needs no reveal. The display ends with the panel. Enter (or a click) on a listing row opens the same panel again. The page fetches the row's sentinel from the daemon and shows it, so the sentinel reads back on demand. The panel is one surface for the row, opened at mint and after. Closing the panel clears its text.

items.title: Revoking a mint
items.text:
The TUI allows this via "x".

msks secret revoke --name github_api retires the daemon-wide row of that label everywhere at once. msks secret revoke --workspace myws --name github_api retires the scoped row whose coverage is exactly that set. The targeting mirrors the mint's, and msks secret renew selects its row the same way. msks secret ls lists every row with its coverage (* for the daemon-wide row, the workspace list scoped).

A workspace can exempt itself from daemon-wide placeholders: msks create --secret-coverage scoped (or msks secret coverage myws scoped later) means only placeholders minted directly at that workspace arm it. A daemon-wide sentinel used from a scoped workspace publishes an off-allowlist sighting and swaps nothing. Every new workspace accepts daemon-wide coverage unless its own setting says scoped, and flipping the setting back to all arms it with any live daemon-wide row.

items.title: The unlock window
items.text: The daemon holds no plaintext of its own: a mint leaves only the per-recipient ciphertext blobs, and the plaintext returns through an operator's unlock. The client decrypts the blobs with the workspace identity's private half and posts the values back over the token-authenticated API (POST /api/v1/secrets/unlock, after GET /api/v1/secrets/pending serves the ciphertext and opens the session window the unlock requires).

items.title: The client's half
items.text:
The unlock reads the identity key file the client already uses for ssh: identity_file (the client config, ~/.config/msks/msks.yaml) or MSKSC_IDENTITY_FILE. It decrypts only the blobs that key opens. Possession of the private key is the authority for a value, proven by the unwrap itself. An operator without the key receives ciphertext, uploads nothing, and the daemon stays cold for those rows; two operators keyed to different workspaces each unlock their own.

An agent-held key cannot unlock: ssh-agent exposes signing, and the unwrap needs the private key material directly, so the unlock reads the file where it lives (ssh login still resolves through the agent). A passphrase-encrypted key file prompts once per session: the passphrase loads the identity and every row then decrypts through it.

Three surfaces run the flow:

  • The TUI at start. The tree's mount offers the unlock against the daemon's locked rows: a warm cache stays silent, a cold one with the key present unlocks itself, and the passphrase prompt (when the file is encrypted) is the modal the session opens with. The secrets page's u action runs the same flow on demand, so a window that lapsed mid-session heals the moment it is seen. The page's STATE column (locked / open) and msks secret ls's state column carry the lock state row by row.
  • msks secret unlock, the scripting surface: fetch pending, decrypt, upload, and print one line per unlocked row plus the rows the key could not open. Rows whose ciphertext failed to open give the re-mint they need; rows with no stanza for this key are another operator's and stay ciphertext. The command without a configured identity gives identity_file and exits nonzero.

The window is MSKSD_SECRET_STORE_UNLOCK_TIMEOUT_S (default 86400 seconds, one day). The timer resets on an unlock POST itself (an operator action carrying plaintext) and on nothing else: websocket traffic, keepalives, and scheduled tasks never extend it. Zero holds plaintext only while at least one operator websocket stays connected: the last disconnect drops it, and an unlock over HTTP alone holds nothing past the reply.

Until an unlock stands, the interceptor's swap path refuses a carried sentinel with a named locked error: HTTP 423, msks: locked: no operator session within the unlock window. The request never reaches the origin, and the sentinel never passes through as a value. An unlock also re-encrypts the row's blobs to its current recipient set, so a coverage edit or a workspace key rotation heals at the next operator session.

items.title: Where the real secret lives
items.text:
A mint stores ciphertext blobs in the daemon's database: one age file per covering workspace identity key, wrapped to that workspace's ssh public half, the same file format the reference age tool writes. The daemon holds no key that opens them: only the workspace identity's private half (kept on the operator's client machine) unwraps a blob, which is the whole design: the client decrypts, the daemon swaps. Values exist in plaintext only in the operator's memory, the token-authenticated request, and the daemon's unlock cache for the window.

The per-recipient blobs are the store. The workspace identity keys decide who can read: back up the client machine's identity files alongside the daemon's database. A database copy alone carries ciphertext nobody can open, and a lost identity file means re-minting the values.

items.title: msksd.yaml examples
items.text:
You can change the secret store unlock timeout.

# the unlock window: how long unlocked plaintext lives in the
# daemon after the unlock POST that supplied it
secret_store_unlock_timeout_s: 86400.0

The store itself needs no configuration: the blobs live in the daemon's database beside the placeholder rows, and the only secret-bearing setting is the window above.

items.title: At-rest encryption
items.text: Every minted value is ciphertext at rest (a per-recipient age blob in the database), and no configuration choice changes that posture. The ssh identities, the database, and the token hashes keep their own house postures; the blobs give the secrets' one, and the blob's recipient list is exactly the row's coverage.

items.title: The audit trail
items.text:
Mint, revoke, expiry, and unlock append a row to the daemon database: the placeholder's coverage (the daemon-wide row, or the workspace list), name, destination allowlist, and a timestamp (msks secret ls lists placeholders; the audit view is /api/v1/secrets/audit).

Expiry fires from the status watcher's periodic sweep, which publishes a secret.expiry event and re-evaluates the covered workspaces' redirects in the same pass. The last placeholder's retirement stands the interception down, and one revoke or expiry retires the whole row everywhere at once. The secret value and the sentinel appear nowhere in the audit or the events. The value travels its mint request alone and is never echoed. The sentinel appears only in the mint reply and the on-demand row fetch, never in the audit or the event stream.

items.title: Workspace storage
items.text:
Every workspace owns exactly two persistent artifacts, created with the workspace and kept for its whole life:

  • the root overlay: a qcow2 copy-on-write file over the workspace's base image. Everything the guest writes to the root filesystem (an apt install, an /etc edit) lands in the overlay; the shared base stays pristine, so every workspace on that image starts from an identical, unmodified root.
  • the /home volume: an ext4 filesystem attached as a second virtio-blk disk the guest mounts at /home. User data lives here, outside the root, so it survives even a full factory reset.

Both artifacts have lifetimes separate from the VM's: stop powers the machine off and keeps the data; start boots the same overlay and volume again. Only delete (and factory reset, for the overlay alone) removes them.

items.title: Local backend layout
items.text:
<state_dir>/
├── vms/<workspace_id>/
│   ├── root.qcow2        # the root overlay (plus the VM's runtime files)
│   └── seed.img          # the cidata seed (user_data workspaces only)
└── volumes/
    └── <workspace_id>.ext4   # the /home volume (sparse ext4)

The overlay is created with qemu-img create -f qcow2 -F raw -b <base rootfs>: a one-level chain, never nested overlays. Its backing file is the rootfs recorded at workspace create, so a workspace always runs the image version it was created with: importing a newer image changes what new workspaces boot, never existing ones. (Rebasing an overlay onto a newer base exists as a qemu-img operation and may become an explicit "upgrade workspace image" action later; it never happens implicitly.)

The home volume is a sparse ext4 file. An idle volume costs its metadata, not its nominal size, and it grows as the guest writes.

The seed exists exactly when the workspace was created with user_data. It is a kilobytes-small iso9660 image labeled cidata, built with mkisofs (genisoimage) and attached to the VM read-only. It is installed mode 0600 because the payload can embed tokens; its staging directory is 0700, and the database file that records the payload is 0600. It lives in the workspace's vm directory, so it survives stop/start and dies with the workspace. Factory reset keeps it (it is immutable create-time input, so the reset workspace re-provisions from it), and docs/images.md describes what runs the payload.

A start heals missing artifacts: if the overlay or the volume file is absent (a crash mid-create, or a workspace row created before this scheme existed), the daemon recreates it before the VM boots. Data that exists is never touched.

Creation is atomic per artifact. Each file is built under a private temporary name and installed with one rename, and a failed create rolls back what it made. A missing tool, ENOSPC, or a partial write leaves nothing at the final path, so the retry starts from a clean pair instead of booting a blank disk. A daemon crash mid-create can still leave a finished artifact (or its *.tmp scratch) behind; the removal helpers sweep the scratch files, and the next create reports any leftover instead of adopting it.

Workspace create never reuses an existing artifact. A file found where a new workspace's overlay or volume would live fails the create with a named error. That file is the debris of a previous workspace of the same id, and adopting it silently would hand the new workspace the old one's data. Clear the files and create again.

items.title: Sizing
items.text:
Both sizes are set at workspace create and configurable three ways. Per request: root_mib / home_mib on workspace create. Per daemon: MSKSD_ROOT_MIB, default 10240, and MSKSD_HOME_MIB, default 20480. Per image: the catalog's manifest carries the cmdline the guest boots, which pairs with the sizes. The overlay's virtual size never drops below its base image's size: a smaller disk would truncate the base filesystem.

Create is not the only time sizes move: POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/resize (msks resize) revisits them on a stopped workspace:

  • the /home volume grows or shrinks. The daemon first quiets the filesystem's journal with e2fsck -fy. A volume a hard stop left dirty is corrected here; corrections are that tool's job, not an error. Then resize2fs moves the filesystem and the file follows. A grow truncates the file up first. A shrink truncates down only after the filesystem agreed. resize2fs refuses to shrink below the blocks in use, and that refusal reaches the caller as a named 409: free data in the workspace or shrink less.
  • the root overlay grows only, measured against the overlay's actual virtual size (create clamps it to the base image's size, so it can sit above the row). Its partition table and root filesystem belong to the guest, and the boot's cloud-init growpart fills the larger device on the next start for free. Shrinking it is a factory reset, not a resize.

A resize carries the home-volume moves' guards (free lifecycle statuses, the placement check, the move-lock against a concurrent boot). The artifact files are the truth each side moves. The grow gate reads the overlay's actual virtual size; create clamps it to the base image, and a corrupt overlay (one qemu-img probes as raw or empty) answers a named 503 instead of being truncated. The home move classifies grow-versus-shrink by the volume file, so a volume imported above its row's size reconciles through the same request.

The row follows each side as it moves: msks ls --json and msks storage report the new ceiling immediately, and the bytes move at once on the host. A workspace whose artifact file is absent simply records the new size, and the next start's artifact heal builds the blank artifact at it. A request giving sizes the files already have answers an idempotent 200 that moves nothing. A completed resize is announced on the events channel (workspace.resized, with the new sizes and topology).

items.title: Capacity reporting
items.text:
msks storage answers the operator's three capacity questions, each from its own source of truth:

$ msks storage
state disk    used 23.4G of 40G    free 16.6G    pressure ok

┃ workspace ┃ root cost/ceiling ┃ home cost/ceiling ┃ cost ┃

  • The budget line is the daemon's own statvfs on the state disk: the number that predicts what a full state disk causes (guest-side I/O errors on every workspace). pressure gives the condition: warn past MSKSD_STORAGE_WARN_PCT (default 90) percent used, critical at or below MSKSD_STORAGE_FLOOR_MIB (default 512) free, ok otherwise.
  • Cost is the disk blocks an artifact occupies: the sparse files' real footprint, never their nominal size. An overlay's cost sits a little above the root filesystem usage the guest's own df reports (qcow2 bookkeeping rides along) and stays below its ceiling until the guest fills it.
  • Ceiling is the size fixed at create (root_mib / home_mib): the quota the guest's df shows its user.
  • Imported is when the archive came in, local time to the minute. Rebuilding an image and importing it again adds a second entry under the same reference; the time tells the entries apart, and the short hash msks image ls shows identifies the one msks image rm removes. Re-importing the same archive refreshes the time.

The fullness a workspace user feels is their own df inside the workspace; the daemon never guesses at it from outside a running VM (the ext4 journal lags the host's view of it).

The watcher probes the state disk every MSKSD_EVENT_POLL_S and publishes a storage.pressure event on each change (a steady condition announces once, with the daemon's first known pressure announced as a baseline), with a named log line at warn and critical. Below the floor, workspace creates, image imports, and home-volume imports answer 507 giving the floor and the reclaim path. msks storage gives the consumers; msks rm and msks image rm remove them. Lowering MSKSD_STORAGE_FLOOR_MIB admits writes at less headroom, if that is the deployment's choice. Raising the floor refuses more writes, not fewer.

Imports are sized when the size is knowable. An image import must fit the floor plus twice the archive's bytes: the retained copy plus its unpacked cache. A home-volume import must fit the floor plus the upload's Content-Length when the client sent one. A chunked upload carries no length and gets the floor alone. Existing workspaces keep running below the floor; their own writes can still fill the disk, so a warn line is the cue to reclaim before they do.

GET /api/v1/storage serves the same document the CLI renders, and msks storage <id> narrows the workspace table to one workspace.

items.title: Factory reset
items.text:
POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/reset deletes only the overlay. The next start boots the pristine base image again (installed packages and every other root change are gone) while /home keeps its data. The VM is stopped first (the overlay is the running root device); a wedged VM is killed, exactly as delete does.

Because the overlay is the root filesystem, reset also clears any provisioned state the guest keeps there (cloud-init's run-once markers live under /var/lib/cloud), so future provisioning re-runs on the next boot.

items.title: Home volume export and import
items.text:
The home volume travels through the daemon's authenticated listener as byte streams: the interim mechanism for backup, migration to another daemon, and seeding a fresh workspace with data:

GET /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/home    → the volume file's bytes, streamed
PUT /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/home    → replaces the volume from the body

msks home export / msks home import drive both endpoints from the CLI (docs/cli.md); a token holder may also call them with any HTTP client.

The body is the volume file's bytes verbatim: an ext4 image, labeled msks-home when msksd made it. An import installs what it receives: a hand-made ext4 image (or one exported from another workspace) lands exactly as uploaded. The ext-family magic sits ~1 KiB into the image, and the daemon checks it as the body's first bytes arrive; a wrong file is refused with 400 at kilobyte cost, and the workspace's existing volume is untouched. The check cannot judge completeness: the daemon installs the bytes that arrive, so verify a hand-made image (e2fsck -n) before importing it. A transfer that dies mid-body is the disconnect case and installs nothing.

Sparseness survives the round trip: the import writes in 1 MiB windows and turns every all-zero window back into a sparse hole, so a blank 2 GiB volume re-imports at its data's cost, not its nominal size. A volume exported over a slow link composes with any compressor (msks home export ws - | gzip > ws.ext4.gz) because - streams the bytes to stdout.

Both endpoints answer 409 unless the workspace's row says its VM is down. created, stopped, and absent move freely. starting, running, and paused keep the volume: an export under a guest mid-write is a torn image, and an import into a mounted device would be overwritten or lost. unknown refuses too. The seam reports it when a live VMM stopped answering its API, so a possibly-live VM gets the volume's protection. Stop the workspace first (msks stop). Under the move's lock the daemon also asks the seam itself: a row can lag a boot by one watcher poll interval, and the live VMM's answer refuses where the row would pass.

A move, a boot, and a delete serialize per workspace on one lock. A boot that arrives during a move waits for it to finish and boots the volume the move left. A move that arrives after a boot sees the running row and answers 409. A delete orders against an import instead of racing it. A waiter gives up after MSKSD_MOVE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S (120 s default) and answers a named 409 (a volume move is in flight) rather than hanging; a stalled export reader holds its lock as long as its connection lives. A foreign host answers the placement 409 every artifact route shares.

An import whose filesystem size differs from the workspace's recorded home_mib mounts fine either way: an ext4 filesystem smaller than its device is legal. home_mib stays the size a blank rebuilt volume gets, and growing an imported filesystem is a guest-side resize2fs. The install is atomic: a failed or cut-off upload leaves the existing volume in place. Every completed move is announced on the events channel as home.exported / home.imported, with the byte count. An export announces when its stream reaches the end, so a cancelled download publishes nothing.

items.title: Placement and single-attach
items.text: The workspace row records the host that owns its artifacts. On the local backend that is always the msksd host that created the workspace. A start, stop, reset, or delete through a daemon on another host fails with 409 giving where the artifacts live. Booting a workspace with an empty /home, marking a running VM stopped, or dropping the row out from under a live VM are all worse than the refusal. The host name is the daemon's MSKSD_HOST_NAME (default: the host's hostname at daemon start); pin it explicitly when the hostname is not stable (laptops, containers) so a rename does not strand every workspace. Deleting a workspace whose artifacts live elsewhere happens from that host: this one refuses rather than orphan the files. A workspace runs on at most one host at a time; the row's placement is the authority locally, and the volume's single-writer semantics make a double attach impossible.

items.title: Image pinning
items.text: A catalog image with live workspaces cannot be removed (DELETE /api/v1/images/{hash} answers 409 giving the workspace): each workspace's overlay backs that exact image file, and its kernel and initrd are read from the image's cache on every boot. Deleting the workspace releases the pin.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text: Variable Default Meaning MSKSD_ROOT_MIB 10240 Default overlay (root) size for new workspaces, MiB. MSKSD_HOME_MIB 20480 Default /home volume size, MiB. MSKSD_STORAGE_WARN_PCT 90 State-disk percentage used that moves pressure to warn. MSKSD_STORAGE_FLOOR_MIB 512 Free state-disk MiB below which pressure is critical and writes answer 507. MSKSD_QEMU_IMG qemu-img The qemu-img binary that creates overlays. MSKSD_MKFS_EXT4 mkfs.ext4 The mkfs that formats /home volumes. MSKSD_RESIZE2FS resize2fs The resize2fs that moves /home volumes. MSKSD_E2FSCK e2fsck The e2fsck that quiets a volume before a resize. MSKSD_MKISOFS mkisofs The mkisofs (genisoimage) that builds cidata seed disks. MSKSD_HOST_NAME the hostname The host recorded as owning locally-created artifacts. MSKSD_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_S 20 How long stop waits for the guest's clean poweroff before the fallback kill; a stop answers within this bound. MSKSD_MOVE_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S 120 How long a boot, delete, or volume move waits for the workspace's other volume move before answering a named 409.

items.title: The TUI
items.text:
The terminal UI and the command-line client are one program named msks.

The TUI uses the same REST API as the CLI commands, with the same environment variables, config file, and daemon aliases. It reads no daemon state directly. Every page uses the API.

A bare msks (no arguments at all) launches the TUI. The default page is a full-screen workspace tree. msks tui is the same command, and msks tui my-workspace opens that workspace's page directly.

items.title: The workspace tree
items.text:
The tree is rooted at the workspaces list: one row per workspace, newest first. The CREATED column's arrow shows the sort direction. The list's keys: c creates a workspace, s starts it, S stops it, D removes it (after a confirmation), e opens the secrets page, and r refreshes. / jumps to the first workspace whose name starts with what you type. Enter opens the workspace's page.

The list re-reads the daemon every five seconds. A workspace changed from another surface (the CLI, another operator) appears without a keypress.

items.title: Workspace creation
items.text:
When you create a workspace, it looks like this:

The only required field is name. You may need to import an image before you can successfully create a workspace. There are Debian, Fedora, and NixOS images available for import. You can also build your own.

You can change vcpus, memory, root, and home values after a workspace is created. The rest are fixed for the lifetime of the workspace.

items.title: The secrets page
items.text:
You can register secret placeholders to use in workspaces instead of putting actual secrets into VMs.

The secrets page lists every placeholder the daemon holds, in columns: coverage (* for the daemon-wide row, otherwise its workspace ids), name, destinations, remaining lifetime, and created date.

The lifetime cell is a live countdown (2h, then 1h), repainted every second. An unbounded row reads never. x revokes the focused row after a confirmation that explains what a revoke does: the row retires everywhere at once. r opens the duration picker with TTL-appropriate choices, an hour to thirty days. The choice nearest the row's remaining lifetime is highlighted. Picking one extends the row in place.

c opens the mint form. The name field comes first, then repeatable destinations: an exact host or a label-anchored suffix, comma-separated in one field. Coverage follows: the daemon-wide row, or a multi-select fed by the tree's workspace list.

The lifetime field offers unbounded by default, with an hour to thirty days beside it. Submit checks the secret store first for dupes, then mints.

A successful mint replaces the form with the sentinel's panel. The sentinel opens masked: the prefix shows its reach (mskssec1_ is scoped to the chosen workspaces, mskssec2_ goes to every accepting workspace), and the body renders as bullets. s shows and hides it again. c copies the sentinel to the terminal's clipboard over OSC 52. A terminal that honors the sequence answers the copy (over ssh included, with no reveal needed).

The display ends with the panel: closing it clears its text, and the minted row stays in the page's list. Enter (or a click) on a listing row opens the panel again. The page fetches the row's sentinel from the daemon and shows it with the same show and copy actions. The sentinel therefore reads back on demand, both at mint time and after.

items.title: The workspace page
items.text:
The workspace page operates on an already-created workspace. Its two-line header: the workspace's name on the first line with its status beside it, in the state's color, then the id, image, host, and created date on the second.

Below the header, two status lines share one shape: a muted label, then the value. The consent line shows the mode and one granted scope with its expiry. Two or more grants show as a count with the nearest expiry (5 grants · next expires 4h). Grant details are listed on the workspace's egress consent screen.

When the workspace mounts host shares, a mounts line follows the same shape. It carries one entry per mount (projects:/mnt/projects:rw), a skipped mount's kind beside its spec (refs:/srv/refs:ro · skipped), and an applies at next start note while a change is pending.

The page's fixed actions sit in three groups — use, configure, and power. The configure group holds the egress consent screen, the sizes-and-topology edit dialog, the mounts editor, and Clone: the full-fork copy of the cloning chapter, taken with a name prompt. The daemon owns the stopped-source rule — a refusal names itself on the page's consent line.

items.title: The mounts page
items.text:
The mounts editor shows the workspace's mounts one row each, in the CLI's HOST_PATH:GUEST_PATH:MODE grammar with the mode always shown. a adds a row (a single-line input), Enter edits the focused row (seeded with its current spec), r removes it, and Escape closes the editor with the last saved set.

Every change posts the whole list to the daemon's mounts route. The reply repaints each row with its derived state (healthy, or the skip's kind and reason). A refusal appears on the editor's note line, and the refused list is rolled back.

The daemon owns the rules: a host path outside the allowed roots, or one under a root the daemon's VM does not mount, is refused with the remedy stated. The mounts chapter and the configuration rows describe the behavior. The CLI's msks mount uses the same route.

items.title: The images page
items.text:
i: the images page — a full page with its key bindings on the footer row. The catalog group comes first, with the default marker, each row's hash prefix, and each import's date. Then the published channel's rows follow, with their descriptions, sizes, hash prefixes, and membership markers.

The published group lists only the rows this daemon's machine can boot: a row that declares another architecture stays off the page. A row that declares none is shown (msks image import follows the same rule). [imported] marks a row whose archive the catalog holds by exact hash match; [local] marks a row the catalog holds under a different hash.

Enter imports a published row through the daemon's URL import or opens a catalog row's detail.

D deletes a catalog row after a confirmation, the same DELETE msks image rm makes. d designates the highlighted catalog row the default image, the same POST msks image default makes; the row that already holds the designation flashes so. Both groups show the build's hash prefix beside the ref, so a published row matches its catalog row by eye — the same prefix msks image ls prints. The page re-reads the workspace each second, so the dimming follows a start or stop made anywhere, not only on the page.

items.title: The egress consent page
items.text:
The page's Egress action and its e key open the egress consent page: a full-screen view that holds the held-request queue and the in-effect verdicts together. It is the consent decider as a page inside the tree, and the only place verdicts are made.

The page carries the same two-line header as the workspace page beneath it: the workspace's name with its status (and the pending-hold count while any hold waits), then the id, image hash, host, and created date, muted. The workspace's identity stays visible while verdicts are made.

Keys on the page: the arrows navigate the held requests and cross into the verdict rows beneath (and back). a/d allow or deny the focused hold for the default duration (tilrestart); A/D pick a duration first (once / 5m / 15m / tilrestart / forever). The letters act on the holds alone: a press aimed at the wrong zone reports which zone it would act on, instead of deciding silently. x revokes the focused verdict. The row leaves on the daemon's refreshed frame, never optimistically.

m opens the mode picker (allow / static / interactive, the current mode highlighted). Picking a mode switches it through the same endpoint msks egress mode uses, without leaving the page. The status line shows the new mode once the switch takes effect. Picking static while nothing is effectively allowed asks the same offline-workspace confirmation the CLI asks: confirm to switch, decline to change nothing. A refused switch states its reason on the status line.

Enter on a focused hold opens the duration picker: the key answers, the pick decides, and only an explicit letter or a picked duration ever decides. While no hold waits, the verdict keys do nothing and leave the footer until one arrives. See msks egress for what verdicts and rules cover.

items.title: The edit page
items.text:
The page's Edit settings action opens the edit dialog: the create form's layout, seeded with the workspace's current values.

The sizes and topology (root, home, vcpus, memory) are editable. Submit sends the changed values to the same endpoint msks resize uses, and the page's consent line shows the same outcome the CLI prints, including changes that wait for the next boot.

A workspace that is running when you press Apply asks first: confirm and the page stops the workspace, then applies the resize. Decline, and the workspace keeps running with its sizes unchanged. Home size changes apply immediately. Root growth and the new topology apply at the next boot.

A resize the daemon still refuses (a root shrink, among others) states its reason on the consent line. The name, image, and user fields show their current values read-only, marked * as create-time: changing them is a delete-and-recreate, and the dialog refuses a changed value with a note pointing at the field, instead of accepting it silently. A size left blank keeps its current value. Escape closes the dialog and changes nothing.

items.title: Opening a shell
items.text:
By default, the page's Open a shell action runs msks ssh in the TUI's own terminal: the tree exits, the ssh session runs where it stood, and the tree restarts when the session returns the terminal. Configure msks to open shells in new windows using terminal_open_cmd, documented below.

A workspace that ssh cannot reach (no NIC, no identity configured) takes a longer path. The flow boots a stopped workspace first and probes the forward. A probe that reports a refusal opens no session: the tree's first flash leads with a suggestion to use msks console as a fallback and follows with the refusal's first line. The row ellipsizes at its end, so the suggestion stays visible. The full refusal text is logged before the tree restarts.

A host that wants shells in windows beside the running tree configures a terminal launcher (terminal_open_cmd below). The action then spawns the launcher with a msks ssh invocation appended. The spawned shell inherits the tree's resolved connection, so it reaches the same daemon. A launcher that cannot start (a missing binary, one without the execute bit) reports the reason on the tree's first flash, exits to the workspace page.

Every screen is navigable with arrow keys. Lists move with up/down, the create form's fields move with up/down between them, and Escape leaves the screen it is on. q backs out of a page. At the workspaces list, Escape quits the tree. Ctrl+Q exits the client from any screen (the tree, a page, a form field, or a panel stacked over them), the same clean exit q takes at the workspaces list.

items.title: The shell action's terminal settings
items.text: The workspace page's Open a shell action runs msks ssh: in the TUI's own terminal by default, or in a new window through a configured launcher. Two client settings shape those windows. Their environment-variable rows are in the client environment table. Their file keys are documented here.

items.title: terminal_open_cmd
items.text:
terminal_open_cmd is the launcher the workspace page's Open a shell action uses to open workspace shells in new terminal windows. It is the opt-in for hosts that want windows beside the running tree isntead of within. The msks invocation is appended after it, the way most terminals take a command after -e / --:

terminal_open_cmd: konsole --hold -e   # string form (shell-split)
terminal_open_cmd:                     # Linux (list form, no shell quoting)
  - ghostty
  - +wait
  - -e
terminal_open_cmd:                     # macOS (open launches Ghostty.app)
  - open
  - -na
  - Ghostty.app
  - --args
  - -e

Any terminal is supported, but let's explain the options to the Ghostty terminal examples anove. On Linux, Ghostty's -e takes the appended invocation as the window's command, and +wait holds the ghostty process until the window closes — the same hold konsole -e gives. On macOS the ghostty CLI is a helper tool; open -n starts a new Ghostty.app instance and --args hands it the -e. A window opened through open runs with a fresh login environment: nothing from the shell the TUI runs in passes through. The appended client therefore locates its packages and its daemon on its own.

terminal_open_cmd's environment form (MSKSC_TERMINAL_OPEN_CMD) overrides the file value with the string form. Unset (the default), the shell action runs msks ssh in the TUI's own terminal, on every host, with no terminal to launch. A configured launcher that fails to execute (a binary that is missing or not executable) reports the reason on the tree's first flash after the same-terminal shell ends. The shell runs in the same terminal.

items.title: terminal_title
items.text:
terminal_title sets the title of every terminal window the workspace page's shell action opens through a configured launcher. {workspace} resolves to the workspace's id (the token msks ssh addresses; that is what the TUI appends to the launcher), or to shell when the appended command addresses no workspace:

terminal_title: msks — {workspace}

A launcher that runs msks-term-popup writes the title before it attaches tmux, and the launch's own tmux server pins set-titles off. The title stays for the window's lifetime: a workspace shell inside the window cannot rewrite it. Every other launcher gets the title from the appended msks ssh itself: the window msks opens is marked at spawn, and the command sets it before the session starts. A workspace that sets its own title from inside the session (a PROMPT_COMMAND with a title escape, the way stock ssh sessions can) rewrites it there. tmux shields the popup path. Nothing shields the plain path.

terminal_title's environment form (MSKSC_TERMINAL_TITLE) overrides the file value. The default is unset: the terminal emulator's own title stays in place (the command it runs, or whatever its -T / --title flag sets). A msks ssh you type yourself keeps your terminal's title: the setting applies only to the windows msks opens, and a same-terminal shell (the dead-launcher fallback) changes nothing.

items.title: msks-term-popup: the consent-decider terminal
items.text:
msks-term-popup is a shipped client command that runs the appended shell inside a local tmux session and answers the workspace's egress consent prompts right there.

To use, it change your msks.yaml config file such that it's the program opened by terminal_open_cmd. For example:

terminal_open_cmd: konsole -e msks-term-popup
terminal_open_cmd: xterm -e msks-term-popup
terminal_open_cmd: ghostty +wait -e msks-term-popup       # Linux
terminal_open_cmd: open -na Ghostty.app --args -e msks-term-popup  # macOS

The launch also starts the consent-decider app in a hidden tmux session on the same socket, where it holds the workspace's decider registration for the window's whole life.

The app lists every hold the workspace carries, destination and time remaining per row, with the arrow keys moving the selection. a allows until restart and d denies the selected hold. The uppercase twins A and D pick a duration for their verdict (Enter picks, Escape cancels). m switches the workspace's egress mode. The picker offers allow, static, and interactive with the current mode highlighted (Enter picks, Escape or q cancels).

Picking static while nothing is effectively allowed asks the empty-static question first, the same confirmation the consent page asks. The switch goes through the same endpoint msks egress mode uses. The status line shows the current mode beside the connection state, and a completed switch flashes its effect there (in effect now, or takes effect at next start for a stopped workspace). A switch the daemon refuses states its reason on the same line. A hold leaves the list the moment the daemon resolves it (a verdict from another decider window, or the hold's own timeout). The popup viewer hides itself when the list empties.

A hold arriving with the popup closed raises a popup viewer over the shell that attaches to the hidden session. The bindings map runs along the popup's bottom edge: the verdict keys, the mode switch, and the hide/show entry. q, Esc, or C-b hide the viewer. The decider keeps running, its queue keeps living, and C-b p brings the popup back. A popup the app raised returns the same way on the next hold. The session ends with its window, and the decider registration ends with the server. It works with any terminal that runs a command: put your terminal and its command flag in terminal_open_cmd, and msks-term-popup right after it (tmux 3.2 or newer must be on PATH):

On macOS, an open-opened window resolves commands on a fresh login PATH, and msks-setup-macos-host links both client commands there. tmux comes from that PATH the same way. The Linux forms need the same: the window resolves msks-term-popup on its own PATH, and msks-setup-debian-host and msks-setup-fedora-host link it beside msks at /usr/local/bin.

The popup viewer keeps its own attach to the hidden session. A hold that arrives while it is open is already in the list. Verdicts posted from it go through the same REST contract as the consent page. A post that cannot complete (the request resolved in another decider window while the verdict was in flight) reports the reason on the popup's status line.

The session's status bar shows the workspace: the launch resolves the workspace's name and pins it to the bar's left side ([project-x]). The id stands in whenever the lookup fails (the daemon down, the workspace gone, the wait run out), and shell stands for a plain shell. The window list after the label stays empty.

The bar's right side carries the egress mode beside the popup key (#764), as interactive · C-b p popup. The key hint lands at launch. The decider app fills the mode in front of it when its first rules frame lands, and updates it on every change whatever surface decided it. Every workspace carries a mode. A workspace created without egress reads allow. A window with no workspace (a plain shell) ships neither half: no decider stands behind it, and C-b p stays stock tmux's own key.

The hidden consent session runs on the launch's own socket, one small server per window. The app retires when the window has been gone for a while, taking the session and the server with it. The window's own hold flags (konsole --hold, xterm's -hold) keep the window open after the session ends, as they do for a plain shell window.

The tmux pane keeps 10000 lines of scrollback and takes the mouse wheel. Wheel up scrolls into the pane's history, and wheel down scrolls back toward the live output. Reaching the bottom (or pressing q) returns to the plain shell. The keyboard path covers the same history: Ctrl-b [ (or Ctrl-b PageUp) opens tmux's copy mode, where the arrow keys and PageUp/PageDown move through it. Shift-PageUp and Shift-PageDown page through it too, one page per press, entering copy mode on the way up and returning to the shell at the bottom.

A plain drag selects text in tmux's buffer, and holding Shift while dragging selects the terminal's native text (most terminals hand Shift drags to their own selection). A consent popup raised while the pane is scrolled still takes its verdict keys: the popup overlays the scrolled pane, and the next keypress answers it.
